Only guides, topics, and your docs section go in the `docs` root. The others have their own guides: {@link namespace:components}, {@link namespace:templates}, and {@link namespace:themes}.

sections.title: Keep topics in the docs root

content.text: The `docs` field in `astryx.integration.mjs` names the folder that holds your topics. The CLI reads every `.doc.mjs` file under it, in subfolders too.

content.label: astryx.integration.mjs

items: Readers open a topic by its `name`, not its file name. Name the file after the doc, `<name>.doc.mjs`, so each one is easy to find.
A topic with no `placement` is a flat topic: the docs list shows it under Topics, and readers open it by its name.
For a section of your own in the docs tree, see {@link generic:sections-and-placement}.

content.text: In global mode: when users install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI, your doc topics show up in folders outside any project; inside a project, only if the project installs your package. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: agent-guidance
docs.title: Agent guidance
docs.description: Add a few lines of guidance that apps put in front of the AI agents working in their code.

content.text: `integration add agent-doc` adds one line for AI agents that work in apps using your package. Apps show it in their agent file, such as `AGENTS.md`.

content.code: {@command integration add agent-doc 'Use AcmeCarousel for rotating content.'}

content.text: The line lands in `agentDocs.append` in your manifest:
Adding the same line again changes nothing. To reword or remove a line, edit `agentDocs.append` by hand.
Every line costs space in each app's agent file, so the CLI keeps guidance short and few. Put detail in your docs instead.

rows: `integration add` fails: `append may contain at most 8 lines`.
`integration add` fails: `must contain at most 240 Unicode code points`.
32 lines per app, from all its packages
`init` writes no agent block and prints `Could not install agent docs.`

content.text: A line is one line of plain text. Line breaks, control characters, spaces at either end, and managed-block markers such as `<!-- ASTRYX:START -->` are rejected.

Start a command in a line with the word astryx alone, with no runner in front, as in: Run astryx doctor before finishing. The block names the command the app runs once, at its top, for every command below it, so your line works in every app. See {@link generic:cli-command}.
An app's `{@command init}` writes your lines at the end of its managed agent block, each labeled with your package name. The CLI owns the heading, the labels, and the markers.

content.code: {@command init --features agents}

INTEGRATIONS:
- `@acme/astryx-widgets`: Use AcmeCarousel for rotating content.
<!-- ASTRYX:END -->

content.text: The block collects lines from every integration the app has installed, with or without an `astryx.config` entry.

sections.title: Refresh the block in an app

content.text: The block changes only when the app runs `init`, or `upgrade --from <version> --apply`. After an app installs a version of your package with new lines, it runs one of them.

content.code: [ok] Agent docs refreshed -> AGENTS.md

content.text: `upgrade --apply` prints that line; `init` prints `[ok] AI agent docs installed -> AGENTS.md`. Without `--apply`, `upgrade` only reports `Agent docs differ from the installed Astryx and integration configuration.` It refreshes the block even when Core did not change. See {@link command:upgrade}.

In global mode: the agent guide the CLI keeps for the computer carries no integration's guidance, because it serves every folder; your guidance reaches agents through the agent docs `init` writes in an app that installs your package. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:computer-agent-guide}.

docs.name: api
docs.title: API
docs.summary: The programmatic API: functions, the JSON output envelope, error codes, and response types.

blocks.text: To run the whole CLI from your own command-line tool, with its arguments, folder, and command name, use the host entry: {@link generic:host-entry}.

docs.name: author-a-theme
docs.title: Author a theme
docs.description: Create, customize, and build a theme: defineTheme, palette generation, token overrides, component style overrides, custom variants, responsive adaptations, and production builds.

content.text: Use an installed built theme as the base for ordinary customization. Import it into your source and pass it as `extends` to `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`. Build the result, then add the local slug. Only eject when you need to own and maintain a full source fork.

content.label: Add to use, eject to fork

content.text: For an annotated map of the whole surface (every defineTheme field, the token families, and the component override syntax, each with the CLI command that prints its reference), run `{@command theme template}`. It writes `theme.template.ts` into your project to read and copy from (`{@command init --features theme}` writes it as part of project setup).

To apply a theme you created, see {@link generic:use-a-theme}. To generate colors from seed values, see the Palette section below. Before you eject a package theme instead, see when that fits in {@link generic:use-a-theme}.
Name a few seed colors and generate every shade a theme needs, light and dark; {@link generic:generate-a-palette} explains what a palette holds.

content.label: Minimal palette config (palette.config.json)
content.code: {"families": [{"id": "ocean", "seed": "#0074e2"}]}

content.label: Generate and preview
content.code:
# Print the palette without writing files
{@command theme palette generate palette.config.json}

# Write palette + receipt, and open a visual preview
{@command theme palette generate palette.config.json} \
  --out src/themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.ts \
  --preview preview.html

content.text: The command writes a `.ts` file exporting 21 shades (stops 0–100) for both light and dark, plus a `.receipt.json` to regenerate later. Point your theme's tokens at the palette, then run defineTheme (see below).

For the full palette config fields and CLI flags, run `{@command docs cli/commands/theme-palette-generate}`. For the integration-authoring walkthrough of connecting a palette to theme tokens, run `{@command docs authoring/building-blocks/themes/generate-a-palette}`.

defineTheme creates a theme from explicit token overrides and optional scale configs. Existing themes may use `color` to expand an accent seed into neutral, surface, text, border, and related values; it is not an accent-only edit. Keep that configuration when preserving existing output. For new complete palettes, generate and review a committed palette module, then import its `palette` export and reference stable stops from semantic tokens. This keeps mapped roles coherent when the accepted palette is regenerated; generation itself does not rewrite the theme. Other scale configs generate typography, radius, and motion values from parameters. Explicit token overrides always take precedence over scale-generated values, token by token. When an existing `color` config is in use, overriding `--color-accent` in `tokens` re-points `--color-accent-muted`, `--color-text-accent`, and `--color-icon-accent`, but `--color-on-accent` stays baked from the `color.accent` seed. Prefer a `[light, dark]` tuple for `color.accent` over overriding `--color-accent` alone. localTokens accepts any valid CSS custom-property name; prefixes do not establish ownership.

content.label: defineTheme with generated palette references and non-color scale configs

rows: Supported broad scale: accent? (hex or [light, dark] tuple), neutralStyle? (warm|cool|neutral), contrast? (standard|high). Use theme palette generate for new complete palettes.
Every --duration-* token, --ease-entrance and --ease-move (springs don't read them yet)

tempo? (0.75–1.5), character? (crisp|standard|expressive); and/or a duration scale: fast (ms), medium (ms), ratio, slow?, easing?. The scale wins over tempo for the durations it sets, and explicit tokens win over both. Fixed whatever the knobs say: drags and momentum, rubber band, keyboard, press onset/cancel/flash, hover intent, gesture thresholds, Spinner/Skeleton loops, the 200 ms Reduce Motion cap. See {@link generic:motion}.

content.text: For dark mode tuples in token values, see the Dark mode section of {@link generic:use-a-theme}.

`extends` lets you derive a new theme from an existing one, inheriting its tokens, component overrides, icons, and fonts. Only specify what you want to change; everything else carries over from the base theme.

content.label: Extending the neutral theme

rows: Base tokens are copied first, then child tokens override on top.
Deep-merged: child component rules override matching keys from the base.
Shallow-merged: child icons override matching names from the base.
Replaced, never merged: a child that sets iconVariants replaces the base list; a child that omits it inherits the list.
Shallow-merged: child indicators override matching names from the base.
Deep-merged per surface: the base's resolved surface first, then the child's overrides.

Field by field: the child's `fast`, `medium` and `ratio` regenerate the fast and medium duration tokens; `slow` and `easing` left unset keep the base theme's tokens, so an inherited slow band stays at the base's ratio. Each knob (`tempo`, `character`) the child leaves unset keeps the base's.
Child config replaces base entirely (these are scale inputs, not additive).
Width-breakpoint overrides merge by fixed name. Inherited ordered rules keep their relative order; child rules append and re-resolve against the child root axes.

content.text: Inheritance is resolved when the theme is defined, so an extended theme is flat: `{@command theme build}` emits one self-contained stylesheet holding everything the child inherited, and the base theme's CSS does not need to be loaded next to it. A base that is not a theme (most often an import that missed) throws when `defineTheme` runs, rather than producing a theme that silently inherits nothing.
For the integration-specific guidance on mapping a palette to tokens when extending, see `{@command docs authoring/building-blocks/themes/define-the-theme}`.

The `components` field in defineTheme uses semantic component keys and style keys, not raw CSS selectors. Use `base` for all instances, `variant:value` or `stateName` for specific props/states, and let the theme pipeline choose the underlying selector. For raw external CSS escape hatches, prefer the data-attribute selector surface documented in {@link generic:styling-advanced}.

content.label: Component overrides with standard CSS

content.text: Run `{@command theme targets}` for every themeable key in the system (`{@command theme targets <Name>}` to scope it, `--json` to lint a theme against it), and `{@command component <Name>}` for one component's theming targets, public CSS variables, and which standard CSS properties are supported.

items: Write standard CSS properties (borderRadius, padding); the pipeline expands them into internal vars.
Set public CSS vars directly when no standard property equivalent exists.
Set private CSS vars (prefixed --_) directly. Use standard CSS properties instead. `{@command theme build}` will error.
Set a public CSS var the component does not define. It compiles to CSS that never applies, and the build does not warn. Take the names from `{@command component <Name>}`.

content.text: Themes can add new prop values to any component. Any `prop:value` key where the value isn't a built-in gets treated as a new variant. Use `{@command theme build}` to generate TypeScript augmentations for type safety.

content.label: Adding custom variants
Using custom variants

content.text: Custom variants only work when the theme that defines them is active. The component's variant map is extended via module augmentation, with no changes to the component source needed.

Use `adaptations` for opt-in token, theme-local token, and component changes under viewport width, primary-pointer precision, contrast preference, or motion preference. Conditions in one `when` are ANDed. Rules are ordinary ordered objects, and later matching writes win.

content.label: Width and pointer adaptations

content.text: `widthBreakpoints` are fixed named start points. Defaults are 640 / 768 / 1024 / 1280 / 1536 CSS pixels. `from` includes its point; `below` excludes it. Breakpoint configuration alone emits no CSS.

Precedence follows rule order. Root theme values apply first, then every matching rule in declaration order. A later rule may deliberately restore a root value. `onDark` and `onLight` media-surface overrides apply after adaptations and win on the same leaf.
`extends` preserves the base rule order and appends child rules. Inherited conditions use the child's effective breakpoint map. An empty child rule is a no-op, not a removal operator.

A rule may replace a theme-local token only when the exact name is already enrolled by root `localTokens` or an enrolled base. Component writes in a rule are validated exactly like root `components`: same targets, axes, and value domains. The one addition is that a rule may not be the only place a custom value is enrolled: a value that is valid only because a theme enrolls it generates unconditional type augmentation, so declare it on the root theme first and let rules restyle it. Built-in values need no root declaration. When rules can match together, their ordered portable and local token writes are validated as one effective graph; any reachable cycle fails before CSS is emitted.

Adaptations compile to CSS media queries with no resize listener or styling rerender. Runtime and `{@command theme build}` use the same compiler, but only a built theme is present at first paint in an SSR app.
`{@command theme build}` compiles a defineTheme file into production-ready artifacts. Recommended for SSR apps (Next.js, Remix) where styles must be present on first paint.

content.label: Build a theme
content.code: {@command theme build ./src/themes/ocean.ts}

rows: Pre-compiled CSS with token overrides, component overrides, and prose element styles in @scope rules
ES module exporting the theme object with `__built: true` and pre-resolved token values.
TypeScript declarations for the theme and icon registry exports
(Optional) Module augmentations for custom component prop values

content.text: The `__built: true` flag tells Theme to skip runtime `<style>` injection; the CSS file handles it. Load the generated CSS wherever you load the module.

content.label: Using a custom built theme

content.text: After upgrading Astryx, rerun `{@command theme build}` for every custom prebuilt theme. Deploy the regenerated files together. The runtime intentionally trusts `__built: true` and will not repair stale CSS from an older build. The build also warns when the theme names font families it does not load. See {@link generic:font-setup} for the full recipe.
For the runtime vs built tradeoff, see the Runtime vs Built section of {@link generic:use-a-theme}.

sections.title: Built themes with an icon registry

content.text: `theme build` emits an icon import when it detects a named import used by the theme's `icons:` field. It does not compile that registry module. Move the registry to a separate module and use a named import.

content.label: Compiling the icon registry sidecar
content.code:
# Emit the built theme
{@command theme build ./src/themes/ocean.ts -o dist/theme.css --icons-specifier ./icons.mjs}

# Compile the icon registry alongside it
esbuild src/themes/icons.tsx --bundle --format=esm --outfile=dist/icons.mjs \
  --external:react --external:lucide-react --jsx=automatic

content.text: In the example above, the generated theme imports `./icons.mjs` from `dist`. If the second command is skipped, `theme build` can still succeed, but loading or bundling the generated module fails because `dist/icons.mjs` is missing. `--icons-specifier` changes the emitted import; it does not create or verify the target file. Match the specifier to a module that resolves from the generated JS file.

Without `--icons-specifier`, the detected source import specifier is emitted unchanged. In the default flow without `--out`, a bundler can resolve an extensionless `./icons` to the neighboring `icons.tsx` source, but Node ESM does not perform that lookup and reports `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. Moving the output with `--out` also changes where relative imports resolve from.
Keep `react` and the icon library external so the registry does not bundle its own copies of those dependencies.

A registry entry can be a function of `{size, variant}`. The built theme keeps the function, so `Icon` asks it for the size and variant it renders, as the runtime theme does, including for entries inherited from a built or package theme. The built theme's `icons` field and the registry its module re-exports are React nodes, with each function read at size `md`. A function written in the theme file itself cannot be carried, so the build fails; move it into the registry module.

A theme that lists `iconVariants` also writes an `IconVariantMap` augmentation into `<theme>.variants.d.ts`, so `Icon`'s `variant` accepts those names wherever the theme's types load. Its declaration carries the list too, so a theme that extends the built theme types `variant` in its icon entries by that list.

Use family mode when an app switches among one base theme and its selected descendants. The build writes one keyed CSS file containing every member, plus one keyed JavaScript module and one declaration file, beside the root source.

content.label: Build one family
content.code:
{@command theme build} --family \
  ./src/themes/ocean.mjs \
  ./src/themes/ocean-calm.mjs \
  ./src/themes/ocean-calm-deep.mjs \
  --family-key ocean-family

content.text: The family stylesheet eagerly downloads every selected member so first paint is complete. Switching members changes only the theme identity; it does not add, remove, or reorder stylesheets.

Use `tokenVar()` when a non-StyleX styling library wants a CSS variable reference, and `resolveThemeTokens()` when JavaScript needs token values for a specific theme and mode without React context. Themes are registered by name when created with `defineTheme()`; call `registerTheme(theme)` for prebuilt or object-literal themes that need name-based SSR lookup.

content.label: CSS var references for styling-library configs
Resolve token values without a hook

content.text: The `@astryxdesign/core/theme/tokens` subpath is server-safe and does not require React. The main `@astryxdesign/core/theme` barrel also re-exports these helpers for client code that already imports theme APIs.
For styling library interop patterns, see {@link namespace:styling-libraries}.

`useTheme()` reads the nearest Theme and effective color mode from React context. Prefer `dataVars` for CSS-capable SVG and DOM values. Use this hook for canvas, charts, maps, third-party configuration objects, or an SVG API that requires a concrete JavaScript color instead of a `var(...)` reference.

content.label: Access resolved token values in React

content.text: Prefer CSS variables for ordinary styling. See {@link generic:use-a-theme} for the provider setup, and {@link namespace:tokens} for the full token reference.

docs.name: authoring
docs.title: Authoring
docs.summary: Build an npm package that adds components, templates, themes, docs, and codemods to Astryx apps, and look up every field of every file it holds.

blocks.text: In global mode: users can install your integration for their computer, beside the global CLI. It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs it. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

An integration is a way to share things with Astryx users: a package you own and maintain, built on a framework Astryx gives you. Publish one, many, or any mix, and people install it in one step. It works with the Astryx CLI alongside Core. See each kind under {@link namespace:building-blocks}.
For example, ship a carousel as an integration. Any app that installs it can find it with `{@command search carousel}`, and the CLI uses it like any Astryx Core component.
An integration can also replace a built-in template or doc. To start, install `@astryxdesign/cli` and open {@link generic:quick-start}.
Every field of every file you write for an integration is in {@link generic:field-reference}.

Every integration runs `{@command integration check --strict}` in its own build: it is required, not optional, so a doc, prop, or link that stops matching the code fails your build instead of your users' apps. See {@link generic:checks}.

docs.name: block-template
docs.title: Block template
docs.description: Describe a smaller composition, choose its preview shape, and connect it to component examples only when that relationship is real.

content.text: Most blocks stand alone. Start with this shape unless the block is specifically the example or showcase for one component.

content.label: templates/acme-stat-card.doc.mjs

content.text: Do not add `exampleFor` only because the block uses a component. `componentsUsed` records composition; `exampleFor` declares that one component owns the example.
Every field is in {@link schema:template-doc}.
Keep one clear primary owner. Use the `also*` fields only for intentional secondary placements.

content.label: templates/acme-status-card-showcase.doc.mjs
content.code:
/** @type {import('@astryxdesign/cli/authoring').IntegrationTemplateDoc} */
export default {
  type: 'block',
  name: 'acme-status-card-showcase',
  displayName: 'Acme Status Card Showcase',
  description:
    'An account-health summary that demonstrates status, trend, and action states for AcmeStatusCard.',
  isReady: true,
  exampleFor: 'AcmeStatusCard',
  isShowcase: true,
  alsoExampleFor: ['AcmeDashboard'],
  aspectRatio: 4 / 3,
  componentsUsed: ['AcmeStatusCard', 'Button', 'HStack', 'VStack'],
};

content.text: Then check the package-scoped template list ({@link generic:template-doc-overview}) and confirm the entry carries the relationship you set. `{@command component}` does not show integration blocks, so the list is where to check.
Every field is in {@link schema:template-doc}.

Set `aspectRatio` from the value for the closest shape below, render the block at that ratio, and adjust it until it neither clips nor leaves large empty space. These are starting points, not contract defaults.

rows: Wide navigation, banner, toolbar, or tabs
Square button, badge, avatar, icon, spinner, or status
Tall navigation, calendar, list, or tree
Content card, dialog, table, or form group

content.text: `scale` affects only Astryx's own block previews. Integration blocks can leave it out.

docs.name: browser-support
docs.title: Browser support
docs.description: What browsers Astryx targets, which modern platform features it depends on, and how to support older browsers for your own audience.

content.text: Astryx is built on modern web platform features: the [`Popover`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API) API, CSS anchor positioning, and CSS `light-dark()`. These let components stay small, accessible, and dependency-free, but they also set a floor on which browsers render everything correctly.

A design system does not own its traffic; the products built on it do. Their audiences range from evergreen-Chrome-only internal tools to public sites with meaningful older-Safari share. So Astryx does not declare a single hard browser floor the way an app would. Instead it defines tiers that describe what works at each level, and hands the final decision to you. Pick the tier that matches your audience.
Astryx officially supports Tier 1 and Tier 2. Tier 3 is best-effort: components will not crash, but positioning and theming may degrade.

rows: Everything works, including CSS anchor positioning. This is the reference target.
Components open, dismiss, and are fully usable. Only anchor positioning is missing, so layered surfaces (tooltips, menus, popovers) may not be positioned next to their trigger.
Best-effort. The only guarantee is "does not crash." `light-dark()` is unavailable, so theme colors may fall back to defaults.

content.text: Only three modern features carry a browser requirement. Everything else Astryx uses (`:has()`, `color-mix()`, container queries, the `<dialog>` element) has been widely available since 2023 or earlier and needs no special handling.

rows: Positions layered surfaces relative to their trigger (tooltips, menus, popovers, dropdowns).
Opens, stacks, and light-dismisses layered surfaces via the top layer.
Compiles every theme color tuple into a single value that responds to color scheme. Underpins the whole theming system.

content.text: The gap that matters is between Tier 1 and Tier 2: the `Popover` API and `light-dark()` reached wide availability well before anchor positioning. So in Tier 2 browsers, layered surfaces open and dismiss correctly; they just are not positioned. This is the one feature most consumers will need to reason about.
Any component that opens a menu, popover, tooltip, or dropdown carries the browser requirement: it renders that surface in an overlay positioned against its trigger. That includes:

items: Tooltip, HoverCard, and Popover, and any prop that shows one (such as the Button `tooltip`)
DropdownMenu, MoreMenu, and ContextMenu
Selector, MultiSelector, ComplexSelector, Typeahead, and PowerSearch (dropdown surfaces)
DateInput, DateRangeInput, and DateTimeInput (calendar popovers)
Tokenizer (suggestion menu)
The overflow and flyout menus in Breadcrumbs, TabList, TopNav, and SideNav
Carousel (anchored controls)

content.text: If your product opens no menus, popovers, tooltips, or dropdowns, it has no anchor-positioning requirement; it needs only `light-dark()` (Tier 2 and up) for correct theme colors. Page layout, typography, forms, buttons, cards, and tables work down to Tier 2 with no special handling.

items: Components never throw on missing platform APIs. Where a browser lacks the `Popover` API, layers fall back to plain visibility instead of crashing.
Tier 1 and Tier 2 are officially supported and tested.
Non-layered components render correctly down to Tier 2.
Astryx does not guarantee correct layer positioning below Tier 1 (anchor positioning). Closing that gap for a Tier 2 audience is a consumer choice; see below.
Astryx does not ship a `light-dark()` fallback, so theme colors are not guaranteed below Tier 2.

content.text: If your audience includes Tier 2 browsers and you need correct layer positioning, you have three options, cheapest first. All of them are decisions you make for your audience; Astryx does not impose one.

items: Polyfill anchor positioning. Load a CSS anchor positioning polyfill conditionally behind an `@supports` check so it costs nothing on Tier 1. This is the lowest-effort way to get correct positioning; polyfills may not cover every position-fallback feature.

Provide a JS positioning fallback. Detect missing support with `CSS.supports("anchor-name", "--x")` and position layers with a measurement-based library (e.g. a floating-element positioner) when it returns false. More code, full control.

Accept degraded positioning. Document for your users that on Tier 2 browsers, layered surfaces open correctly but may not sit next to their trigger. Cheapest, and often fine for internal tools on evergreen browsers.

content.text: Feature-detect at runtime rather than sniffing user agents:

content.label: Feature detection

sections.title: How These Tiers Move Over Time

content.text: The tiers are rolling, not frozen to specific versions. They track the Web Baseline year:

items: Tier 1 tracks the current Baseline year.
Tier 2 tracks Baseline minus two years.
Tier 3 is everything older, and remains best-effort.

content.text: This is not an arbitrary window: Baseline − 2 is close to where anchor positioning stops being available while the `Popover` API and `light-dark()` still are, so the tier boundary tracks a real capability edge, not a guessed date. The version floors above are reviewed and advanced roughly once a year as new Baseline years land. Always feature-detect rather than hardcoding version numbers, so your app adapts automatically as the platform moves.

docs.name: build-the-template
docs.title: Build the template
docs.summary: Make sure your template works when an app copies it: write the template file, set up its styles, fonts, icons, and images, then package and test it.

docs.name: building-blocks
docs.title: Building Blocks
docs.summary: Add components, templates, themes, docs, and codemods, and configure how it behaves.

blocks.text: In global mode: every kind your package adds also applies outside projects when users install it for their computer, beside the global CLI; inside a project, only if the project installs it. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.
These are everything you can add to an integration. Mix them however you like. You are not limited to any one thing.

items: One component, or a whole library of them.
Components together with themes and templates.
Only docs, if that is all you need.
Agent guidance, so the AI agents in an app follow your library.
Codemods that update app code across your breaking changes.

blocks.text: Each kind below is its own guide. Open one to learn, in depth, how to add it and how to keep it healthy as your package grows.

docs.name: check-the-props
docs.title: Check the props table
docs.description: Compare each props table with the component's TypeScript props, then fix the doc or the code.

content.text: `doctor integration components` compares every props table in your component docs, hidden docs and every family entry included, with the props the component's TypeScript declares. Run it in your package after you change a component or its doc.

content.code: {@command doctor integration components}

severity:  [warn]
component: AcmeCarousel
prop:      loop
kind:      not_in_code
message:   "loop" is documented, but AcmeCarousel's props have no "loop".
doc:       components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
source:    components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
docType:   boolean

1 prop(s) differ between the docs and the code in 1 of 1 component(s) compared (TypeScript 6.0.3). These are warnings: update the doc, or the code if the doc is right.

items: A doc's own `props` describe the export its `name` names. In a family doc, each entry describes its own export. A hook entry documents parameters and returns, so it is not compared.

It reads props with the `typescript` your package installs, and reads your package's `tsconfig.json` the way `tsc -p` does. It finds TypeScript the way the docs check does, TypeScript 7 included ({@link generic:check-your-docs}). Without a usable one it prints `[skip] Props not compared` and the reason.
Findings are warnings and leave the exit code at 0. Read them before you publish. With `--json`, they are in `data.propDrift.findings`.

content.text: Each finding's `kind` says what differs. Fix the doc, or the code if the doc is right.

rows: The doc lists a prop the component's props do not have
Remove it from the doc, or add it to the code. A name an index signature takes, such as `data-*`, counts as present
Your package declares a prop the doc does not list, or builds one with a mapped type, such as `Partial<Record<'sm' | 'md', string>>`

Document it. Props from React, the DOM, or another package are never asked for, and neither are props whose keys another package defines (`keyof CSSProperties`, behind an alias or not), `className`, `style`, `xstyle`, `data-testid`, `ref`, `key`, or a prop whose JSDoc has `@internal`. A deprecated prop is still a prop: document it until you remove it. A prop a mapped type builds from keys the check cannot trace (a template literal, say) is listed under `[info] Props not checked for a doc entry` instead

Set `required: true` exactly when every caller must pass the prop. One your `defaultProps` fills counts as optional, as it is to JSX callers, and so does one only some members of a union require, since a caller can leave it out: say in its description which variants need it. An entry that names several props (`value / onChange`) makes the same claim about each: give them separate entries when they differ
The documented `type` differs from the code's, where both read exactly
Copy the type from the source, or fix the code. The next section says which types are judged
The documented `default` differs from the literal default the component writes in its props destructuring, such as `size = 'md'`
Copy the default from the source, quoted as code: `default: "'md'"`. Quotes and spacing are ignored, and a default that is not a literal on either side (a constant, a call, prose) is not compared

sections.title: Write types the check can judge

content.text: For a prop your package declares, the check also compares the documented `type`, but only where both sides read exactly. It never guesses, so a type it cannot judge is listed, not reported. It needs TypeScript 4.8 or later: with an older one it prints `[skip] Prop types not judged` and judges none.

content.code:
severity:  [warn]
component: AcmeCarousel
prop:      interval
kind:      type_mismatch
message:   "interval" is documented as string, but the code declares number.
doc:       components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
source:    components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
docType:   string
codeType:  number

items: Write the type as the source writes it, such as `ReactNode[]` or `(index: number) => void`. Parameter names, member order, quotes and whitespace may differ. Text that writes `readonly` must match exactly, parameter names included; only whitespace may differ. `React.X` names React's own `X` where the prop is declared, so it matches a bare `X` only where that name is React's: `React.KeyboardEvent` is not the DOM's `KeyboardEvent`.

Name a type as the file that declares the prop names it, so an import renamed there (`Item as BaseItem`) is written as that file writes it. A field (`cfg.level`) takes its prop's file, even when the field's own type is declared in another file.

A type written another way is judged only when both sides are built from exact parts: primitives such as `string` and `number`, string, number and boolean literals, string enum members, arrays and unions of these, and type names that stand for them. Union members may come in any order, and a member another covers adds nothing, as TypeScript passes it there: `undefined` beside `void`, or `string[]` beside `(string | number)[]`.
A mutable array type matches a readonly one, because callers can pass it. A readonly one documented for a mutable array is a mismatch.

When a prop's variants give a field different types, as `{value: string} | {value: number}` does, document every variant's type (`string | number`). The types of only some variants are listed: the prop's variants give this field different types. With more than six variant types, any other type is listed too.
To name an alias and show its values, write `AcmeSize = 'sm' | 'md'` or `AcmeSize ('sm' | 'md')`. Both parts must match.
An optional prop's `undefined` is set aside on both sides. With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, the doc shows `undefined` exactly when the code declares it.
Anything else, such as an object, a tuple, a generic with arguments, `keyof`, an intersection, or a mapped or conditional type written another way, is not compared.

content.text: The check prints how many documented types it judged, then lists the rest by reason: not a form the check judges exactly, a field the prop's variants give different types, a standard prop, or a prop declared outside the package. With `--json`, they are in `data.propDrift.typesNotCompared`.

content.code: [info] Documented prop types judged: 2; not compared: 0. A type is judged when the doc writes it the same as the source (exactly, if it contains `readonly`), or when both are primitives, literals, arrays and unions of those, or names for them.

sections.title: When a component is not compared

content.text: When the check cannot read a component's props exactly, it lists the component under `[info] Props not compared`, with the reason, instead of reporting findings that might be wrong.

content.code:
[info] Props not compared for 1 documented component(s):

component: AcmeCarousel
doc:       components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
reason:    AcmeCarousel depends on `@acme/motion` (imported in AcmeCarousel.tsx), which the compiler could not resolve, usually a dependency that is not installed. Install the package's dependencies and run this check again

rows: It depends on a package or file the compiler could not resolve
Install the package's dependencies, then run the check again
It depends on a type the compiler can't work out
Make the types compile with `{@pm exec tsc --noEmit}`, then run the check again
The package's TypeScript config has an error
Fix `tsconfig.json` until `{@pm exec tsc -p .}` reads it
Give the component a props type
Some prop names come from a type parameter
Nothing to fix: a component that renders an element the caller picks takes props known only where it is used
The file has no export named by the doc's `name`
Change `name` or the export so they agree

docs.name: check-your-docs
docs.title: Check your docs
docs.description: Check the docs tree, links, overlaps, doc fields, read size, and CLI peer.

content.text: Run `doctor integration docs` in your package to check the docs tree, every link, and overlaps with Core topics, and to list any passage two topics repeat. Pass a package name to check an installed package.

content.code:
Checking integration docs: @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

[ok] The docs tree and every link in these docs check out.

[ok] No doc topics overlap with Core.
[ok] No topic copies a passage from another.
[ok] No filler phrases or low-density topics.

content.text: Write each fact in one topic. When two of your topics, or one of yours and a Core topic, repeat 10 or more words of prose word for word, the check lists the pair as a `copied_passage` warning. It names the topic that keeps the text (a Core topic, or of your two the one the passage fits) and the line in the other where to put the link instead ({@link generic:links}). Code and examples are not compared, and a topic may carry the text of the Core topic it replaces. A run with fewer than 4 distinct content words (words other than function words such as "the", "in" or "it"), or one that three or more topics share (a series lead-in), is not listed. Each listed pair is also a warning (`copied_passage`): `doctor integration docs` still exits 0, and `integration check --strict` fails until you fix it.

Keep docs dense. The check lists, as a `doc_fluff` warning, each padding phrase in your prose, with its file line and what to write instead, and each topic of 80 or more prose words in which fewer than half the words carry content (words other than function words such as the, and, in), with its measured share and the floor of 0.5. `doctor integration docs` still exits 0, and `integration check --strict` fails until you cut it. Code, examples, and quoted text are not read. The phrases: `it's important to note`, `it is important to note`, `important to note that`, `it's worth noting`, `it is worth noting`, `worth noting that`, `it should be noted`, `please note`, `note that` (opening a sentence), `as mentioned above`, `as mentioned earlier`, `as mentioned before`, `as noted above`, `as you can see`, `needless to say`, `in order to`, `due to the fact that`, `for the purpose of`, `at this point in time`, `in other words`, `basically`, `essentially`, `obviously`.

Point at another doc with a link, never by writing `{@command docs <name>}` in prose: `{@link generic:<name>}` for one of your package's topics, or `{@link @astryxdesign/cli:generic:<name>}` for a Core doc (`namespace:` for a Core namespace). The CLI prints the link as the command that opens the doc, and doctor checks that the doc exists. The check lists each written pointer to a doc that exists as a `stray_doc_pointer` warning, with the link to write instead. A command with more words, or one in a code block, is a walkthrough and is not listed.
Its arguments and exit codes are in {@link command:doctor integration docs}.

A doc that does not load, an accidental Core overlap, a `reference` block that names no doc, or a failed namespace or placement fails the check with exit code 1. A link that names no doc only warns, and the exit code stays 0.

rows: A doc that does not load, such as an unknown section field or block type
A topic with a Core topic's name and no `replaces` or `extends`
A placement that fails, which hides the doc
A `reference` block whose target names no doc
A link that names no doc

content.text: Read the warnings before you publish. With `--json`, they are in `data.issues`, with `severity: "warning"`.

sections.title: Check each doc against its type

content.text: `doctor integration validate` reads every doc your package ships against the type `@astryxdesign/cli/authoring` publishes for its kind, the way `tsc` would: a `hidden` doc and a second doc for one name too. Test fixtures under `__tests__` in the components or docs root, which those readers skip, are counted, not checked. It reports a field the type does not have (`unknown_field`), a missing required field (`missing_field`), and a value outside the field's type (`wrong_type`).

content.code: {@command doctor integration validate}

Checking 1 doc(s) against the authoring types (TypeScript 6.0.3)

severity: [warn]
doc:      components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
line:     7
export:   default
type:     ComponentDoc
field:    summary
problem:  unknown_field
message:  Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'summary' does not exist in type 'SingleComponentDoc'.
fix:      Remove `summary`: SingleComponentDoc has no field `summary`.

items: The folder decides the type: `ComponentDoc` in your components root, `IntegrationTemplateDoc` in your templates root, `ThemeDoc` in your themes root, and in your docs root the type the doc's `type` names. Keep the `@type` comment above each doc's export too, so your editor shows the same problems as you type.
Every finding is a warning, so the exit code stays 0. With `--json`, they are in `data.docTypes.findings`.

It uses the `typescript` your package installs. Where `typescript` is missing or has no JavaScript compiler API, as TypeScript 7 does, it uses `@typescript/typescript6`, the TypeScript 6 API package, if your package installs it. Without either, it prints `[skip] Docs not type-checked` and the reason.
Every field of every doc type is in {@link generic:field-reference}.

content.text: `{@command doctor}` also measures every read and warns on one over 32 KB. Run it in your package or in an app that installs it; `doctor integration docs` does not check size.

content.code: {@command doctor}

id:      docs-progressive-disclosure
status:  [warn]
label:   Documentation navigation and size
message: acme/deploying build-before-you-ship: 46 KB, over the 32 KB one read may return

content.text: Split a section over the limit into smaller ones, each with its own key. See {@link command:doctor}.

`integration verify` fails a package that ships a docs section, a placed guide, or a doc section with an `id` without an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer of `>=0.6.4`. It does not run the docs check, so run both.

content.code: {@command integration verify}

- [fail] The package ships a namespace doc or a placed guide but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer. A stable CLI before 0.6.4 does not read the docs tree, and can hide every doc topic the package ships. Declare "@astryxdesign/cli": ">=0.6.4" in peerDependencies (optional in peerDependenciesMeta, if the CLI is not required).

items: `integration add doc --parent` writes the peer for you.
`integration verify` passes a hidden guide and an accidental Core overlap; only `doctor integration docs` catches them.
Everything else it checks is in {@link command:integration verify} and {@link generic:checks}.

docs.name: checks
docs.title: Check an integration
docs.description: Pick the check for each problem, learn what fails and what only warns, and run every check in CI.

content.text: Run these in the package folder. The four `doctor integration` checks read your source, and `integration check` runs all four; `integration verify` checks the package npm would publish.

rows: The manifest loads, each root holds contributions the CLI can read, and each doc matches its authoring type. Notes list a malformed `cliCommand` (`invalid_cli_command`) and, for each topic, a command written with a package runner (`runner_command`), bare (`plain_command`) or for one package manager (`package_manager_command`), and a token that does not parse (`doc_token`; see {@link generic:doc-syntax}). Notes fail nothing by default; `integration check --strict --next` fails on the ones marked `next`, and the next minor release counts them

A declared root is missing (`missing_root`), a contribution does not load (`invalid_doc`, `invalid_component`, `invalid_theme`), or two templates in the package replace one Core id (`ambiguous_template_replacement`)

The manifest has a key this CLI does not know (`unknown_manifest_key`), or a doc field does not match the doc's authoring type: a field the type does not have, a missing required field, or a value outside the field's type. It also warns on what no reader can serve: a prop listed twice (`duplicate_prop`), a `propDescriptions` key that names no documented prop (`unknown_translated_prop`), a section with no content (`empty_section`), two sections of a topic with one key (`duplicate_section_key`), or a `.doc.zh.mjs` or `.doc.dense.mjs` overlay beside no topic file (`orphan_doc_overlay`). Since 0.7.3 it also lists, from source and without failing, what the package tells apps to import that they cannot: a component's import (the doc's `import`, or the one the CLI derives) or a template's public import whose subpath package.json `exports` does not declare (`component_import_not_exported`, `template_import_not_exported`) or that names another package (`component_import_other_package`); an example that imports an undeclared subpath (`example_import_not_exported`); a template that imports a path outside the templates root (`template_import_outside_root`) or a path its package or Core does not export (`template_private_import`). It lists the same way a component's import whose module does not export the component (`component_import_missing_name`), an example or a template that imports a name its package does not export (`example_import_missing_name`, `template_import_missing_name`), and a template source with no default export (`template_no_default_export`). Each is a note, printed with its fix, that fails `--strict` from the next minor; an import it cannot judge, such as an `exports` target not built yet or a deep path into a `dist/` not built yet, is listed under `publicImports` as not checked. It checks docs with your installed `typescript`, or, where that is missing or has no JavaScript compiler API (TypeScript 7), with an installed `@typescript/typescript6`; without either, it prints `[skip] Docs not type-checked`. With no `astryx.integration.mjs` it prints a hint and exits 0
No component name clashes with a Core component, each `replaces` names one Core component, and each component doc's props match the component's TypeScript props

Core is not installed (`core_not_found`). In a package that declares the CLI range that turns replacement on, a `replaces` target is missing (`missing_component_replacement_target`) or invalid (`invalid_component_replacement`), or two components replace one Core component (`ambiguous_component_replacement`)

A name clashes with Core, a component sets `replaces` in a package without that range (`inactive_component_replacement`, plus any missing, invalid, or duplicate `replaces` reported as a warning), or a documented prop differs from the code: it is missing there (`not_in_code`), the doc omits a prop the package declares (`not_in_doc`), or its `required` (`required_mismatch`), type (`type_mismatch`), or literal `default` (`default_mismatch`) disagrees, or a `{@link}` in a component doc names no doc (`invalid_doc_graph`). It reads props with your installed `typescript`; without it, it prints `[skip] Props not compared`
Each `replaces` names a Core template of the same type
A `replaces` target is missing (`missing_template_replacement_target`) or of the other type (`invalid_template_replacement`), or two templates replace one id (`ambiguous_template_replacement`)
A template id matches a Core id without `replaces`
Your docs tree, every link, topic names against Core, passages two topics repeat word for word, padding phrases and low-density topics, and written pointers to docs
A topic takes a Core topic name without `replaces` or `extends`, a doc is invalid (`invalid_doc`), or a namespace or placement fails, which hides the doc (`invalid_doc_graph`)

A link names no doc (`invalid_doc_graph`), two topics repeat a passage word for word (`copied_passage`), prose pads with a listed phrase or falls under the density floor (`doc_fluff`), or prose, a description or summary, or the text of a component doc writes `{@command docs <name>}` where a link would be checked (`stray_doc_pointer`)
Everything the four `doctor integration` checks prove, in one command, for your build
Any of the four would exit 1 on its own. With `--strict`, also any warning, and any check that did not run, such as a package with no `astryx.integration.*`
Anything the four warn about, unless you pass `--strict`
The packed package holds every file, shows the same contributions, resolves every public import, and declares the CLI it needs
Anything `validate` fails on, no manifest, a file left out of the `.tgz` file, an import that does not resolve, or a missing CLI peer
Anything `validate` warns about, or a component sets `replaces` and the package does not declare the CLI range that turns it on (`component_replaces_needs_cli`)

content.text: Pass a package name, such as `{@command doctor integration validate @acme/astryx-widgets}`, to check an installed copy from an app instead. To fix a props finding, see {@link generic:check-the-props}.

sections.title: Run every check in every build (required)

content.text: Every integration runs `integration check --strict` in its own build, so every build keeps your docs, types, and links in sync; this is required, not optional. The strict check fails on every copied passage the docs check lists ({@link generic:check-your-docs}). Run `integration verify` before you publish. Install devDependencies first, because the components check needs Core, and `tsc --noEmit` needs `typescript` and a `tsconfig.json`. In package.json:

content.code: "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit && astryx integration check --strict"

items: `integration check` runs `validate`, `components`, `templates`, and `docs` in that order, prints each result, then a summary, and exits 1 when any of them would.
`--strict` also exits 1 on any warning and on any check that did not run. Without it, warnings keep exit code 0: use that while you fix the warnings a package already has.

Its exit codes and JSON are a contract for your build: a new check, or a new failure code, joins only in a minor release that names it in the release notes. A patch can still ship a Core component, template, or CLI topic whose name conflicts with one of yours.

`integration verify` runs `validate` but none of the other three: a Core name clash, a `replaces` that names no Core template, a topic that takes a Core name, or a hidden guide still passes it. Run both before you publish: `astryx integration check --strict && astryx integration verify`.
Bare `{@command doctor}` in the package also warns about a doc section over 32 KB, which no check above measures.

content.text: `integration verify` packs your package with npm, unpacks it into a temporary app, and checks that the app sees everything your source has. It publishes nothing and leaves no `.tgz` file or temporary folder behind.

items: It runs `{@pm-only npm "the tarball the registry receives" pack}` the way `{@pm-only npm "npm is the client the registry publishes from" publish}` would, including your `prepack` script.
It checks that every contribution file is in the `.tgz` file. A root missing from `files` fails with `Add "templates" to "files" in package.json.`
It lists the components, templates, themes, docs, and codemods the temporary app sees, and compares them with your source.

It resolves each component's `import`, and each template's public import, the way Node does, and checks that the module exports the component under the name its doc documents, or a default export for a template. A type-only export does not count.

For each theme, it rebuilds the source, compares the built module and production CSS with the authored outputs, and proves the module, CSS, and optional font CSS exports resolve from the packed package.

It fails a package that needs an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer and lacks it: `>=0.6.6` for a template that sets `keywords`, and `>=0.6.4` for a template that sets `replaces`, a docs section, a placed guide, a doc section with an `id`, or a theme.

content.text: `integration pack --check`, the name this check had before published 0.6.5, still runs it and prints a note; it will be removed in a later release. The options and exit codes are in {@link command:integration verify}.

docs.name: ci-and-containers
docs.title: CI and containers
docs.description: What Astryx does in CI and containers: no update checks or notices, the project's version as always, and how to cache versions or work with a read-only home folder.

items: Most CI services set `CI=true`. When `CI` is set to anything but empty, `0`, or `false`, Astryx never checks for updates and never prints a notice; `CI=false`, `CI=0`, and an empty `CI` do not count. `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER`, set to anything, does the same anywhere.

Add `@astryxdesign/cli` to the project as a devDependency at the same version as `@astryxdesign/core`; then CI runs the version pinned in the repo, and nothing is fetched. A global install in a CI image also works: in a project, it runs the project's version.
Use `--json` for output a script reads; it never carries the answered-by line or a notice.

content.text: When the project installs its own CLI and you install the project's dependencies first, there is nothing to cache. Astryx downloads into its cache only the CLI version a project whose own CLI cannot start needs, and, outside a project, the Core of a global install for commands that read components. In CI it downloads nothing in the background, so a global install in a CI image fetches that Core on its first component command. To skip those downloads on every run, cache this folder between runs:

When the cache cannot be written, a project whose own CLI cannot start is answered by the global install, with a warning naming the folder. Point `XDG_CACHE_HOME` at a writable absolute path, or reinstall the project's dependencies. The global install's daily check and agent guide are skipped quietly when they cannot be written.

sections.title: Machines that keep only the home folder

content.text: Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone; the guide says to run the command that installed the CLI, such as `{@pm install @astryxdesign/cli --global}`, when that command is not found, and `astryx doctor` names the same step. To keep the CLI across restarts, install it into a folder in your home and put its `bin` folder on your PATH, as for a permission error ({@link generic:install-once}), or run that command when the machine starts.
This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works.

docs.name: cli
docs.title: Astryx CLI
docs.summary: Commands, programmatic APIs, and output contracts. Building an integration is under {@link namespace:authoring}.

blocks.text: Use the CLI in any folder: install it once for your computer, and every project still gets the release that matches its Core. See {@link namespace:global}.

docs.name: cli-command
docs.title: CLI command
docs.description: Name the command your users run the CLI with, so every command the CLI prints in their apps starts with it.

content.text: The CLI ends most answers with the next command to run: a hint, an error fix, a Doctor fix, or a doc example. By default each one starts with a command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs, such as `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`, when the app's own CLI answered, and otherwise the CLI package pinned to that release, such as `{@pm dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.2}`.

Set `cliCommand` only when your users run the CLI some other way, such as a wrapper your company ships that runs it with your package loaded. Otherwise the commands the CLI prints send them, and their agents, to a CLI that answers without your package. Most packages leave it out.
Add `cliCommand` to `astryx.integration.mjs`: the command, without a subcommand.
In an app that installs your package, the CLI then prints every command with it:

content.code: Error: Theme "ocean" is not added. Run `acme astryx theme add ocean` first.

content.text: That covers hints, errors, suggestions, Doctor fixes, `--help`, the setup reminder, the agent block `init` writes, and doc text. `--json` output keeps every command without a runner, as in `"command": "astryx theme add ocean"`, so a script reads the same fields in every app.

sections.title: How the CLI picks the command

items: The `cliCommand` of the packages the app loads, when they name one command.
The command a host tool names when it runs the CLI for the app. Nothing in a plain project names one.

A command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs when the app's own CLI answered, such as `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`; `astryx` outside a project when the CLI installed for the computer answered; otherwise the CLI package pinned to that release, such as `{@pm dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.2}` (see {@link generic:who-answers}).

content.text: Two packages that set the same command agree, and the CLI uses it.

If two packages an app loads set different commands, the CLI uses neither: it prints commands with what the app's package manager runs, even when a host tool named a command. `{@command doctor}` warns in its `cli-command` check and names both packages:

content.code:
status:  [warn]
label:   CLI command
message: Loaded integrations declare different CLI commands: @acme/astryx-widgets (`acme astryx`), @other/kit (`other astryx`). Neither is used, so printed commands start with `pnpm exec astryx`.

content.text: The app fixes it by removing the package that does not belong, or the packages agree on one command.

An invalid value is ignored, and the rest of your manifest still loads. `{@command doctor integration validate}` reports it as `invalid_cli_command`. A valid `cliCommand` is one line of plain text without spaces at either end, at most 120 characters.

In an app that installs your package, `{@command doctor}` passes its `cli-command` check and names your package as the one that set the command. A CLI released before this field reports `cliCommand` as an unknown key and prints the package manager's command.

In global mode: outside a project, the `cliCommand` of integrations installed for the computer applies; when none is declared, commands start with the plain command of the CLI installed for the computer. Inside a project, only the project's integrations count, so a `cliCommand` from a package installed for the computer never changes the project's printed commands. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: codemods
docs.title: Codemods
docs.description: Ship codemods that `{@command upgrade}` runs to migrate app code, and know which of them an app runs.

content.text: `integration add codemod` writes a codemod into a folder named after a version. Apps run it with `{@command upgrade}` to migrate their code.

content.code: {@command integration add codemod rename-delay --to 0.7.0}

codemods/
  0.7.0/
    rename-delay.mjs         # the codemod
    rename-delay.test.mjs    # skipped: a test file
    __tests__/               # skipped: a test folder

content.text: The first add declares `codemods: './codemods'` in `astryx.integration.mjs`. The codemod's id is its path inside the version folder, without the extension: `rename-delay`. An id must be unique across all version folders in the package.

The loader skips `*.test.*`, `*.spec.*`, and `*.fixture.*` files and everything under `__tests__/` or `__fixtures__/`, so tests can sit beside the codemod. The folder name decides when an app runs the codemod; see "Choose when a codemod runs".
A codemod default-exports a plain object with a `type`, a `title`, and a `transform` function. `transform` returns the new source, or `null` to leave the file as it is.

`type: 'code'` rewrites the app's source files that match `fileExtensions`. `type: 'config'` rewrites the app's `astryx.config` file instead, and runs before code codemods. `title` shows in the upgrade output, and `api.jscodeshift` is a jscodeshift instance for the file. Every field is in {@link schema:codemod}.
Two rules decide whether an app's `{@command upgrade}` runs your codemods: the app's Core versions, and whether the app names your package.

items: Version folders are matched against the app's `@astryxdesign/core` versions, not your package's version. `upgrade --from <version>` runs each folder above `--from`, up to and including the Core version installed in the app. With Core 0.7.0 installed, `--from 0.6.3` runs `0.7.0/`, and `--from 0.7.0` runs nothing. A folder named after your own release, such as `1.0.0/`, waits until the app has Core 1.0.0.

`upgrade` runs your codemods only when the app lists your package in `integrations` in its `astryx.config`, or passes `--integration @acme/astryx-widgets`. Having your package installed is not enough: the run then skips your codemods with no warning.

content.text: An app previews codemods with `{@command upgrade}` and writes the changes with `--apply`. Without `--apply`, nothing on disk changes.

content.code:
Integrations: @acme/astryx-widgets
<n> codemods to run (dry run)
Applying integration codemods...
  Rename AcmeCarousel delay to interval (v0.7.0, @acme/astryx-widgets)
!     ~ src/Hero.tsx (would change)

content.text: `<n>` counts Core's codemods for the same versions too: they run first and print above `Integrations:`. To run only yours, as when you test it, add `--codemod rename-delay`.

`--from` is the Core version the app had before it upgraded. The run scans `./src` unless the app passes `--path`, and it never writes a file the app marks as generated, vendored, or ignored; see {@link command:upgrade}. `upgrade --list` shows only Core codemods.
An integration manifest has no `hooks` field. Commands that run after codemods, such as a formatter, are the app's to set, in `hooks.postCodemod` in its `astryx.config`.

In global mode: inside an app, `upgrade` runs with the release equal to the app's Core, whichever copy of the CLI the user starts, and only the codemods of integrations the app installs run. Outside a project, `upgrade` lists codemods and migrates nothing. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link command:upgrade}.

docs.name: color
docs.title: Color
docs.description: Semantic color tokens for surfaces, text, icons, borders, and status indicators.

content.text: Colors are semantic: tokens describe purpose, not appearance. Every color adapts automatically between light and dark modes via CSS light-dark(). Themes override the resolved values, so your code never references raw hex colors.
Layered surface hierarchy: body → surface → card → popover. Each level sits visually above the previous one.
Semantic colors for consistent theming. All colors use light-dark() for automatic mode switching.
Status roles: pick the token by the surface. `<status>` is info, success, warning, or error.

rows: Status text on the page or a card (4.5:1 or more).
Status icons on the page or a card. Defaults to the text colour.
Status borders on the page or a card, such as an invalid field. Defaults to the text colour.
Strong status fill, such as a Badge or StatusDot.
Text and icons on the strong fill (4.5:1 or more).
Pale status fill, such as a Banner.
Text and icons on the pale fill (4.5:1 or more).

content.text: Import the typed color tokens and use them in `stylex.create()`; they resolve to the active theme and color mode.

content.label: Applying color tokens

items: Use semantic tokens (--color-text-primary) instead of raw hex values.
Rely on the surface hierarchy (body → surface → card → popover) for layering.
Use status colors (success, error, warning) only for their semantic meaning.
Hardcode hex values, since they won't adapt to dark mode or custom themes.
Mix accent colors with status colors in the same context.
Use --color-on-accent on non-accent backgrounds.

docs.name: commands
docs.title: Commands
docs.summary: Every command and subcommand: usage, options, examples, exit codes, and what it does outside a project.

blocks.text: In global mode: each command declares its behavior outside projects (`outsideProject`). Most answer like a new project; some write nothing and name the project they need; `doctor`, `init`, and `upgrade` behave differently. Commands with different behavior describe it in their `In global mode:` note, and CLI tests run each command in an empty folder against its declared value. Inside a project, the project's Astryx release runs every command, whichever astryx command you type. See {@link namespace:global}.

docs.name: component-family
docs.title: Component family
docs.description: Adapt a single-component doc when one module exposes several public components or hooks that belong to one family.

content.text: Start with a complete single-component doc. Convert its top-level `props` into a `components` array only when one source module or component directory exposes several public components or hooks as one family. The family doc keeps the shared usage guidance; each array entry owns one public export.

items: Put the primary or most-used export first.
Use a full entry when this file owns that export's description and signature.
Use `props` for a component entry. Use `params` and `returns` for a hook entry.
Do not add private implementation helpers or exports that people should not use directly.

content.text: Every field is in {@link schema:component-doc}.

content.label: components/AcmeTabs.doc.mjs

content.text: The public module named by `import` must export every component or hook named by a full entry. Apps then list, search and open each component in the family by its own name. A full entry the module does not export is not listed, and `integration verify` does not report it: check the family with `{@command component --list}`. When `import` names output your pack lifecycle builds (such as `dist`), the members are listed once that output exists, and `integration verify` compares them as they are listed after the pack builds it.

A member's source is the `.tsx` file in the family doc's folder, or below it, that declares it: the one the family's own file or the module `import` names reaches, else the one in that folder that declares the name, as when `import` names built output. A member that only a bundle or a file outside that folder declares is still listed, with no source for `--source` or `swizzle`. A member is not listed when a doc's file or a Core name your package replaces already has its name. A member that shares a name with Core opens with `--package`.

sections.title: Give a member its own file

content.text: When one family member needs its own doc, replace its full entry with `{name: 'MemberName'}` and move the details into a sibling doc. The parent keeps the family relationship without copying the child's content. Continue with {@link generic:subcomponent}.

docs.name: component-imports
docs.title: Resolve the import
docs.description: Keep the component doc import and package exports map aligned, then verify the packed package.

content.text: Apps copy the component doc's `import` field into their code, so that exact specifier must resolve from your packed package. `integration add` writes it together with an `exports` entry in package.json.

content.label: package.json

content.text: Add writes the entry only when package.json already has an `exports` map, so start every package with `"exports": {}`.

A file does not have to be named after its component. When `Slides.tsx` exports `AcmeCarousel` and nothing named `Slides`, keep the doc beside it as `Slides.doc.mjs` and set its `name` to `AcmeCarousel`: apps list, search and open the component by that name, and `integration verify` checks that its import exports `AcmeCarousel`. A file that exports its own name keeps that name. A package that names its files in kebab case works the same way: `acme-gallery.doc.mjs` beside `acme-gallery.tsx` sets `name: 'AcmeGallery'`.

The file name still opens the doc. A name that Core or another doc's file already has stays theirs, and so does a Core name your package replaces: with `Badge.doc.mjs` naming `AcmeBadge`, `{@command component Badge}` opens Core's `Badge`, and `--package` with your package name reaches yours.

`integration verify` unpacks the packed package into a temporary app, resolves each documented import, and checks that the module exports the documented component name. Its `--json` output names each failure by code.

content.code: {@command integration verify}

items: `component_import_unresolvable` means the exports map has no entry for the documented import.
`component_export_missing` means the module does not export the documented name, or package.json has no exports map.
`typescript_extension_in_specifier` means the public import ends in `.ts` or `.tsx`.

content.text: To import from the package root, set `import: '@acme/astryx-widgets'` and re-export the component from the file that `exports["."]` points to. See {@link command:integration verify}.

In global mode: outside a project, imports the CLI prints name packages installed for the computer, which a new app must install before it can build them; inside a project, only packages the project installs are printed. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: component-lookups
docs.title: Component lookups
docs.description: Look up one or several exact component identities, choose a focused projection, and handle complete batch receipts.

content.text: `{@command component}` accepts exact selectors as a variadic positional argument. With no selector it browses the catalog. With one selector it keeps the normal single-component response. With two or more it prints one complete ordered batch receipt.

content.label: Several component docs
content.code:
{@command component Button Badge Text}
astryx --json component Button Badge Text

content.text: Every selector gets one row in input order. Duplicate selectors stay duplicate rows. A missing or ambiguous component does not hide successful neighbors or stop later selectors from resolving.

A batch accepts at most 100 selectors, including duplicates, in every projection mode. A larger request returns a top-level `ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT` before any component resolves. It emits no `component.batch` receipt and no partial results.
Focused component controls apply to every found row. Use the same control you use for one component:

content.label: Focused batch lookups

content.text: A selector is an exact component identity, not free-text search. Use one of these forms:

items: `Button` for an unqualified component name.
`widgets/Button` for a component in an unscoped package.
`@acme/widgets/Button` for a component in a scoped package.
`@acme/widgets@1.2.3/Button` to require that exact installed package version.

content.text: A version qualifies the package, never the component. The lookup does not fall through to another installed version. An unqualified name owned by several installed packages is `ambiguous` and lists every candidate. Use a package-qualified selector or `--package` to choose one.
`{@command discover}` remains free-text package discovery. Its words form one query; they are not component batch selectors.

JSON uses `component.batch` with `{count, results}`. Each row echoes `selector` and has one status: `found`, `not_found`, `ambiguous`, or `error`. A found row carries the normal single-component `{type, data}` under `result`. Failed rows carry `code` and `error`, plus `suggestions` or `candidates` when available.

content.label: Outcome and duplicate examples
content.code:
astryx --json component Button Badge                 # all found, exit 0
astryx --json component Button MissingWidget         # mixed, exit 1
astryx --json component MissingWidget MissingPanel   # all failed, exit 1
astryx --json component Button Button                # two ordered rows, exit 0

content.label: A complete failed JSON receipt
content.code: astryx --json component MissingWidget MissingPanel

content.label: The same receipt in text mode
content.code:
Component batch

count: 2

Results

MissingWidget

selector: MissingWidget
status:   not_found
code:     ERR_UNKNOWN_COMPONENT
error:    No component named "MissingWidget"

MissingPanel

selector: MissingPanel
status:   not_found
code:     ERR_UNKNOWN_COMPONENT
error:    No component named "MissingPanel"

content.text: The CLI emits every row first, then exits 1 when any row is not `found`. This includes mixed receipts and receipts where every row failed. JSON and text use the same exit status. A batch where every row is `found` exits 0.

The argument shape chooses the response shape. Omit the argument for the catalog, pass a string for the existing single-component response, and pass an array for `component.batch`. An array always means batch, including empty and one-item arrays, so filtering a selector list cannot silently change the response type. The published `ComponentBatchResponse` specializes the shared `BatchResponse` and `BatchRow` types.

content.code:
import {component} from '@astryxdesign/cli/api';

const catalog = await component(); // component.list
const button = await component('Button'); // component.detail
const empty = await component([]); // component.batch, count 0
const oneRow = await component(['Button']); // component.batch, count 1
const batch = await component(['Button', 'Badge']); // component.batch, count 2
await component(Array(101).fill('Button')); // ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT before lookup

content.label: Exact empty-array response
Handle every row without losing partial results

docs.name: component-migration
docs.title: Component Migration
docs.description: Move the app frame first, map shadcn and Radix primitives to components, and wire up command palette, settings, and theme controls.

content.text: Start with AppShell so page migration happens inside the final navigation, spacing, surface, and responsive frame. This also exposes theme and color issues early because every route shares the same shell.

rows: Use for product identity, global actions, account entry, and command/search trigger.
Use sections and nested nav items for route groups. Keep selection state driven by the router.
Let the shell own persistent structure; let route components own page content.
Verify focus, close behavior, and route changes on narrow viewports.
Use as the home for theme mode and app preferences.

content.text: Do not wrap old shadcn components in design system styles. Replace the primitive with the component that owns the behavior, accessibility, state classes, and token usage.

rows: Use Button for labeled commands and IconButton for icon-only toolbar actions.
Keep validation state in status props rather than ad hoc border classes.
Use when multiline editing is the primary action.
Use for persisted boolean settings, including theme mode when represented as a binary choice.
Use list variants for grouped selection.
Use when one option must be selected from a visible set.
Use Selector for bounded options and Typeahead for searchable async options.
Use route state or current page state as the source of truth.
Keep app-specific search sources outside the shell and feed searchable items.
Use MoreMenu for compact overflow actions.
Use Banner for page or section messages and Toast for transient feedback.
Use AlertDialog for destructive confirmation and Dialog for task flows.
Prefer ListItem for selectable rows instead of styling Button as a row.

content.text: Move global search to CommandPalette once the shell exists. Treat the palette as a view over app commands: routes, contextual actions, create actions, filters, recent items, and entity results. Keep data normalization in app code so search sources always return arrays of searchable items.
Put light and dark mode controls in the settings popover or account menu. The switch or selector should update the mode passed to Theme, not toggle isolated body classes.

content.label: Settings popover theme control

docs.name: components
docs.title: Components
docs.summary: Add components to an integration, document their public contract, and make them work in every app that installs the package.

blocks.text: In global mode: components from an integration installed for the computer show up outside projects; inside a project, only components from integrations the project installs. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: computer-agent-guide
docs.title: The agent guide on your computer
docs.description: Your global install keeps one short Astryx skill in your home folder and links it into the folders agent tools read, so agents anywhere know Astryx is there. `{@command init --user}` writes it now or turns it off.

content.text: A project's agent docs reach only agents working in that project. Your global install also keeps one skill file, `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, which most coding agents read. It tells agents that Astryx is on this computer, when it is relevant (building or changing UI), and to start with `{@command search}`. It names no version, so it never goes stale. Inside a project, the project's own agent docs come first.
It is written in the background on the first run and again after you upgrade, so no command waits for it. Installing the package does not write it, because some package managers skip install scripts.

Agents that read only their own skills folder get a link to the skill's folder, so they read the same one file: a folder symlink with a relative target (a junction on Windows, or a copy where neither can be made). Continue's scanner skips links, so it gets a copy, refreshed with the file:

rows: When Xcode's coding assistant folder exists

content.text: Astryx never replaces anything it did not create at one of these folders, and never writes a folder another tool manages; `{@command doctor}` names any it skipped, and any link whose skill folder is missing, as in a container that mounts only one agent's folder.
