items: Cloud and background agents read only the repository, so the project's own agent docs, the block `{@command init}` writes into AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, are what reach them.
Apps that take an uploaded skill: upload `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, or a zip of its folder.

content.text: If your agent reads skills from another folder, link it to the skill:

content.code: ln -s ~/.agents/skills/astryx <your agent's skills folder>/astryx

content.text: On Windows, in PowerShell:

content.code: New-Item -ItemType Junction -Path "<your agent's skills folder>\astryx" -Target "$HOME\.agents\skills\astryx"

sections.title: Write it now, or turn it off

content.code:
{@command init --user}
{@command init --user --remove-agents}

items: `init --user` writes the file and the links now.
`--remove-agents` removes the file and every link Astryx made, and turns it off until you run `{@command init --user}` again.
A file you edited is never overwritten or removed; delete it to get the current text.
Outside a project, `{@command doctor}` says whether the skill is there, current, edited, or turned off, and where it is linked.

content.text: This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works. A project's own agent docs: {@link command:init}.

docs.name: computer-integrations
docs.title: Integrations installed globally
docs.description: Integrations installed next to your global install work in folders outside any project. Inside a project, only the integrations the project installs work, and the others are listed as ones you could add.

content.text: Install the integration the same way you installed the CLI, so the two sit side by side:

content.code: {@pm install @astryxdesign/cli @acme/widgets --global}

content.text: A tool that installs the CLI together with integrations in one folder, and runs the CLI from there, counts the same way. `npx` and the cache of project versions never count.

In a folder outside any project, Astryx loads each integration installed next to your global install the way a project loads its own: its components, templates, docs, themes, and discover source show up, and a command name it declares starts the commands Astryx prints. One whose `@astryxdesign/core` or `@astryxdesign/cli` peer range leaves out your global version is skipped, and `{@command doctor}` says why.

sections.title: Inside a project, only the project's

content.text: A project's answers must match what it installs: a component from a package it does not install would not build. So inside a project, an integration installed only globally adds nothing. `{@command discover}` lists it among the packages the project could add, with the project's install command, when it supports the project's version and loads. When the project installs the same integration, the project's copy is the one used.

items: Outside a project, `{@command doctor}` lists the global integrations it uses and warns about each it skips.
Inside a project, `{@command doctor}` and `{@command discover}` list the ones the project could add.

content.text: This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works. Building an integration: {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: configuration
docs.title: Configuration
docs.summary: Set how your integration behaves in an app: agent guidance, the command your users run, debug and gap reports, and more as it grows.

blocks.text: In global mode: installed for the computer, beside the global CLI, your package's manifest is read as it is in a project and applies in folders outside any project; peer ranges are checked against the global CLI's release. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

Beyond the things you ship, an integration can set how it behaves in an app: the guidance it gives the AI agents working there, the command its users run the CLI with, and the record it keeps of each CLI run. Open one below to set it up.

docs.name: css-and-stylex
docs.title: CSS & StyleX
docs.description: Core integration principle, plain CSS / CSS Modules, and StyleX typed-token imports.

content.text: Keep the system as the source of truth for theme values. Components read design tokens from CSS custom properties such as `--color-text-primary`, `--color-background-surface`, `--spacing-4`, and `--radius-container`. Other styling libraries should map their own semantic tokens, utility names, or theme objects to those system CSS variables whenever possible.

Use CSS variables for ordinary DOM styling because they inherit through the tree, follow `data-theme` color mode, respect nested `data-astryx-theme` scopes, and update when themes switch. Use token resolver APIs only for non-CSS consumers such as SVG attribute values, canvas, chart configuration, color calculations, or static config generation.

For available token names and values, run {@link namespace:tokens}. Focused references are also available with {@link generic:color}, {@link generic:spacing}, {@link generic:shape}, {@link namespace:typography}, {@link generic:elevation}, and {@link generic:motion}.

Choose the narrowest integration path that fits the styling library. Most DOM styling should stay on the CSS-variable path; JavaScript token resolution is for APIs that cannot consume CSS custom properties.

rows: The library ultimately writes CSS and accepts string values
You are writing StyleX styles in application code
You want utility classes backed by active system tokens
JavaScript needs token values for charts, canvas, SVG, or config objects

items: Map by semantic intent: text, surface, border, accent, status, radius, spacing, typography.
Let the system own color mode. The root Theme syncs `data-theme="light|dark"` and `data-astryx-theme` to `<html>` for portals and first-level theme scope.
Prefer CSS variables for runtime theme switching and nested themes.
Copy raw hex/px values into a second theme object when a `var(...)` reference would work.
Run a second unsynchronized dark-mode provider that disagrees with Theme.
Make another library's CSS variables the source of truth for the system. Some consumers need token values outside the DOM.

content.text: The simplest integration is direct CSS variable usage. CSS Modules scope class names, but system token variables are global/inherited values supplied by package CSS and the active theme.

content.label: Card.module.css

content.text: Sass variables are compile-time only. They are useful for generating static CSS, but they do not update when the system switches theme or color mode. Use native CSS custom properties for themeable values.

For StyleX styles, prefer the typed token exports from `@astryxdesign/core/theme/tokens.stylex`. They provide autocomplete and catch token-name typos while still resolving through the same system CSS variables at runtime.

content.label: Typed token imports

content.text: Use `xstyle` for component overrides and `stylex.props()` for your own DOM nodes. Use `className` when integrating a non-StyleX styling library.

docs.name: debug-and-gap-reports
docs.title: Debug and gap reports
docs.description: Receive a record of each CLI run in apps that use your package, and handle the gap reports they send about it.

content.text: Export a `debug` function from `astryx.integration.mjs`; the CLI calls it once per command run in an app loading your package.
The event is a `DebugEvent` with `command`, `outcome`, `exitCode`, `durationMs`, `error`, and more, its values scrubbed (`redacted: true`). Every field is in {@link schema:debug-event}.

Keep the function synchronous: the CLI calls it as the process exits and never waits for a promise. The app's own `debug` handler runs first, then yours. A handler that throws is skipped, and the command's output and exit code stay the same.

An app records every command only when its `astryx.config` names `integrations` or `debug`, as listing your package does. Otherwise your handler runs only for commands loading the app's project, such as `component` and `docs`, never for `--version` or a mistyped command. In an app whose config names neither word, those commands also print a stderr warning.
`debug` is a named export, not a manifest field, so an older CLI ignores it and loads the rest of your manifest.

sections.title: Turn off debug in an app

content.text: An app can refuse every integration's `debug` handler and keep its own. It sets `inheritDebug` in its package.json:

content.code: {"astryx": {"inheritDebug": false}}

content.text: Your handler then no longer runs in that app.
Export a `gapReport` handler, and `{@command gap-report}` in an app sends it each gap report, such as a missing component or variant. The handler files the report and returns a receipt.
Every handler in the app gets every report, so check `report.target.package` and skip reports about other packages.
Every field is in {@link schema:gap-report-handler}.

The CLI waits 30 seconds, then aborts `signal`. A throw, a timeout, or an invalid receipt fails your delivery, and the command exits 1; the other handlers still run. Like `debug`, `gapReport` is a named export that older CLIs ignore.
Set `audience: 'public'` when your handler writes somewhere the public can read. The CLI runs it only when the caller passes `--confirm-public`; an `'internal'` handler always runs.

content.code: {@command gap-report AcmeCarousel --category missing_variant --reason 'Need a vertical layout'}

handlerType: integration
handler:     @acme/astryx-widgets
audience:    public
status:      consent_required
message:     Rerun with --confirm-public to file this report.

content.text: With `--confirm-public`, the same delivery reads `status: filed` and shows your `url`. The report goes to the package named by `--package`, else the package that owns the component, else Core.
With no `gapReport` handler in the app, the CLI routes the report to the target package's manifest `issuesUrl`.

items: A GitHub issues URL, such as `https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues`, gets an issue filed with the GitHub CLI, `gh`, once the caller passes `--confirm-public`.
Any other URL comes back as a `routed_only` receipt for the caller to open.
With no `issuesUrl`, the command fails: `Package "@acme/astryx-widgets" provides neither a report handler nor an issues URL.`

content.text: One handler anywhere in the app, from the app or from any package, turns the fallback off for every report. So does a listed package that fails to load: the CLI cannot tell whether it has a handler, so the report fails for that package instead of going to another tracker. See {@link command:gap-report}.

sections.title: Let the person choose where a report goes

content.text: When an app loads packages naming their own `issuesUrl`, a report can go to the default (the handlers, or the fallback above) or to one of those packages. `{@command gap-report --list-categories}` and the receipt of a report filed without `--to` list every destination, with a line telling the agent to ask the person.

items: An agent asks the person where to file. It never picks a package destination on its own.
`--to <package>` carries the person's choice: the report goes only to that package's `issuesUrl`, under the same `--confirm-public` rule, and no handler runs.
Without a choice, leave out `--to`; the report goes to the default.
A `--to` that names no destination fails before anything is sent and lists the destinations.

content.text: In global mode: when users install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI, its `debug` function receives runs in folders outside any project too; inside a project, only if the project installs it. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: define-the-theme
docs.title: Define the theme
docs.description: Point theme tokens at the palette, keep light-dark() to colors, and avoid Core internals.

content.text: A theme token is a named slot that Astryx components read for a value — `--color-accent` for the accent color, and so on. Components never read your palette directly; they read tokens. Defining a theme means pointing each token at a palette shade, so the components wear your colors.
Import the palette in `oceanTheme.ts` and point your tokens at its stops. Each token takes a `[light, dark]` pair — the shade to use in light mode and the one in dark mode.

Local imports must stay inside the theme folder. One that leaves it, such as `../../shared/colors`, fails with `invalid_theme`, and every theme in the package disappears from `theme list`. `{@command theme template}` writes a file that explains every `defineTheme` field. For the full token set and component theming, read {@link generic:author-a-theme}.

To base a theme on an existing one, `extends` it: import the base theme and override only the tokens you change. Add the derived theme with `integration add theme ocean-contrast`, and import the base from its built package export, since local imports cannot leave the theme folder. The derived theme keeps a live link to the base and picks up its later changes when you rebuild it — unlike `--from`, which forks a copy ({@link generic:add-a-theme}).

Each `[light, dark]` pair compiles to a `light-dark()` value, which switches only colors. Give it colors. For a value that is not a plain color — a gradient — put `light-dark()` on each color stop, not around the whole value: `light-dark()` takes two colors, so wrapping whole gradients makes the value invalid where the token is used, and `theme build` does not warn.

sections.title: Do not set Core private variables

content.text: Core private variables start with `--_`, such as `--_field-radius`. They are internals and can change in any Core release, so `theme build` reports each one it finds as an `[error]`. Set the standard CSS property instead — `borderRadius`, `padding` — and let the build emit the internal variable where Core needs it.

The theme imports `@astryxdesign/core/theme`, so declare Core as a peer dependency, with the range of Core versions you test the theme against — a range, not an exact version, so a Core patch release does not force a republish. `integration add theme` already declared the optional `@astryxdesign/cli` peer that reads themes:

docs.name: describe-the-component
docs.title: Describe the component
docs.summary: Write and maintain the default component doc, then adapt it when one family owns several exports or a member needs its own file.

blocks.text: A component's `.doc.mjs` is part of the integration's public contract, not optional commentary. Astryx uses it for CLI output and search, and people and agents read it to decide whether the component fits and how to use it.

items: Change the source and its `.doc.mjs` together.
Update the doc whenever the public name, import, behavior, props, defaults, examples, or accessibility requirements change.

`integration verify` checks the doc shape and packed import, and `doctor integration components` compares each props table with the component's TypeScript props ({@link generic:check-the-props}). Neither can prove the prose still matches the component.

blocks.text: Every component doc has one stable identity and enough usage guidance for a reader to choose it correctly. Pick the shape below that matches your module.
After every source or doc change, read the component back. This output is what people and agents receive.

docs.name: doc-syntax
docs.title: Doc syntax
docs.description: The tokens a doc writes for links, Astryx commands and package-manager steps, which the CLI shows each reader in their own package manager.

content.text: A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table cells and code blocks.

rows: the command that opens that doc
a step only one package manager can do
`npm pkg set name=x` (only with npm: why)

content.text: In prose a token prints as a code span; in a code span or code block it prints as the command alone. `--json` carries the same commands, a `{@@command}` token as the bare command that starts with astryx, which a reader that shows the doc prefixes itself.
A `{@@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.

rows: `yarn global add x` (Yarn 1); npm on Yarn 2 and newer

items: Flags: `--dev` and `--exact` with `install`, `--global` with `install` and `remove`, `--latest` with `update`. `--exact` takes one version, never a range: only npm pins a range.
Everything after the name of a script (`run`), a binary (`exec`) or a package (`dlx`, `create`) is passed to it as written.
`{@@pm install x --global}` on pnpm needs `pnpm setup` once per computer.

sections.title: A step only one package manager can do

content.text: Some commands exist in one package manager only, such as `npm pkg set` or `pnpm setup`. Write `{@@pm-only <manager> "<reason>" <command>}`: the manager is one of npm, pnpm, yarn, yarn-classic or bun, and the reason, in double quotes, is shown to readers beside the command. Use it only when no `{@@pm}` step does the same: doctor names a one-manager step that every package manager can run, with the `{@@pm}` token to write.

`doctor integration validate`, and so `integration check`, lists each of these as a note with its file, line and the token to write. A note fails nothing today; the next minor release turns them into warnings, so `integration check --strict --next` fails on them now. Run it to fix them ahead.

rows: a code span or shell line written for one package manager, such as `npm install -D x`
an Astryx command written with a runner, such as `pnpm exec astryx docs`
an Astryx command written bare, where `{@@command docs}` checks that the command exists
a token that does not parse, or a name that is not a doc token

content.text: In global mode: outside a project, a `{@@command}` token prints the way your global install prints every command, and a `{@@pm}` step prints for npm unless the CLI detects another package manager. In a project, the project's own runner and package manager decide. See {@link namespace:global}.

docs.name: docs
docs.title: Docs
docs.summary: Write docs that ship with your package and that people and agents find by search or one level at a time.

blocks.text: In global mode: docs from an integration installed for the computer show up outside projects; inside a project, only docs from integrations the project installs. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: document-the-template
docs.title: Document the template
docs.summary: Write the doc that helps people and agents find, choose, and trust your template: its name, description, readiness, preview, and any Core replacement.

docs.name: document-the-theme
docs.title: Document the theme
docs.description: Document a theme by extending the core theme topic, so an app reads it in {@link generic:theme}.

content.text: Give your theme a doc topic that extends the core `theme` topic, so an app that lists your package sees your theme at the end of {@link generic:theme}. Add it with `extends: 'theme'` ({@link generic:extend-or-replace}).

Keep the section short: how to install the package, run `theme add`, apply the generated module ({@link generic:use-a-theme-in-an-app}), and customize with `extends`. When the theme uses a custom font, name the families and the optional exported font stylesheet that `theme add` imports ({@link generic:fonts-and-assets}). Extend `theme` rather than a topic another package replaces, or an app that loads that package after yours drops your section.

Do not put theme usage in `agentDocs`. Agent lines land in every app's agent file and are for guidance needed every session; a theme's install-and-use steps belong in a doc topic that people and agents read on demand. See {@link generic:agent-guidance}.

docs.name: elevation
docs.title: Elevation
docs.description: Shadow tokens for visual elevation and inset state rings.

content.text: Elevation tokens create depth through box-shadow. Three levels (low, med, high) establish a visual hierarchy for floating elements. Inset shadows provide focus and selection rings for interactive components.
Each level adds stronger offset and spread. Shadow color adapts to dark mode automatically via light-dark().
Elevation shadows (low to med to high) and inset shadows for input state rings.

Pick the level by how far the surface sits from the page, not by how much shadow you want. Elevation encodes stacking order: a higher level means the surface is layered over more of the UI. Use exactly one level per surface, and only raise a surface above `none` when it actually sits above other content.

rows: The component is flat and embedded in the surface; it is part of the page, not layered above it. This is the default for every surface except ChatComposer.
A Card in a grid, an inline Banner, a standard Button

The component is in the normal page flow but should read as distinct from the background. Use for emphasis or to separate the component from the surface behind it; the component still sits on the page, it is not floating over other content.
A raised Card that needs emphasis, a ChatComposer
The component sits over other content on the same page; it floats above nearby elements but not the whole screen.
A Popover, a floating Banner, a floating action Button
The component is placed over the entire UI; it is the topmost layer and typically has a backdrop or takes focus from everything else.
A modal Dialog, a full-screen overlay surface

content.text: If two surfaces overlap, the one on top takes the higher level. If a surface does not overlap anything, it is `none` or `low`; never `med` or `high`.

Configurable surfaces expose a single `elevation` prop instead of asking consumers to hand-write a box-shadow. It takes the graded enum `none | low | med | high`, narrowed per component to the steps that surface needs: Card, ClickableCard, SelectableCard, Button, IconButton, ButtonGroup, ToggleButton, and Banner expose the full scale, while ChatComposer exposes only `none | low`. `none` is a flat literal (`box-shadow: none`); the other levels map to the `--shadow-*` tokens above, so a surface stays theme-agnostic.

Prop defaults preserve current appearance: every surface defaults to `none` except ChatComposer, which defaults to `low` to keep its raised look. Set `elevation="none"` to flatten it; the flat composer draws a border with the same rest / hover / focus treatment as a text input.

content.label: Raising a surface with the elevation prop

content.text: Always float; no prop: intrinsic overlays (Dialog, Popover, Tooltip, Toast, HoverCard, DropdownMenu, and the components that compose them) bake their elevation in and never expose the prop. Flow content (inputs, Text, layout) is never elevated; input fields use inset rings, which are a separate concept from elevation.
When building a custom surface, read elevation from the token scale rather than a hand-rolled shadow; the same tokens the elevation prop resolves to.

content.label: Applying elevation

items: Reach for the `elevation` prop on a configurable surface before writing any custom shadow.

Choose the level by how far the surface sits from the page: `none` when flat/embedded, `low` when in-flow but distinct, `med` when over page content, `high` when over the whole UI. See "Choosing a level".
Use inset shadows for input focus/selection states; they compose better than outlines.
Hand-write a `box-shadow` in app code; set the `elevation` prop or read `shadowVars` instead.
Raise a surface that does not sit above other content; a non-overlapping surface is `none` or `low`, never `med` or `high`.
Stack multiple elevation levels on the same element.
Use elevation shadows for decorative borders. Use --color-border tokens instead.

docs.name: experimental
docs.title: Experimental features
docs.summary: Features you can try now that may change or be removed in a patch release.

blocks.text: Everything here is experimental: its commands (under `astryx experimental`), configuration (under `experimental` in astryx.config and in an integration manifest), output, and docs may change or be removed in any patch release, with no deprecation period. Nothing here changes what the rest of Astryx does unless you use it. A feature leaves this section when it becomes stable.

docs.name: export-template-assets
docs.title: Export the template and assets
docs.description: Make sure the published package contains and exposes everything the copied template imports.

content.text: `integration verify` resolves each template through a public package path without a file extension, such as `./templates/acme-dashboard`, and fails when that path is missing.

content.label: package.json

items: `integration add` writes this entry when `package.json` has an `exports` map ({@link generic:start-a-template}). Without a map it writes nothing, because creating one would make existing deep imports private. Add the map yourself, then the entry.
Keep the public path without `.tsx`. Only the target file ends in `.tsx`.
Do not point the entry at a barrel file that loses the template default export.

content.text: Add a public path for every package-owned component, helper, icon, or stylesheet that the copied source imports. Keep implementation-only files private.

content.label: Relevant package.json entries

content.text: If a block is also loaded directly as a live `.tsx` preview, add a pattern that keeps the extension, such as `"./templates/*.tsx": "./templates/*.tsx"`. Keep the generated entry too; `integration verify` resolves the template through it.
An export can point to a file that npm leaves out. When `package.json#files` exists, list the integration manifest, the templates directory, and every directory the copied file depends on.

content.label: package.json
content.code:
{
  "files": [
    "astryx.integration.mjs",
    "templates",
    "components",
    "icons",
    "styles",
    "assets/fonts"
  ],
  "sideEffects": ["**/*.css"]
}

items: `integration add` appends the manifest and templates directory when a `files` list already exists. Add the other directories yourself.
If `package.json` sets `sideEffects`, include CSS in it, as above, so bundlers keep side-effect stylesheet imports.
Run `{@pm-only npm "the tarball the registry receives" pack --dry-run}` and read the real file list instead of reasoning from the workspace.

sections.title: Declare what the copied file imports

content.text: A copied file imports from the app, so the app must install every package it imports. Declare the Astryx peers as described in {@link generic:versioning}. For other packages:

rows: Libraries the copied source imports, such as an icon library. List them in `devDependencies` too, so the package itself builds.
Runtime packages used only by package-owned modules, which should travel with the integration
Everything needed to build and test the integration itself

content.text: Use only ranges you test. A package that resolves only because a workspace hoisted it is not declared.

docs.name: extend-or-replace
docs.title: Extend or replace a topic
docs.description: Take over a topic or guide, or merge sections into it.

content.text: Set `replaces` to take over an existing topic, such as Core's `getting-started`. Readers who open the old name get your topic.

content.label: docs/acme-getting-started.doc.mjs

content.text: The docs list shows your topic in place of the old one. Because your topic has its own `name`, the old name keeps resolving to it, so links and agents that learned the old name still land on your topic.
Set `extends` to merge sections into an existing topic instead of owning it. A section replaces the base section it matches, and a section that matches none is added at the end.

content.code:
{@command integration add doc acme-theming --extends theme}
{@command docs theme --index}

content.label: docs/acme-theming.doc.mjs

items: Read the base topic's keys with `--index`, and give a section that replaces one that key as its `id`. A section that replaces one keeps its place. A section without an `id` matches only a base section with exactly its title, or one whose `id` is the key its title makes, so `Integration Themes` is added beside a base `Integration themes` that has no `id`.

Set `before` or `after` to a base section's key to add a new section there instead of at the end. A key that names no section adds it at the end, and `astryx doctor integration validate` lists a note. An older CLI rejects these fields, so declare an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer range that starts at the release that reads them; `astryx integration verify` warns without it.
The topic keeps the base's title and description, and readers open it by the base's name.
Replace the `Overview` placeholder that `integration add` writes, or it is added to the base topic.
Extend a topic to correct or add to it. A copy made with `replaces` stops getting the owner's fixes.

sections.title: Replace or extend a CLI guide

content.text: A guide in the CLI's docs tree has a route rather than a topic name. Set `replaces` or `extends` to that route to change the guide for every app that installs your package: say what differs for your users on the page agents already read.

content.label: docs/acme-quick-start.doc.mjs

items: Your doc stays a flat topic: do not give it a `placement`. Readers open the guide by its route, never by your `name`.
With `replaces`, readers of the route get your doc, under your package. With `extends`, each section you add or replace names your package.
A name that holds no topic or guide, such as a namespace, changes nothing; `astryx doctor integration validate` lists it as a note, with the guides below a namespace.

content.code:
# Every guide route, by namespace
astryx docs authoring --depth all
astryx docs cli --depth all
# The keys to place sections by
astryx docs authoring/quick-start --index

content.text: A topic sets `replaces` or `extends`, never both, and a placed guide sets neither. A topic that uses a Core topic's name with neither is an accidental conflict: apps keep reading the Core topic.

content.code: {@command doctor integration docs}

severity:     [info]
topic:        acme-getting-started
relationship: replaces
coreTopic:    getting-started
message:      Intentional override: "acme-getting-started" replaces the Core topic "getting-started".

severity:     [fail]
topic:        color
relationship: accidental
coreTopic:    color
message:      Accidental conflict: "color" is already a Core topic. Rename it, declare replaces: 'color' to take it over, or declare extends: 'color' to merge sections.

items: An intentional overlap prints as `[info]`. An accidental one fails with exit code 1.
A topic that sets both fails as `invalid_doc`, and so does a placed guide that sets either one.

content.text: In global mode: a doc that extends or replaces a topic from a package installed for the computer applies in folders outside any project; inside a project, only those from packages the project installs apply. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: font-setup
docs.title: Font Setup
docs.description: Font families, custom font loading, geometric font sizes, and semantic font weights.

content.text: Typography is built on a geometric type scale: base size × ratio^step, with 14px and 1.2 as defaults. Every text style is a semantic token that composes font size, weight, and line-height, so components express intent (heading, body, label) rather than raw values.

Two layers work together: raw size tokens (--font-size-xs ... --font-size-5xl) form the geometric scale, and semantic type scale tokens (--text-heading-1-size, --text-body-leading, etc.) reference them by var(). Themes override the entire scale by adjusting base and ratio in defineTheme; all semantic tokens recompute automatically.

Three font roles: body (UI text), heading (titles and headings), and code (monospace). By default, body and heading share the same system font stack; code uses a monospace stack. Custom themes can assign different families per role; heading inherits from body when not explicitly set.
Font family stacks for body, code, and heading text.

rows: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

content.text: Astryx never loads font files. defineTheme and the built CSS only set font-family: naming a webfont (Fraunces, JetBrains Mono, and so on) makes every browser look for it, and quietly fall back when the app has not loaded it. `{@command theme build}` warns when a theme names families that are neither CSS generics nor common system fonts and prints the snippet to add; loading the font is always the app's job.

content.label: Google Fonts: add to your document <head>
content.code:
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com" />
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin />
<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Fraunces:wght@400;600;700&family=JetBrains+Mono&display=swap"
/>

content.label: Self-hosted: one @font-face per family and weight

content.text: Always pair a webfont with a real fallback stack (metric-similar system fonts plus a generic) so text stays readable before the font loads and wherever it never does: defineTheme({typography: {heading: {family: 'Fraunces', fallbacks: 'Georgia, serif'}}}).

Geometric scale: round(base × ratio^step), expressed in rem. The default scale is 14px × 1.2, producing 12 steps from 4xs (6px) to 5xl (42px). Adjusting base and ratio in defineTheme regenerates every size token while preserving proportional relationships.
Geometric type scale: round(14 × 1.2^step). Base is 14px (--font-size-base).

Four semantic weights: normal (400, body/code), medium (500, labels/data), semibold (600, headings/titles), bold (700, strong emphasis). Type scale tokens reference these by var() so themes can remap numeric values.
Font weight values for body, emphasis, and headings.

docs.name: fonts-and-assets
docs.title: Fonts and assets
docs.description: Name the fonts in the theme, then export an optional font stylesheet that `theme add` imports with the built theme.

content.text: A theme names its typefaces in `typography`: `body`, `heading`, and `code`, each with a `family` and `fallbacks`. These set the `--font-family-*` tokens every component reads. Always give real `fallbacks` so text stays readable before the font loads, or if it never does. `heading` inherits `family` and `fallbacks` from `body` when you omit them.
The full type scale and font roles are in {@link generic:author-a-theme}.

Naming a family does not load it. When the theme uses non-system fonts, add `<slug>.fonts.css` beside the built module and production CSS, then export it as `./themes/<slug>.fonts.css`. `theme add` imports that stylesheet with the built theme.

The stylesheet can contain self-hosted `@font-face` rules or import a hosted stylesheet. A hosted `@import` is simple, but it delays loading compared with a preconnected `<link>`; choose that trade-off deliberately. Doctor warns when it cannot prove the loader — a hosted `@import`, or no font stylesheet while the app loads the family itself — but the warning does not fail the app.

items: Load every weight and style the theme uses. Do not let the browser synthesize bold or italic.
Include self-hosted font files and their licenses in the packed package.
Keep CSS and font assets side-effectful so a bundler does not remove the loader.
Run `integration verify`; it fails when an exported font stylesheet cannot resolve, but it does not check the font files the stylesheet names.

content.text: Before publishing, run `integration verify`. Then install the package in a clean app, run `theme add`, apply the generated theme, and open it in a browser. The source, packed exports, and applied result form one chain; check the last step too.

items: Text renders in the named families at every weight and style — the italic face resolves, not a synthesized slant.
Every font request succeeds; nothing silently falls back to a system font.
Color pairs still meet contrast in both light and dark mode.

docs.name: generate-a-palette
docs.title: Generate a palette
docs.description: Turn a few seed colors into full light and dark color ramps, saved in the theme folder.

content.text: A theme needs dozens of related colors — shades of each brand color for backgrounds, borders, text, and states, in both light and dark mode. A palette is that full set of shades. Rather than hand-pick every one, you name a few seed colors and generate the rest, so the shades stay consistent.

You write a short config naming each color family and its seed, then run `theme palette generate`. It expands each seed into a full light and dark ramp — the scale of shades — and writes the result into the theme folder, where your theme tokens point at it (see {@link generic:define-the-theme}). Keep the config and the generated palette together in that folder.
The smallest config is one color family: an `id` to name it and a `seed` color to grow it from. Save it as `themes/ocean/palette.config.json`:

content.code: {"families": [{"id": "ocean", "seed": "#0074e2"}]}

# Print the palette without writing files
{@command theme palette generate themes/ocean/palette.config.json}
# Write the palette and its receipt
astryx theme palette generate themes/ocean/palette.config.json \
  --out themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.ts

[ok] Wrote themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.ts

[ok] Wrote themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.receipt.json

Review and edit the candidate before adopting it as theme-owned palette data.

content.text: The command writes two files. `ocean.palette.ts` is the palette your theme tokens will read: it exports `black`, `white`, and `palette` — a ramp of 21 shades (stops `0` to `100`) for both `light` and `dark`. The `.receipt.json` beside it records the exact seeds and settings, so you can regenerate the same palette later. A second run leaves both files alone unless you pass `--overwrite`.

Add `--preview <file>.html` to also get a web page showing every shade, so you can eyeball the palette in a browser. Write it outside `themes/` so it does not ship in your package. Every option is in {@link command:theme palette generate}, and the config it reads is described in {@link function:generateTonalPalette}.

docs.name: getting-started
docs.title: Getting Started
docs.description: Add the design system to your project and start building.

content.text: Paste this into your AI coding tool and let it handle the setup:

content.label: Set up the design system
content.code: Install @astryxdesign/core, @stylexjs/stylex, @astryxdesign/theme-neutral, and @astryxdesign/cli in this project, then run `{@command init}` to set up agent docs. Read the generated files to learn the conventions.

content.text: Then give it a look. Every app gets a theme whether or not anyone picks one, so it is worth one question at setup rather than revisiting screens later that were built around the wrong look:

content.label: Give it a look
content.code: Ask me what look and feel this app should have. Run `{@command theme list}`, install the closest theme package, and run `theme add <slug>`; use `--package` when owners share a slug. Import `themes` and `defaultThemeSlug` from the generated module once and pass `themes[defaultThemeSlug]` to `<Theme>`. Customize with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`. Use `theme eject` only when I ask for an independent source fork. Default to neutral if I have no preference, and show me the result before moving on.

content.text: Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
Add the core package and its `@stylexjs/stylex` peer dependency, plus a theme and the CLI.

content.label: Terminal
content.code: {@pm install @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @astryxdesign/cli}

content.text: Then run `{@command init}` to install the AI agent cheat sheet (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md). It's non-interactive; no prompts; so it's safe for AI agents, CI, and scripts. Add `--all` for pointers to the theme and page-building workflows.

content.label: Terminal
content.code: {@command init}

content.text: Install the CLI once for your computer too, and the astryx command works in any folder, for you and for any coding agent, even before a project exists. Inside a project, the project's own version still answers, so a global install never changes what your team and CI get. Keep it in the project as well; that is the recommended setup.

content.label: Terminal
content.code: {@pm install @astryxdesign/cli --global}

content.text: Project, global, or both: {@link generic:project-global-or-both}. Everything else about global mode: {@link namespace:global}.

sections.title: Add base CSS and a theme

content.text: Import the reset and base styles in your global CSS. Then run `{@command theme add neutral}`; the generated app module imports the theme’s production CSS and font CSS.

content.label: globals.css
content.code:
@import '@astryxdesign/core/reset.css';
@import '@astryxdesign/core/astryx.css';

content.text: Run `{@command theme list}` to see every theme.

content.label: App root

items: `@astryxdesign/theme-neutral`: muted and minimal; a good starting point
`@astryxdesign/theme-butter`: warm, golden tones with blue accents
`@astryxdesign/theme-chocolate`: rich chocolate and caramel tones
`@astryxdesign/theme-gothic`: dark-only theme with ink and noir influences
`@astryxdesign/theme-matcha`: earthy greens and botanical tones
`@astryxdesign/theme-stone`: warm neutrals inspired by sandstone
`@astryxdesign/theme-y2k`: playful early-2000s pop aesthetic

content.text: These stylesheets are cascade-layered: the reset loads in @layer reset and component styles in @layer astryx-base. If your project has existing global CSS, a legacy reset, or Tailwind, declare the layer order explicitly and assign every stylesheet to a layer deliberately: unlayered styles and later layers both override astryx-base regardless of specificity. Before building screens, read the two cascade layer sections of {@link generic:migration-setup}.
Run {@link generic:use-a-theme} for the full theming guide.
Import each component from its own entry, the path `{@command component <Name>}` prints. This keeps bundles small and makes intent clear.

content.label: app/page.tsx

content.text: Astryx components support various styling solutions, from plain CSS and `className` to Tailwind and CSS-in-JS. See {@link namespace:styling} for the full guide. Astryx also has a deep integration with [StyleX](https://stylexjs.com/), an atomic CSS-in-JS library: create styles with `stylex.create()` and pass them to components with the `xstyle` prop.

content.label: Style overrides

content.text: For a full working project, clone one of the example apps from the repo. These are complete setups with routing, theming, and components wired together.

content.label: Clone and run an example

content.text: The CLI is your reference for components, tokens, templates, and docs. For reliable invocation (especially with AI assistants), add this script to your package.json:

content.label: package.json

content.text: Then discover what's available:

content.label: Terminal
content.code:
{@command component}          # list all components
{@command component Button}   # props, usage, theming for Button
{@command docs}               # list all doc topics
{@command template --list}    # available page templates
{@command docs tokens}        # spacing, color, radius reference

docs.name: global
docs.title: Global mode
docs.summary: Install Astryx once on your computer and use it in any folder. Each project still runs its own version of Astryx, so a global install never changes what a project gets.

blocks.text: Global mode means installing the Astryx CLI once for your computer, so the astryx command works everywhere: in your projects, in an empty folder, and for every coding agent. Inside a project, the project's own version of Astryx answers, so your global install never changes what a project gets.
What you get

items: Docs, components, templates, and search in any folder, before you have a project.
Every coding agent on your computer knows Astryx, through a short guide the CLI keeps where agent tools look.
Each project keeps its own version: in a project, the project's version answers, whichever astryx command you run.

blocks.text: Which version runs

rows: The project's own CLI. In a project that installs only `@astryxdesign/core`, the astryx command you started, with a hint once a day to add the CLI.
Commands for your computer, such as `{@command init --user}`
Your global version, in any folder.

blocks.text: Not sure whether you want a project install, a global one, or both: {@link generic:project-global-or-both}. The details: {@link generic:who-answers}.
Updates
Your global install never upgrades itself or a project. When a newer version is out, a command that succeeds ends with a two-line notice, at most once a day: {@link generic:updates}.
Agents
The CLI keeps a short Astryx guide where agent tools look in your home folder, so an agent working anywhere knows Astryx is there: {@link generic:computer-agent-guide}.
Integrations

Integrations you install next to your global install work outside projects. Inside a project, only the project's own integrations do: {@link generic:computer-integrations}. Building one: {@link generic:global-integrations}.
More

items: Install, and work offline: {@link generic:install-once}.
Monorepos and nested folders: {@link generic:monorepos}.
CI and containers: {@link generic:ci-and-containers}.
Something looks wrong: {@link generic:problems}.
Uninstall and reset: {@link generic:uninstall}.
Every path, setting, JSON field, and error code: {@link generic:reference}.
What each command does outside a project: {@link namespace:commands}.

docs.name: global-integrations
docs.title: Make your integration work globally
docs.description: People can install your integration next to their global Astryx install, where it works in every folder outside a project; inside a project, only the project's own integrations work. A checklist, with the exact commands to try it.

sections.title: First: your peer ranges must include the global CLI's version

content.text: Your `@astryxdesign/core` (and, if you use it, `@astryxdesign/cli`) `peerDependencies` ranges must include the version of the CLI installed globally. If they do not, Astryx skips your package outside projects, and `{@command doctor}` warns and names the range.
Inside a project that does not install your package, `{@command discover}` offers it, with the command that adds it to that project, once your peer range admits the project's release.

items: Installed in an app: it works in that app, as always, whichever `astryx` the person runs, because the app's version of Astryx answers there.

Installed next to the global install (`{@pm install @astryxdesign/cli your-package --global}`), or in the same folder as the CLI by a tool that installs them together: it works in every folder outside a project. People and agents there see its components, templates, docs, themes, codemods, and discover source.

Installed only globally, inside an app that does not install it: it adds nothing there. When it supports the app's version and loads, `{@command discover}` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command.
Installed both ways: the app's copy is the one used in that app. In your own package folder, your working copy is used.

content.text: Astryx loads a global integration with the same loader and checks as an app's, so nothing extra goes in your manifest.

items: Declare the `@astryxdesign/core` (and, if you use it, `@astryxdesign/cli`) `peerDependencies` range your package really supports. Outside a project, Astryx skips your package when that range leaves out the global version, and `{@command doctor}` says why: too narrow, and global users lose it after an upgrade; too wide, and it loads against a Core it may not build with.
Keep imports in your docs and templates to packages an app installs with yours, since outside a project there is no app to check them against.

If you set `cliCommand`, know that outside a project it starts every command Astryx prints, and that two global integrations naming different commands cancel out, falling back to `astryx` ({@link generic:cli-command}). Inside an app, only the app's integrations count.
Try it globally before you publish, with the steps below.

content.text: Pack your package, install it next to a global CLI, and look at it from an empty folder:

items: `{@command discover}` lists your package as installed, with what it adds.
`{@command docs}` lists your topics, and `{@command search <one of your component names>}` finds them.
`{@command doctor}`'s `computer-integrations` check lists your package as used, with no warning.
In an app that does not install it, `{@command discover}` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command, and none of its components or docs show up.

content.text: Remove it again with `{@pm remove your-package --global}`.
How global mode works for the people who install your package: {@link namespace:global}. Their side of global integrations: {@link generic:computer-integrations}.

docs.name: headers-and-footers
docs.title: Headers and footers
docs.description: Pin a header or footer while the body scrolls, so the title and commit actions stay reachable.

content.text: A region can pin a header or footer while its body scrolls. Both are Layout slots, and padding set once on Layout reaches all three, so header, body, and footer share one content line.

items: LayoutHeader in the header slot: the region title and its primary action
Toolbar instead of LayoutHeader when the header carries interactive controls
LayoutFooter in the footer slot: actions that commit the work and must stay reachable
defaultHasDividers on Layout fences both at once, rather than hasDivider per slot

content.label: Pinned header and footer around a scrolling body

content.text: Verify: scroll the body. The header and footer stay put, their dividers run full-bleed, and all three still share one left content line.

docs.name: help
docs.title: Help
docs.summary: Find a CLI message and how to fix it.

docs.name: host-entry
docs.title: Host entry
docs.description: Run the Astryx CLI from your own command-line tool: the inputs `runHostedCli` takes, what it returns, and when the process ends instead.

content.text: A tool that carries the CLI for its own users starts one run per process with `runHostedCli` from `@astryxdesign/cli/host`. The run behaves as the CLI's own command does with the same arguments in the same folder, and the commands it prints start with your tool's command.

rows: The command-line arguments, without the command name.
The folder the run works in. It must exist.
The command your users type, such as `acme astryx`: a non-blank single line of at most 120 characters, with no surrounding spaces.
Why you did not run the project's own CLI, such as `untrusted`: a non-blank single line of at most 120 characters. That CLI then never runs.

Your package sets, in order of preference: folders whose `node_modules` each hold a CLI, the Core of the same release, and integrations. A run never installs a release; it takes the release a project needs from the first set that holds it.
Integrations you approve for use outside a project, by package name.
Your own discover sources. `{@command discover}` reports each as the host's.

items: It resolves with `{status, packages}`: the exit status the CLI's own command would exit with, and each package the run used, with its version and whether it came from the project or a package set.
When another release answers from one of your package sets through its own host entry, that entry runs in the same process with the same inputs, and the call resolves with its result.
It rejects with a `TypeError`, before anything runs, for an unknown option or an invalid value, and with an `Error` when a run already started in the process. Start each run in a new process.

content.text: Like the CLI's own command, a run ends the process with its exit status, and the call never resolves, when it:

items: prints help or the version (`--help`, `-h`, `help`, `--version`, `-V`, `--version --json`);
rejects the command line, such as an unknown command or option;
reports an error it stops on, including every error in `--json` mode;
meets an unexpected error;
hands the run to another CLI's own command: the project's CLI when you pass no `declinedProjectCli`, or a package set whose CLI has no host entry.

docs.name: i18n-library-integration
docs.title: Library Integration
docs.description: Override astryx's default text, coexist with react-intl / i18next / next-intl / LinguiJS, or use astryx as your i18n library.

content.text: Use `overrides` to change individual strings without shipping a full catalog. Overrides are keyed by locale and merged on top of the built-in and user-supplied catalogs.

content.label: Change one string in English
content.code:
<InternationalizationProvider
  locale="en"
  overrides={{en: {'@astryx.pagination.next': 'Next →'}}}
>
  <App />
</InternationalizationProvider>

content.text: Overrides win over both bundled English and any `messages` catalog for the same key. Use them for brand voice tweaks or one-off wording changes.

sections.title: Using astryx with your own i18n library

content.text: Astryx components render astryx strings through astryx's provider. Consumer components render consumer strings through whatever i18n library you already use: react-intl, i18next, next-intl, LinguiJS, and so on. The two systems coexist and read from the same source of truth for the active locale.

content.label: Astryx + react-intl side by side

content.text: Keep the two providers in sync on locale, and each library owns its own catalog. Astryx never sees your app strings, and your i18n library never sees astryx internals. Runtime locale swap works the same way: re-render both providers with a new `locale` prop and the whole tree updates live.

Single-catalog usage (where an external i18n runtime like react-intl or i18next resolves both your app strings AND astryx's strings through one provider) is on the roadmap via a `Translator` adapter. Track [meta/astryx#4029](https://github.com/meta/astryx/issues/4029). For now, run the two providers side by side as shown above.

sections.title: Using astryx as your i18n library

content.text: For production apps with substantial localization needs, we recommend a dedicated i18n library such as react-intl, i18next, next-intl, or LinguiJS. If your app is small or you do not want another runtime, you can resolve your own strings through astryx too. Keep app keys in a separate namespace from `@astryx.*`, and include your own `en` catalog because astryx's built-in English fallback only contains astryx component strings.

content.label: Translate app strings with astryx

content.text: `Catalog` types the rich `{defaultMessage, description?}` authoring shape. `RuntimeCatalog` types the generated key-to-message string map. `ProviderMessagesByLocale` accepts either shape for the provider, while `MessagesByLocale` keeps the original rich-only context shape.

docs.name: i18n-quick-start
docs.title: Quick Start
docs.description: Wrap your app in InternationalizationProvider, load a locale catalog, and swap languages at runtime.

content.text: Internationalization ships with `@astryxdesign/core`. There is nothing to install. Wrap your app in `<InternationalizationProvider>` and set the active `locale`; astryx components pick up localized strings from that provider.

content.label: Wrap your app

content.text: The provider always has the built-in English catalog. Pass additional catalogs through `messages` when you enable another locale.

content.label: Load an astryx locale catalog

content.text: Astryx ships English and first-party translations for supported locales. Compact runtime modules from `@astryxdesign/core/locales/*.generated.js` contain only the messages apps need; the existing `@astryxdesign/core/locales/*.json` files retain translator context. Until a locale is available, apps can pass a local catalog in either shape. Missing keys fall back through the locale chain to English (for example, `pt-BR` walks to `pt`, then to shipped `en`).
Locale catalogs only affect astryx strings. Your app can continue using its own i18n system for product copy.
Re-render `<InternationalizationProvider>` with a new `locale` prop and every astryx string updates live. No reload, no separate API call.

content.label: Toggle between locales

content.text: Persisting the user's choice (localStorage, cookie, URL segment, account setting) is up to the consumer. Astryx reads whatever `locale` you pass in.

docs.name: i18n-rtl-and-testing
docs.title: RTL & Testing
docs.description: Text direction (RTL), pseudo-locale testing, and contributor guidance for developers and translators.

content.text: Astryx tracks text direction (`'ltr'` or `'rtl'`) alongside the locale. By default the direction is derived from the `locale` you pass to `<InternationalizationProvider>` via [`Intl.Locale.getTextInfo()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Locale/getTextInfo), so RTL locales such as Arabic (`ar`), Hebrew (`he`), Farsi (`fa`), and Urdu (`ur`) resolve to `'rtl'` automatically.

You don't wire anything per component. Once the direction is set, astryx components mirror on their own: layout and spacing flip via CSS logical properties, directional icons (chevrons, carets) flip in place, keyboard arrow keys swap left/right, and overlays position on the correct side. Set the direction once and the whole component tree follows.

content.label: Direction derived from locale

content.text: Pass the optional `dir` prop to force a direction. This overrides the locale-derived default; useful for RTL layout testing under an English catalog, or to skip derivation when you already know the direction.

content.label: Explicit direction override

content.text: There's one more step: tell the browser about the direction too. Add a `dir` attribute to your page; usually on the `<html>` tag. This is what makes text align to the correct side, punctuation and mixed-language text flow correctly, and layouts mirror. The provider handles astryx components; the `dir` attribute handles everything else on the page.

Astryx doesn't set `dir` for you; you set it, alongside the same direction you pass to the provider. If your app is server-rendered (like Next.js), the `getLocaleDirection()` helper computes the direction from a locale so you can set it while the page renders:

content.label: Set <html dir> in a Next.js root layout

content.text: In a plain client app, set the same attribute on `<html>` whenever the locale changes. (`getLocaleDirection()` safely returns `'ltr'` for anything it doesn't recognize, so you can call it with any locale string.)

To make just one part of a left-to-right page right-to-left; say an Arabic quote or a comment thread; wrap that part in its own `<InternationalizationProvider dir="rtl">` and add `dir="rtl"` to the element around it. Pop-up overlays; menus, dialogs, popovers, tooltips; opened from inside that region mirror too: they position with logical CSS anchor placement, so they land on the correct side and inherit the region's direction automatically.

Astryx generates a `pseudo` locale that wraps every string in `⟦…⟧` and replaces letters with accented look-alikes. Turn it on in development to catch hardcoded astryx strings and layout issues caused by longer text.

content.label: Turn on pseudo-localization

content.text: Developers
Astryx component authors read strings with `useTranslator()` rather than hardcoding user-facing text.

content.label: Read an astryx string

content.text: Astryx's own strings live in `packages/core/locales/en.json`. New user-facing strings must go through `useTranslator`; this is enforced by the `@astryx/no-hardcoded-i18n-string` ESLint rule. See the AI contribution guide for the alias-and-resolve pattern used when adding new keys.
When you author a component that needs to respond to direction, resolve it from the DOM, not from a render-time JavaScript read, and reach for the lightest tool that works. In priority order:
1. CSS logical properties first

Use `insetInlineStart`, `paddingInlineEnd`, `marginInline`, and friends instead of physical `left`/`right`. Most mirroring needs nothing more; the browser flips it from the ambient `dir`. The `@astryx/no-physical-properties` ESLint rule enforces this.
2. Directional icons: mirror with CSS, not a name-swap

Render one fixed glyph and wrap it in the shared `rtlStyles.mirror` (a `scaleX(-1)` that only applies under `[dir="rtl"]`). It flips from the ancestor `dir` through the cascade, so it works on the server with no hydration flash. Do not pick `chevronLeft` vs `chevronRight` in JS. This is how Pagination, Calendar, and Carousel handle their chevrons.

content.label: Mirror a directional icon with CSS

content.text: 3. Behavioral logic: read the DOM lazily, on the event

For things CSS can't express; keyboard arrow-key mapping, drag/scroll math; read direction at interaction time with `isRtlElement(el)` (a `getComputedStyle().direction` check), never during render. The focus primitives (`useListFocus`, `useGridFocus`, `useTreeFocus`) already auto-detect direction from their container, so arrow keys flip for free; don't pass a direction flag to them.
4. useDirection() context: the last resort

Reach for it only when you genuinely need the direction value during render and none of the above fit. It's SSR-safe and returns `'ltr'` outside a provider (matching `useTranslator`'s silent fallback), but it's the one path that can mismatch on hydration if the provider's `direction` disagrees with `<html dir>`; so prefer the options above, which resolve purely from the DOM. As of the CSS-mirror migration, no astryx component reads direction from context at render time.
Translators

Crowdin is the preferred way to contribute; [join a language](https://crowdin.com/project/astryx), translate strings in the web UI, and your work syncs back to the repo without opening a PR. Direct PRs against `packages/core/locales/*.json` also work if you prefer that flow.

docs.name: icon-definitions
docs.title: Icon definitions
docs.summary: Every icon definition: what an icon stands for, and the shared name icon sets map their icons to.

blocks.text: An icon definition is one thing an icon stands for, such as `close` or `delete`. Every icon set registers its icons against definitions in its data file's `map`, and templates are written against definitions, so a project that switches icon sets gets the same definition from the new set. Built-in definitions, marked [built-in], are the shared names Core renders (the semantic icon names in `astryx docs icons`); every set maps them, and `integration check` fails until it does. The others are optional: map each one your library draws. `map` keys a definition by its camelCase name, shown after the id (`eyeSlash`); `experimental icon map` and `--pairs` take either spelling. A set may add its own definitions; in a project that sets `experimental.iconSet`, they are listed here with the package that ships them. `astryx experimental icon <definition>` finds the icon each installed set draws for it. Icon definitions are experimental: they may change or be removed in a patch release.

docs.name: icon-sets
docs.title: Icon sets
docs.description: Ship an icon set: register each icon against an icon definition, so apps find icons by meaning and templates use your icons.

content.text: Icon sets are experimental: the `astryx experimental icon` commands, the `experimental.iconSet` key in astryx.config, the `experimental.iconSets` key in an integration manifest, the data file, icon definitions, and the output and JSON of all of them can change, or go away, in any patch release without a deprecation period. A project that does not set `experimental.iconSet` sees no change in any stable command, apart from: the marked `experimental` group in help and in `astryx manifest` (its command, and its `responseTypes` and `jsonSupported` entries); the marked experimental entries in the CLI reference listings; and a search for "experimental", which also finds the stable `stability` field of the field reference. Templates, discover, and doctor answer as they do with no icon set installed. With a package that ships icon sets installed and no opt-in, the warnings an older CLI gives about the manifest key `experimental` (in `astryx doctor` and `astryx doctor integration validate <package>`, and the one-line nudge other commands print to stderr) are gone. `astryx search` never returns icons or these docs; to find an icon by meaning, use `astryx experimental icon <words>`.

Astryx keeps a list of icon definitions: one file per meaning, like `close` or `delete` (`astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-definitions`). An icon set registers which of its icons draws each definition, in the `map` of its data file; one icon may draw several definitions (`file` and `document` can both be your `document` icon). Templates say which definition each of their icons draws, so a project that uses your set gets your icon for every definition you map. Every set maps the built-in definitions, the names Core renders itself.
The CLI knows no icon library. You, or your agent, pick each icon from the library you wrap; the commands below verify it, write the files, and check the set.

content.code: astryx experimental icon new-set outline

content.text: `outline.doc.mjs` is the descriptor: name, display name and description (`--display-name`, `--description`), and `license`, the SPDX license of the artwork (it starts as your package's own). `outline.icons.json` starts with no icons and an empty `map`; its `module` is your package name. `outline.generated.js` is the set's generated module, with its declaration file `outline.generated.d.ts`: the CLI writes both, and every icon and the theme map are exports of it. Every field is in {@link schema:icon-set-doc} and {@link schema:icon-set-data}.

The set's icons import from your package by name, so your package's entry must re-export the generated module. The command writes only the set's own files: your entry, `exports`, `main`, `types`, `files`, peers, and scripts are yours, and the receipt names each change to make as text to copy. For an entry file in the package (and the declaration file package.json names) that is the line `export * from './icon-sets/outline/outline.generated.js';`, relative to it; for a package with no entry, `index.js` and `index.d.ts` with that line and the package.json `main`, `types`, and `exports` that name them; for a built or CommonJS entry, the line to add to the source it is built from. `integration check` names the same change until you make it, and the receipt also names the peers and the `typecheck` script to add. `integration check --strict` type-checks the set's doc files with your package's TypeScript; the receipt says when it is missing (`npm install -D typescript@6`).

sections.title: Add icons one at a time

content.text: Pick an icon from the library and ask which definitions fit it. Nothing is written yet. To read every icon a set already has, one line each with its words and the definitions it draws, run `astryx experimental icon --set <set> --all-icons`; `astryx experimental icon <set>/<id>` reads one, or says the id does not exist:

content.code: astryx experimental icon add Bin --from @acme/glyph-library

content.text: Each row is an Astryx definition (or one your set declares) with the exact command that adds the icon for it. Run one:

content.code: astryx experimental icon add Bin --from @acme/glyph-library --definition delete

content.text: The CLI reads the library's exports without running them and refuses a name the module does not export, suggesting close names. It adds the icon as `BinIcon` (id `bin`, words from its name), writes `export {Bin as BinIcon} from '@acme/glyph-library';` to the set's generated module, and sets `map.delete = "bin"`. Running it again changes nothing. Do not copy the definition's words into the icon: `astryx experimental icon` matches an icon by its own words and by the name and words of every definition it is mapped to.
When no Astryx definition fits, add your own in the same command. It needs no pull request:

content.code: astryx experimental icon add Dice5 --from @acme/glyph-library --new-definition random --description 'Pick something at random.' --words dice,shuffle,chance

content.text: `experimental icon map <definition> <icon>` points a definition at an icon the set already has (a definition is named in camelCase, `eyeSlash`, or by the kebab id the definitions list shows, `eye-slash`; an icon by its id, its export name in any case, or another name its library exports it as, such as `trash-2`, never by one word of its id), `experimental icon map --pairs close=x-mark,search=magnifying-glass` writes many entries at once (checked together, all or none; an entry the map already has is replaced, and the receipt shows what it was), and `--remove` drops an entry. `experimental icon new-definition <name> --description ... --words ... --icon <id>` adds your own definition for an icon you already have. `experimental icon --definitions` lists every Astryx definition, built in or not, with its words (`--json` for a script).

content.code: astryx experimental icon new-set outline --from @acme/glyph-library

content.text: Every component the library exports becomes an icon (an alias of one component is recorded once), named `<Name>Icon`, with an id from its name (`Squares2X2Icon` is `squares-2x2`: a dimension stays one word). `map` is filled only where a definition's name is an icon's id (`delete` → icon `delete`), and the receipt lists those entries under Mapped by name: a library can draw another meaning under the same name (one library's `delete` is a backspace key), so check each. An icon whose id is only one of a definition's words (`trash` for `delete`) may mean something else in this library, so the receipt lists it under Suggestions, with the `experimental icon map <definition> <icon>` command for each, and writes nothing for it: check the meaning, then run the ones that fit. Run it again after a library release to refresh the icons that library supplies; `map` entries whose icon still exists are kept, and the receipt names any icon the library dropped, any icon `--exclude` left out, and the `map` entries each took with it. Icons you added from your own files or another library are left as they are. An icon you already have is known by the library export it re-exports, so it keeps its export name exactly, its `map` entries, variants, and words, even when a newer CLI spells its id differently or your `--exclude` lets a library prefix come off new ids; the receipt lists each changed id under `renamed`. A refresh with `--dry-run` writes nothing and prints the Mapped by name and Suggestions lists again; `--display-name` and `--description` on a refresh rewrite the descriptor. Variants added with `add --variant … --all` are kept too; run that `add` again to pick up icons the release added. `experimental icon --list` shows how many definitions the set maps.

With a package or package subpath, it also records the installed library and version as the data file's `source`, so `integration check` warns when your dependency moves to another version; copies the library's LICENSE (and NOTICE) files into the set directory; and sets the descriptor's `license` to the library's. A set you started without `--from` gets the same the first time a refresh records its source, unless you already changed `license`: a `license` you set is kept (the receipt names the library's), and every later refresh keeps it too. Your package.json `license` is never changed. Edit `license` when the artwork's license differs from the library's package license.
A library with a module per style supplies variants. Declare them when you create the set, then add a variant for every icon in one run:

content.code:
astryx experimental icon new-set heroicons --from @heroicons/react/24/outline --variants outline,solid --default-variant outline --description 'Heroicons, outline and solid.'
astryx experimental icon add --variant solid --from @heroicons/react/24/solid --all

content.text: A library that redraws its artwork for small sizes (Heroicons' 20px mini and 16px micro) ships each of those as its own set in its own package (their export names match the 24px ones), not as variants: a variant's size comes from CSS. `--variants` lists the variants; `--default-variant` names the one each icon's own export draws (the first variant when omitted). `--all` adds the variant for every icon whose id an export of `--from` has (`TrashIcon` in the solid module becomes `TrashSolidIcon`, the solid variant of `trash`), and the receipt lists the icons the module has no export for. Running it again changes nothing.

A library whose icons are data (objects or SVG strings) has no components to find: create the set, declare an `adapter` in its data file (see library shapes), and run the command again; every data export then becomes an icon through the adapter. When every icon export shares a leading word, such as `feather` in `featherEye` and `featherSun`, ids and export names leave it out: `featherEye` becomes id `eye`, exported as `EyeIcon`. The prefix is read over icon-like exports only: SCREAMING_CASE constants (`README`, `VERSION`), number and boolean exports, and, next to components or icon objects, plain strings are never icons. Components named `…Provider` or `…Context` are never icons either. Leave out any other export that is not an icon with `--exclude meta,version`: the data file keeps the list in `exclude`, so a refresh leaves them out too. When a library exports one icon under several names (`Trash2` and `Trash`), the icon is recorded once and its other names become words, so `experimental icon trash-2` finds it and `experimental icon map delete trash-2` maps it. `experimental icon add` reads the prefix the same way, and reuses the icon an export already has, so its commands need no `--id`.
Every icon is a named export of your package's public entry, so apps, templates, and theme maps all import components from one place:

items: The data file's `module` is your package name or one of its package.json `exports` subpaths, never a file path. `integration check` fails otherwise.
A variant is a named look the set supplies (for example outline or solid); size comes from CSS. List the names in `variants` in the data file and the one each icon's own export draws in `default`.
Each export is named `<Name>Icon`, and a variant `<Name><Variant>Icon`, such as `TrashSolidIcon`. `experimental icon add` names them that way; `integration check` warns on another name.
Each export is a React component: a function, a class, `forwardRef` or `memo`, or what your adapter returns. `integration check` fails on a plain object or string.

It accepts SVG props (`className`, `style`, `aria-*`, `width`, `height`), draws with `currentColor`, and fills its box (`1em` or `100%`), so `<Icon icon={TrashIcon} size="sm" />` sizes and colors it like a built-in icon. The CLI cannot check this statically; the test below can.

content.text: `experimental icon add` writes the set's generated module (`generated` in the data file) and its declaration file, which re-exports each component's own types and types each adapted icon as `ComponentType<SVGProps<SVGSVGElement>>`. Add this line to your package's entry and its types; `experimental icon new-set` names the exact line and file in its receipt (see add an icon set):

content.code: export * from './icon-sets/outline/outline.generated.js';

content.text: An optional render test you can copy. Save it inside your package directory and run it there, since it imports your package by name through its `exports`, and install `react-dom` first (`npm install -D react-dom`). A library may add its own classes beside yours, so it checks the class list. A library that sets `width` and `height` attributes (24, say) still fills its box: CSS sizing, such as the `Icon` component's, overrides SVG size attributes.
`--from` is any import specifier: a package, a package subpath, or a `./` path inside your package. Use the row that matches the library:

rows: `experimental icon add --variant solid --from @acme/glyph-library/solid --all` for every icon at once, or `experimental icon add Bin --from @acme/glyph-library/solid --id bin --variant solid` for one (the set must declare the variant: `new-set --variants`)
One file per icon, default export
Declare an `adapter`, then `experimental icon add Rocket --from @acme/glyph-data --definition rocket`
Declare an `adapter` that renders them, then `experimental icon add` as above

`experimental icon add Rocket --from ./src/icons/rocket.js --definition rocket`, and `--id rocket --variant solid` for its other looks. The file exports a component named as written (no library prefix is taken off), with a declaration file beside it (`rocket.d.ts`) or written in TypeScript, since the set's types re-export its own; when package.json lists `files` and none covers it, the receipt names the `files` array that publishes its folder.

content.text: An export that is not a component goes through your adapter: a function in your package that turns it into one. Declare it in the data file, `"adapter": {"module": "./src/adapt.js", "export": "adapt"}`, and `experimental icon add` writes `export const RocketIcon = adaptIcon(RocketIconSource);`:

The generated module also exports `themeIcons`: one entry per built-in definition in `map`, each an element of your own icon, hidden from assistive technology and sized `1em`. The CLI rewrites it on every `experimental icon add` and `experimental icon map`, so you never write it by hand, and `integration check` proves it matches `map`. A theme uses it in one line:

`astryx integration check` reads the set without running your icons. An unmapped built-in definition is an error that names the definition's description and words and the `experimental icon map <definition> <icon id>` command that fixes it, so you or your agent can pick the icon. It names a search of your set (`experimental icon <word> --set <set>`) only when that search finds icons, and suggests one icon: the first of the suggestions `experimental icon new-set` gives for that definition. It never matches part of a word, and never writes a suggestion. Its icon-set codes:

items: `invalid_icon_set` (error): the descriptor, data file, or a definition file is invalid, for example a repeated `id`, an icon with no words, or a `map` key that is neither an Astryx definition nor one in your `definitions` folder. The set is withdrawn: apps do not see it.
`icon_builtin_definition_missing` (error): a built-in definition is not in `map`.
`icon_definition_unused` (warning): a definition you declared is not in `map`.
