`icon_definition_shadowed` (warning): a definition you declared now exists in Astryx; map to Astryx's and remove yours.
`icon_module_not_public` (error), `icon_export_name` (warning), `icon_not_component` (error): the export contract above.
`icon_export_missing` (error): an export, the generated module, or the adapter does not exist.
`icon_module_invalid` (error): the set's module, a file it re-exports, or the generated module does not parse; reported once, instead of a missing export per icon.
`icon_generated_types_mismatch` (error): the generated module's declaration file is missing or does not match it.
`icon_theme_map_mismatch` (error): the theme map disagrees with the built-in entries of `map`.
`icon_source_version_drift` and `icon_license_notice_missing` (warnings): the data names another library version than the package depends on, or a set with an upstream ships no license notice.

content.text: The other Astryx definitions your set leaves unmapped are not issues: a library need not draw every definition. They are listed under "Unmapped icon definitions (optional)", and in the JSON as the validate result's `iconSets`: for each set, `unmappedDefinitions` (each `{name, description, words}`) and `suggestions` (each `{definition, icon}`, for any unmapped definition one of your icons fits). They are never counted and never fail a check.

An export fails only when the reader proves it absent; what it cannot judge it does not fail either. An icon export whose module is an `exports` target you have not built yet; an icon or adapter export it cannot prove either way (behind a re-export it cannot follow, bound to a default or namespace import, or imported from a package that is not installed); and a theme map or theme-map entry it cannot read are listed under "Not checked", and in the JSON as each set's `unchecked` (each `{icon}`, `{adapter}`, or `{entry}`, with its `reason`). Build the package, install the package it imports from, export the icon by name, or write the entry as a binding or element to have it checked. An export your built module lacks is still an error.

Errors fail the check. Warnings fail only with `--strict`. A set that maps every built-in definition and every definition it declares passes `--strict`, which integrations run in their build ({@link generic:checks}). The flow, start to finish: `experimental icon new-set` → `npm install -D typescript@6` when the receipt asks → `integration check` → `experimental icon add` (or `experimental icon map`) for each definition it lists → `integration check` passes.

items: Run `astryx integration verify` yourself before publishing. Do not put it in `prepublishOnly`: under `npm publish --dry-run` its own `npm pack` becomes a dry run too, and it checks nothing.

Declare `@astryxdesign/cli` as an optional peer (`peerDependenciesMeta`). A required peer an app cannot satisfy makes npm remove the app's CLI without a word. Icon sets are experimental, so no version range promises them, and the format may change in a patch release. A CLI reads a set only when it knows every key the set's data file uses: a key it does not know withdraws the set, naming the key. `exclude` is read only by a CLI whose data-file reference lists it ({@link schema:icon-set-data}); a set without `exclude` is read by every CLI that has `astryx experimental icon`. A CLI without it reads `experimental` as a manifest key it does not know: `astryx doctor` there warns that your package was published against a newer Astryx CLI, other commands print a one-line nudge to run it, and your icons, icon definitions, and template icon mapping do not appear ({@link generic:versioning}).

Every built-in definition needs an icon, because Core renders it. When your library has no icon with that exact meaning, map the closest one, or add your own artwork as a component file in your package (`experimental icon add <Name> --from ./src/icons/<name>.js --definition <definition>`; a ./ path is named as written). Artwork you draw is yours: note its license beside the library's, for example in a NOTICE file in the set directory.
The generated declaration file imports React types, so declare `@types/react` as an optional peer for TypeScript users.

Keep the wrapped library in `dependencies`: your generated module re-exports its components, so apps get it with your package, and `integration check` compares its range with the version the data file records.
`integration check --strict` type-checks the set's doc files; it does not type-check the generated declaration file against React's types. Run `tsc` with `@types/react` installed to check those.

Your package needs `react` (the theme map and adapter use it) as a peer, as Core does. The `experimental icon new-set` receipt names the peers your package.json does not declare yet, as the JSON to add: `react` (`>=18`), and `@types/react` and `@astryxdesign/cli` (from the release that wrote the set) as optional peers; and the `typecheck` script (`astryx integration check --strict`) when there is none.

sections.title: Share a definition with every set

content.text: Your own definitions need no change to Astryx. To share one with every set, open a pull request that copies its file into the CLI's icon definitions folder, with a description and words. Its name must not clash with another definition.

content.code:
astryx experimental icon delete              # ranked matches with import lines
astryx experimental icon outline/bin         # one icon and every variant
astryx experimental icon --list              # installed sets and their definition coverage
astryx experimental icon use outline         # make it the project's icon set

content.text: A template declares, in its descriptor's `icons`, the definition each imported icon draws (`{TrashIcon: 'delete'}`). Once the project sets `experimental.iconSet` in astryx.config (`experimental icon use` writes it), each declared icon becomes the set's icon for that definition. An icon the set does not map keeps its original import, and the copy reports every icon as mapped or kept. Nothing is guessed from names. A mapped icon loses its library's sizing props (`size`, `strokeWidth`, `absoluteStrokeWidth`), since a set's icons take their size from CSS; the report names them as `dropped`. Comments on a rewritten import line are kept.

Each `icons` key is the name the template imports from its module, not a local alias. When a template imports the same name from two modules, such as `TrashIcon` from a library's outline and solid modules, one key covers both: both draw the same definition. Each then becomes the project set's variant of the same name when its module belongs to an installed set that declares the variant (so solid stays solid), else the set's default.

Every place the CLI reads or reports icon sets, all experimental. Outside `astryx experimental icon`, each appears only in a project that sets `experimental.iconSet`; `astryx search` never returns icons:

rows: The project's icon set, by set name or as `<package>/<set>`, and the opt-in: templates, discover, and doctor read icon sets only when it is set. `astryx experimental icon` ranks its icons first, and without it treats the only installed set as the project's. `astryx experimental icon use` writes it.
The folder that holds the package's icon sets, relative to package.json. `astryx experimental icon new-set` declares it.

The icon definition each imported icon draws (`{TrashIcon: 'delete'}`): a named import by the name it imports, a default import by its local name. `astryx template`, shown or copied, then writes the set's icons and reports `icons` (status, set, mapped, kept): every key is mapped, or kept with why (no match, a namespace or type-only import, a re-export, an Astryx or project-set import, or no import at all). `integration check` notes a key the template's source never imports (`template_icon_not_imported`), never failing.
A package's sets (`iconSets`) and, for `@scope/name/<set>`, the set's display name, license, icon count, and definitions; `--type icon-set` keeps only sets.

In an app, the `icon-sets` check: fails when `experimental.iconSet` names a set that is not installed or was withdrawn (an invalid set, or one whose module does not resolve), saying why, and warns when two packages ship a set by that name or a set was withdrawn. In your icon-set package, check with `astryx integration check` instead: plain `doctor` diagnoses an app.

`icon.search`, `icon.detail`, `icon.list`, `icon.setIcons`, `icon.definitions`, `icon.use`, `icon.map`, `icon.mapMany`, `icon.add`, `icon.addVariants`, `icon.definitionMatches`, `icon.newSet`, and `icon.newDefinition`, from the matching `astryx experimental icon` command.

docs.name: icons
docs.title: Icons
docs.description: Semantic icon names available in the design system. These adapt to the active theme's icon registry.

content.text: Components that accept an icon prop use IconType: either a semantic name string or a direct SVG component. The semantic names below are resolved through the global icon registry.

rows: Jump to first, skip to start
Jump to last, skip to end

content.text: For icons not in the semantic list, pass an SVG component directly. Any ComponentType<SVGProps<SVGSVGElement>> works; Icon applies size and color styling automatically.

content.label: Using custom SVG components

content.text: Themes can replace the default SVGs for any semantic name with the `icons` field in `defineTheme()`. This lets you swap the icon set (e.g. heroicons → lucide) without touching component code, and keeps lookup scoped to the active theme instead of mutating global defaults.

content.label: Theme-scoped icons

content.text: An entry can also be a function of the request, so the theme maps Icon's size to its icon library's own props or artwork. `Icon` calls it with `{size, variant}`, where `size` is the size it renders at (`xsm`, `sm`, `md`, or `lg`: an explicit `size`, else the owning component's default, else `md`). Reads that return one node — `getIcon()`, `useIcon()`, `getIconRegistry()`, and the theme's `icons` field — call it with `{size: 'md'}`. The same entry shape works in `registerIcons()`.

content.label: A size-aware icon entry

content.text: Keep the function pure and synchronous: it computes its result from the request only, with no hooks, DOM or SVG measurement, browser globals, network access, mutable module state, or side effects. Its result is final. Returning `null` draws no glyph instead of falling back to a registered or built-in icon, while a `null` or `undefined` node entry still falls back. A child theme that sets an entry for a key replaces the inherited entry for that key.

A theme lists the icon variant names it supports once, with `iconVariants` in `defineTheme()`. The list belongs to the whole theme, never to one icon, and Astryx defines no names of its own. Inside `defineTheme`, an entry function receives `variant` typed as the listed names, or `undefined`, so a misspelled name is a type error. An entry that receives `undefined` draws its normal artwork.

content.label: Listing variants and mapping them to artwork

content.text: A theme that `extends` another inherits its list unless it sets its own; a list it sets replaces the inherited one instead of merging with it.

Request a variant with `Icon`'s `variant` prop. The entry receives it only when the active theme lists it; an entry the theme inherited also needs the theme that defined it to list it. Otherwise the entry receives `undefined` and draws its normal artwork, so an unlisted variant never breaks rendering. A `registerIcons()` entry receives the variants the active theme lists, and a node entry draws the same node for every variant. An icon component passed directly to `Icon` never receives `variant`, and `variant` is never written to the DOM: it selects artwork, so there is no theming selector for it.

content.label: Requesting a variant
content.code:
<Icon icon="info" variant="filled" />  // brandTheme: the filled artwork
<Icon icon="info" />                    // the normal artwork

content.text: An application declares the variant names it uses by augmenting `IconVariantMap` from `@astryxdesign/core/Icon`. `IconVariant` is those names, and an entry passed to `registerIcons()` receives `variant` typed as `IconVariant`. `astryx theme build` writes this augmentation for a built theme's list.

content.label: Declaring the variant names an application uses

content.text: A glyph that belongs to one component or library gets a namespaced key (`numberInput:stepperDown`, `richtext:bold`) instead of a new semantic name. It resolves through the same registry and a theme overrides it the same way, but the shared IconName list stays reserved for glyphs the whole system uses, so adding one does not make every downstream icon registry grow a key.

content.label: Owning and theming a namespaced icon

content.text: Outside core, pass a fallback to `getExtendedIcon(key, fallback)` so the glyph renders with no theme.

docs.name: illustrations
docs.title: Illustrations
docs.description: Illustration guidelines for empty states, onboarding flows, and feature highlights.

content.text: Consistent illustration usage reinforces brand identity and helps users understand context at a glance. Use illustrations in these contexts:

rows: No data, first-time experience, search with no results
Welcome screens, feature introduction, setup wizards
Permission denied, not found, service unavailable

items: Keep illustrations consistent in style across the product.
Use simple, flat illustrations that work in both light and dark mode.
Size illustrations proportionally to the container, typically 120–240px.
Place illustrations centered with supporting text below.
Mix illustration styles from different sources.
Use illustrations as decoration without purpose.

content.text: For an empty state, pass the illustration to the `icon` slot of `EmptyState`, which centers it above the title and description. Typical illustration sizes range from 120px for inline empty states to 240px for full-page onboarding screens. Always pair the illustration with a title and a description that says what to do next.

content.label: Empty state with illustration
content.code: } title="No results found" description="Try adjusting your search or filters." />

docs.name: install-once
docs.title: Install Astryx globally
docs.description: Install the Astryx CLI once for your computer with npm, pnpm, Yarn, Bun, or Volta, and what happens when you are offline.

content.text: Install the CLI package with your package manager. One astryx command then works in every folder.

content.code:
{@pm install @astryxdesign/cli --global}
# with Volta: volta install @astryxdesign/cli

content.text: Keep the CLI installed in each project too: that pins its version for teammates and CI ({@link generic:project-global-or-both}). Inside a project, whichever astryx command you type, the project's version answers. Outside a project, your global install answers with its own version, and a version you name, such as `{@pm dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.0}`, answers as exactly that version.
If `npm i -g` fails with `EACCES`, do not use `sudo`. Give npm a global folder you own, then add its `bin` folder to your PATH, or use a Node version manager such as nvm, fnm, or Volta:
Astryx's update notice then names that folder in its upgrade command.

When a project's own CLI is installed but cannot start, Astryx runs the CLI version equal to the project's Core instead, installing it once into a cache in your home folder and reusing it. It uses npm for that, so your npm registry, proxy, and offline settings apply. Deleting the cache is safe: versions come back when a project needs them. Where it lives: {@link generic:reference}.

Your global install answers offline in a project with only Core, and so does any project that installs its own CLI. Outside a project, commands that read components, such as `{@command component Button}`, need your global version's Core: after any command you run online, your global install downloads it once into the cache in the background, so they work offline from then on (not in CI, where nothing downloads by itself: {@link generic:ci-and-containers}; and not on Windows, where the first component command downloads it). Only a project whose own CLI cannot start needs a version installed or cached; when it is neither and cannot be fetched, your global install answers with a one-line warning, and Astryx waits 2 minutes before trying to download it again (10 minutes after a second failure in a row). {@link generic:problems} has the exact message.
This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works. Next: {@link generic:who-answers}.

docs.name: is-my-code-good
docs.title: Is my Astryx code good?
docs.description: Check whether a product surface fits its app and uses Astryx well, require evidence for every claim, and improve it with a repeatable agent review.

content.text: Do not judge a file or surface in isolation. First learn the app context that makes a pattern correct, inconsistent, or incomplete.

items: Name what the app is for, who uses it, and the task this surface helps them complete.
Trace where the surface sits: its route, entry point, navigation path, parent shell, and the page or block pattern it is meant to use.
Inspect sibling surfaces that do the same or adjacent jobs. Record their shared headers, actions, layout primitives, spacing, density, states, and narrow-screen behavior.
Read project guidance, including the root and relevant nested `AGENTS.md` files. Record app-owned wrapper components and intentional app conventions.

Record the installed `@astryxdesign/core`, `@astryxdesign/cli`, and integration-package versions from the project manifest and lockfile. Run the installed invocation of `{@command component --list}` to see core and integration components, then inspect app-owned wrappers that do not appear in that catalog.
List the real data states, roles and permissions, supported locales and RTL behavior, and mobile or narrow-width needs that affect the task.

content.text: Keep this context with the review. Mark anything you could not learn as `not inspected`. Do not flag a documented, intentional app convention merely because it differs from a generic pattern; cite the convention and verify that the user task and accessibility requirements still work.
Review one exact revision and one named product surface, route, or component in its app context. Pick the smallest review that can answer your question.

rows: A fast check for raw elements, direct icons, custom styles, and unsupported imports
Source findings plus app context visible in the project. It cannot call the rendered product good.
App fit and task completion plus source quality, rendered layout, states, assets, project checks, and accessibility evidence.
An integration template that people copy
The shared criteria plus versioned scoring, metadata, packaging, copy, and clean-app checks in {@link generic:grade-template-with-agent}.

content.text: If all you have is one source file, run the source check anyway and use any project context that is available. Report clear source blockers; list missing app purpose, route, sibling patterns, shell, theme and density, installed components and versions, real states and roles, locale and mobile needs, revision, runnable app, rendered states, and project checks; and do not call the full product good.

`astryx` in this guide means the project's installed CLI invocation, such as its local binary or existing package script. If the project has no installed invocation, report that evidence gap instead of downloading a different CLI version for the review.

A screenshot can prove a visible result, but it cannot prove which imports, components, or styles produced it. Source alone cannot prove responsive behavior, interaction, color modes, or whether an asset loads. Mark anything outside the supplied evidence as `not inspected`.

Mark each category `good`, `needs work`, or `not inspected`. Cite the route, sibling surface, project guidance, theme, component catalog, or user requirement behind every context-dependent result; cite a file and line for every source result; and name the rendered state for every visual result. Never turn missing evidence into a pass. A blocker is a finding that prevents the surface from building, rendering, operating, letting the target user complete the task, or meeting an accessibility requirement. Other departures from the rubric are `needs work`.

rows: The surface uses the app's established shell, page pattern, theme, density, wrappers, integrations, and interaction conventions unless a deviation is intentional and evidenced. The target user can complete the surface's job across the real states and permissions in scope.
Astryx owns each visible or interactive pattern for which it has a suitable component. Raw elements remain only when their native semantics are necessary or Astryx has no equivalent.
Icons render through `Icon`, `IconButton`, or the receiving component icon prop, not as raw SVG or a library component used directly.
Component props and design tokens do the work before custom StyleX declarations, inline styles, or classes. Each custom rule has a reason because no supported Astryx surface fits.
Astryx layout primitives express the visible structure, hierarchy, spacing, and responsive behavior without rebuilding the same patterns in raw containers or CSS.
Every image, font, and other asset is intentional, accessible, stable, and working from the product build path.
Public imports resolve, client boundaries are necessary, reachable states are handled, and no dead code or wrapper hides a finding.

content.text: Before calling a pattern custom or wrong, compare sibling surfaces and the installed component catalog. Reuse an app-owned wrapper or integration component when it already owns the job. A documented app convention is not a finding merely because it differs from a generic pattern; cite the convention and verify the user's task and accessibility requirements.
Common component replacements

Keep a native element when its semantics are necessary and Astryx has no equivalent. Common examples are a `form` that provides native submission, `input type="hidden"` for native form state, and an `img` when no general Astryx image component fits.

items: Compare the route with sibling surfaces that do the same job. Identify the app's shared header, actions, shell, page pattern, spacing, and density before judging the target.
Inspect every JSX opening tag. Moving raw HTML behind a PascalCase helper does not make the underlying pattern an Astryx component.

Count every raw SVG element used as an icon, including `svg`, `path`, `circle`, `rect`, `line`, `polyline`, `polygon`, `ellipse`, and `g`. For an inline SVG helper, count its raw SVG elements once in the helper definition, not again at each render. Count each icon-library component rendered directly outside an Astryx icon surface.
Look up a possible replacement with `{@command component <Name> --dense}`. Do not invent a component or prop that the installed version does not provide.
Run the installed `{@command component --list}` and inspect app-owned wrappers before rebuilding a pattern. Prefer the component the app or one of its installed integrations already uses for the job.
Inspect every `stylex.create` declaration, inline style, `className`, and `stylex.props` use. Look for a component prop or token first.

When replacing a literal spacing value, read `{@command docs spacing --full}` for the matching step or token and the target component doc for the prop's accepted scale. Do not guess a pixel-to-step mapping.
Choose the root that matches the surface. Use `Layout` for a page, `Center` for centered content, and `AppShell` only when the surface owns global application chrome.
Render realistic empty, loading, error, long-content, and interactive states. Check narrow and wide widths plus each supported color mode.
Verify the target roles and permissions, supported locales and RTL behavior, and mobile needs. Follow the real task from entry to completion instead of judging only the static page.
Run the product build, type check, tests, and accessibility checks. Keep a missing or failed check visible instead of calling the result good.

content.text: This shared rubric has no numeric score. It answers whether ordinary product code uses Astryx well without pretending that an inapplicable template field or missing browser state earned points. Integration templates add a versioned score in {@link generic:template-grading-rubric}.

items: Record the exact revision, named surface, route, and source files in scope. If the files are outside version control, record a content hash for each file and say that no project revision was available.
Write down the app's purpose, target users, surface task, entry point, navigation path, parent shell, expected page pattern, and sibling surfaces used for comparison.
Record project guidance, theme, density, installed Astryx and integration versions, the relevant output of `{@command component --list}`, and app-owned wrappers or conventions.

List the states and context that matter, including real data shapes, roles and permissions, empty, loading, error, long content, interaction, narrow width, wide width, supported color modes, locales, and RTL behavior when they apply.
Run the product and capture each named rendered state. Use screenshots or a live browser result for visible claims, and follow the target user task from entry to completion.
Run the build, type check, tests, and accessibility checks. Keep their commands and results with the review.
For each Astryx component whose replacement, prop, or composition is in question, read `{@command component <Name> --dense}`.

content.text: Start with a read-only pass so the original findings stay visible. Replace every angle-bracket value in this prompt.

content.label: Agent evaluation prompt
content.code:
Evaluate how well <surface> at <revision> fits <app> and uses Astryx. Do not edit files during this first pass.

`astryx` below means the project's installed CLI invocation, such as its local binary or existing package script. If none is installed, report that evidence gap instead of downloading a different version.

Before evaluating:
1. Read `astryx docs is-my-code-good --full`.
2. Read the root and relevant nested `AGENTS.md` files plus other project guidance. State what the app is for, who uses it, and the task this surface supports.
3. Trace the surface's route, entry point, navigation path, parent shell, and expected page or block pattern.
4. Inspect at least two sibling surfaces that do the same or adjacent jobs. Record their shared headers, actions, layout, spacing, density, states, and narrow-screen behavior.
5. Record the app's theme, density, app-owned wrappers, and documented intentional conventions.
6. Read the project manifest and lockfile for the installed Astryx, CLI, and integration versions. Run `astryx component --list`, then identify relevant integration components and app-owned wrappers.
7. List the real data states, roles and permissions, supported locales and RTL behavior, and mobile or narrow-width needs.
8. Inspect every source file in scope and its public imports.
9. Run `astryx component <Name> --dense` for each Astryx component whose replacement, prop, or composition you question.
10. Read `astryx docs spacing --full` and the target component's docs before mapping a literal spacing value to a prop or token.
11. Render every supplied state at narrow and wide widths and in each supported color mode.
12. Read the build, type-check, test, and accessibility-check results.

If only source is supplied, continue with a source check. Report blockers visible in the source, list every missing app-context and product-evidence item, and do not call the full product good. Do not leave the blocker list empty only because no checks were supplied.

Judge the code against the app as well as Astryx. Ask whether it matches sibling surfaces, uses the right shell and page pattern, reuses app or integration components instead of rebuilding them, preserves intentional app conventions, and lets the target user complete the task.

For each rubric category, return `good`, `needs work`, or `not inspected`. Every context-dependent finding must cite the route, sibling file, project guidance, theme, component catalog, wrapper, or user requirement it relies on. Cite file and line evidence for source findings and name the rendered state for visual findings. Mark context you could not learn as `not inspected`. Do not flag a documented intentional app convention merely because it differs from a generic pattern. Never turn missing evidence into a pass. Do not hide raw HTML or custom styles behind a helper. Do not calculate a template score for ordinary product code.

Return:
- app purpose, target users, surface job, route, and entry path
- app context inspected and app context missing
- product evidence inspected and product evidence missing
- one row per rubric category with result, evidence, and fix
- task-completion, functional, or accessibility blockers visible in the source or found by the supplied checks
- the top three fixes in order
- every claim that still needs a person to verify

items: Reject a `good` result without app-context, source, and rendered evidence. Open every cited route, sibling file, guidance file, and source location, and reproduce every named visible state.
Check that documented intentional app conventions were not flagged merely for differing from a generic pattern, and that context the reviewer could not learn stayed `not inspected`.
Fix task-completion, build, functional, and accessibility blockers first.
Reuse the app shell, page pattern, wrappers, and installed integration components before replacing unnecessary raw elements, direct icons, and custom styles.
Follow the target user task again, render the full state set, and rerun the project checks.
Repeat the read-only review on the new revision. Keep the first report so the improvement and every remaining tradeoff stay visible.

content.text: For an integration template, finish with the scored package and copy workflow in {@link generic:grade-template-with-agent}. Ordinary product code stops with the evidence-backed category report and does not receive a template publication grade.

docs.name: layout
docs.title: Layout
docs.summary: Build an app layout outside-in: scaffold the regions, structure the content, tune the spacing, then adapt across widths.

blocks.text: Build a layout outside-in. Settle the shell and its region budgets before any content exists, then work inward. Content-first layouts drift into a padded column of cards, because every section ends up inventing its own container.

items: Scaffold: pick the shell, budget each region, and choose navigation
Structure: rank each region's content and choose its container
Spacing: align each region to one content line, then set gaps and density
Breakpoints: decide what each region does as width changes

blocks.text: This guide decides layout, not component APIs. Run `{@command build "<idea>"}` to start from the closest template for your app type, and `{@command component <Name>}` for a component's props.

docs.name: layout-spacing
docs.title: Layout spacing
docs.description: Hold one content line per region, then tune gaps and density.

content.text: Hold one content line per region, then tune gaps and density. Alignment, Rhythm, and Density and size each build on these rules.

items: Let the container own padding; children zero their own margins
Hold one content line per region: text on the line, hover backgrounds bleed to the edge
Hold one padding token across a region header, body, and footer
Contrast tight and generous gaps so grouping reads without borders
One control size per row; match density to use frequency
Double padding: a component indented past its Section heading (keep one inset owner)
Raw px for interior spacing; tokens only, px is for structural widths
One repeated gap everywhere, which flattens grouping
Mixed control sizes in a single row

content.text: The container owns padding and child gaps; children zero their margins, and interior spacing is always a token. Pick one content line per region and hold it constant, not the padding: `container_inset = content_line - component_intrinsic_inset`.

items: Text and Heading carry no inset, so the container takes the full padding
List, Tab, Menu, and nav items carry a small inset, so the container gives up its padding and the component owns the line
Table cells carry a larger inset, so the container gives up its padding and the cell owns the line

content.label: One content line, two inset owners

content.text: Verify: draw one vertical line down the left of the region. Every label touches it; only hover and selected backgrounds cross it.
Grouping comes from contrast between tight and generous gaps, not one repeated value. If every gap is the same step, proximity does no work.

items: Tight gaps bind: the smallest steps, used inside an item or field
Generous gaps separate: several steps up, used between sections
Reach for the in-between steps to tune cadence, rather than rounding everything to the same two values

content.label: Tight inside, generous between
content.code:
// Tight binds at gap={1}–{2}, generous separates at gap={4}–{6}.
// In-between steps tune cadence: gap={3} = 12px, gap={5} = 20px.
<VStack gap={6}>
  <VStack gap={1}>
    <Text weight="semibold">Retention</Text>
    <Text color="secondary">Logs are kept for 30 days</Text>
  </VStack>
  <VStack gap={1}>{/* next label and value */}</VStack>
</VStack>

content.text: Verify: with every border removed, you can still name the groups from spacing alone. If you cannot, the intervals are too uniform. Form fields are the exception: FormLayout owns their spacing.
Match density to how often a region is used, and give every control in a row the same size so heights share a baseline.

items: Compact: high-volume regions scanned fast, like logs, monitors, and large datasets
Balanced: most Table and List surfaces
Spacious: low-frequency or high-stakes rows, like settings or a short selection list

content.label: Density paired with control size

content.text: Verify: every interactive element in a row shares one size, and that size is paired with the density of the region it sits in.

docs.name: links
docs.title: Links
docs.description: Link one doc to another so the link keeps working when the doc moves.

content.text: Write `{@link [provider:]kind:name}` in prose, list items, and table cells to link another doc. The CLI prints the command that opens it, so the link keeps working when the doc moves.

content.code:
{type: 'prose', text: 'Before you ship, read {@link generic:deploying}.'},
{type: 'list', style: 'unordered', items: ['All guides: {@link namespace:acme}.']},
{type: 'table', headers: ['Task', 'Guide'], rows: [['Ship', '{@link generic:deploying}']]},

content.text: Each link reads as a command. This link, {@link generic:extend-or-replace}, opens the next guide.

items: The kind is `generic` for a topic or guide, `namespace` for a docs section, `command` or `function` for a CLI command or API function, `schema` or `enum` for a schema or a fixed set of values, `component` for a component, and `page` or `block` for a template.
Name a component by its export name and a template by its id. Its link reads as the command that opens it, such as `{@command component AcmeCarousel --package @acme/widgets}`.
Inside backticks or a code block, link syntax prints as written.

content.text: A link without a provider resolves against your own package. To link the CLI's docs, or another package's, start the target with that package's name, such as `@astryxdesign/cli:`.

items: Name a CLI command the way you type it, spaces included, such as `@astryxdesign/cli:command:doctor integration docs`.
In a topic that `extends` another package's topic, your sections still resolve against your package, so a link to the base topic's docs needs its provider.

sections.title: Fix a link that names no doc

content.text: A link that names no doc prints as written, and `doctor integration docs` warns. The warning names a search that finds the right target.

content.code: {@command doctor integration docs}

severity: [warn]
code:     invalid_doc_graph
message:  acme/deploying § check-before-you-ship: "command:doctor" names no doc. Find it with `astryx search doctor --type doc`, then name it as `[<provider>:]<kind>:<name>`.

items: The warning keeps exit code 0, so read the report before you ship; see {@link generic:check-your-docs}.
Published 0.6.4 and later read links. An older CLI, such as published 0.6.3, prints each one as written; see {@link generic:versioning}.

docs.name: migration
docs.title: Migration
docs.summary: Migrate an existing Tailwind, shadcn, or Radix app to the design system incrementally — setup, component replacement, and verification.

docs.name: migration-setup
docs.title: Setup
docs.description: Install the theme, wire CSS layers, audit resets, and run the foundation smoke test before migrating any surface.

content.text: Treat migration as a product-shell and workflow migration, not a global class replacement. Start by putting the app inside Theme and AppShell, then move one route or surface at a time to design system primitives while keeping existing data, routing, and business logic intact.

Tailwind can coexist during migration. Use it for legacy wrappers and local layout while replacing interactive controls, navigation, command surfaces, forms, alerts, dialogs, and settings UI with components.

items: Install the packages and run `{@command init}` for agent docs, then add the reset, `astryx.css`, and theme CSS imports (see Theme and CSS Setup below).
Wrap the app root with Theme and choose the initial light, dark, or system mode behavior.
Make Tailwind and design system CSS layer order explicit before replacing components.
Render the foundation smoke test page and confirm primitives keep their padding before migrating any surface.
Move the persistent frame first: AppShell, TopNav, SideNav, page content, and mobile navigation. See {@link generic:component-migration}.

Replace shared primitives: Button, IconButton, TextInput, NumberInput, Switch, CheckboxInput, RadioList, Selector, TabList, Dialog, AlertDialog, Banner, Toast, Badge, Card, Table, and ListItem. See {@link generic:component-migration}.
Replace global workflows: command palette, settings popover, theme toggle, search, filters, create flows, and destructive confirmation dialogs.
Remove legacy Tailwind classes from each completed surface, keeping only token-backed layout utilities or local wrappers that still need to be migrated.
Verify both light and dark modes, keyboard navigation, responsive layout, and empty/error/loading states before moving to the next route. See {@link generic:migration-verification}.

content.text: Use the CLI as the migration checklist. Read the docs for the pattern you are about to touch, inspect a matching template skeleton, then read the exact component docs before editing.

content.label: Migration-oriented CLI pass

content.text: For a shorter read to paste into an AI coding tool, see {@link generic:working-with-ai}. Use `--json` when building automated migration reports.

content.label: Short and JSON modes
content.code:
{@command docs migration --full --detail brief}
{@command component Button --json}

content.text: Mount Theme at the app root so every migrated component reads the same token set. Keep the mode in application state if users can switch between light and dark themes.

content.label: Root provider with explicit mode

content.text: When Tailwind remains in the app, declare layer order once in the global CSS file. Load the Astryx reset and theme CSS before Tailwind utilities so migrated components keep design system defaults while legacy utility classes still work. On Tailwind v4, use the imports and layer order in {@link generic:tailwind}.

Import the global CSS file first in the root layout or app entry, before anything that imports Astryx or theme CSS, including the `astryx-themes` module and a root component like the `AppRoot` above. Why the order matters, and what to do when it cannot come first, is in {@link generic:tailwind}.

content.label: Root layout or app entry
content.code:
import './globals.css'; // first: declares the cascade-layer order

import {AppRoot} from './AppRoot';

content.text: On Tailwind v3 there is no preflight.css to import, so wrap the @tailwind base directive in a named layer instead. Keep utilities unlayered so existing app utility classes still win everywhere. Put the `@layer` order line in its own `layers.css` and import it first, before `globals.css`: Next.js (webpack or Turbopack) and other bundlers that hoist CSS imports move the imported files above an inline `@layer` line, so the order would arrive too late.

content.label: layers.css (imported first)
content.code: @layer reset, tw-preflight, astryx-base, astryx-theme;

content.label: globals.css (Tailwind v3 coexistence)
Root layout or app entry (Tailwind v3)

content.text: In a stylesheet with no layers at all, a zero-specificity reset like `* { padding: 0 }` loses to any class selector, so most developers treat resets as harmless. Layers change the rules twice: unlayered styles beat every named layer, and a later layer beats an earlier one, both regardless of specificity. The same reset therefore wins against every component style either by staying unlayered or by landing in a layer declared after astryx-base. Same CSS, opposite outcome, and no error or warning when it happens.

This is the most common way an adoption breaks, through one of two @import mechanisms. A top-level @import without the layer() keyword keeps the legacy reset unlayered, where it overrides every design system layer. And an @import nested inside a file that was itself imported into a layer inherits that surrounding layer, so a reset can silently land in a consumer layer above astryx-base. Either way the fix is the same: import the legacy reset into the lowest layer explicitly.

content.label: Legacy reset, explicitly layered
content.code:
/* was: @import "./legacy-reset.css";  (unlayered: beats every layer) */
@import "./legacy-reset.css" layer(reset);

content.text: Before building screens, check every stylesheet against the cascade layer audit below.
Audit the layers around the design system with this checklist before building screens.

items: Declare the canonical @layer order once, before any @import. With Next.js (webpack or Turbopack) and other bundlers that hoist CSS imports, the order declaration must live in its own CSS file imported first, such as layers.css, because the bundler hoists @import content above the inline CSS that follows it.

Audit every pre-existing global or reset stylesheet and assign each one to a layer deliberately. Top-level imports without layer() stay unlayered and beat every layer; imports nested inside a layered file inherit that layer.
Remove or demote the app legacy reset. The design system ships its own :where() reset in the lowest layer, so any app reset belongs in that same reset layer and never in a layer above astryx-base.

Layer Tailwind preflight. On Tailwind v4, import preflight.css with layer(base). On Tailwind v3, wrap the @tailwind base directive in a named layer (see the snippet in Theme and CSS Setup). Unlayered preflight overrides theme CSS silently.
Set moduleResolution to bundler or node16 and newer so subpath imports like @astryxdesign/core/reset.css resolve.

Theme with defineTheme and the accent family API instead of hand-writing individual color tokens. Derived tokens like --color-on-accent are generated from the accent scale automatically; hand-writing only --color-accent leaves --color-on-accent at its stale white default with no contrast guarantee against the new accent.
Run the foundation smoke test below and view a few components in both light and dark mode before migrating any route.

content.text: One more mental model shift: a className or utility class you write on a component still reaches the DOM either way, but whether it overrides the component is a layer question, not a source order question. Keep app utilities in the utilities layer so they keep winning.

A broken layer order fails silently and identically on every page, so catch it before feature work instead of after N migrated screens. Render one throwaway page with a few primitives as the first migration step.

content.label: Foundation check page

content.text: If the button renders with visible padding, a filled primary background, and the input and card have borders and internal spacing, the foundation is sound. For an assertion that can run in any test runner or a dev-only effect, check that a primitive keeps non-zero padding:

content.label: Foundation assertion

content.text: When this fails, the fix is almost always in the layer order: find the stylesheet that zeroes padding, and move it into the reset layer or delete it.

docs.name: migration-verification
docs.title: Verification
docs.description: Post-migration verification checklist and an AI migration prompt to paste into your coding tool.

items: Run the app in light and dark mode and check that surfaces, borders, text, icons, hover states, focus rings, and status colors flow together.
Open the command palette from the shell, type into it, select items by keyboard, and confirm focus returns to the trigger.
Check the SideNav at collapsed, expanded, active, hover, nested, and mobile states.
Verify settings popovers and dialogs in jsdom and in a real browser because the native dialog and [`Popover`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API) APIs may need test shims.
Search for leftover hardcoded Tailwind colors, arbitrary hex values, and one-off hover colors after each route migration.
Run component tests, build, and at least one browser screenshot pass for each migrated route.

content.text: When using an AI coding agent, give it an explicit migration loop instead of asking for a full-app rewrite.

content.label: Paste this into your AI
content.code:
We are migrating this existing Tailwind/shadcn app to Astryx incrementally.

First run:
- astryx docs migration --dense
- astryx docs theme --dense
- astryx docs styling --dense
- astryx template AppShellTopNavWithSideNav --skeleton

Then migrate one route or shell surface at a time. Keep business logic and routing intact. Replace shadcn/Radix/Tailwind primitives with Astryx components, remove hardcoded colors, verify light and dark mode, and take screenshots before moving to the next surface.

docs.name: monorepos
docs.title: Monorepos and nested folders
docs.description: How Astryx finds the project a folder belongs to, and which version answers in a monorepo, a nested app, or a cloned repository inside another project.

content.text: Astryx searches upward from the current folder: `@astryxdesign/core` or `@astryxdesign/cli` installed there or a few folders above, else the nearest `package.json` declaring either, up to the repository root. Folders without any are outside projects.

items: A workspace member declaring Astryx is its own project, even with packages hoisted to the repository root. A root CLI answers it, as always; a member with its own Core and no CLI anywhere gets answered by the astryx command you started.
A folder without its own `package.json`, such as `src/` or `scripts/`, belongs to the project above it.
A repository that builds the CLI itself, with the CLI in `packages/cli` next to Core in `packages/core`, runs that CLI.
Folders inside another project, such as nested apps or cloned repositories, answer with the enclosing project's release.
Folder names compare as your file system compares them: a folder reached through a link, or typed in different letter case on macOS or Windows, answers like the folder itself.
In a Yarn Plug'n'Play project, Astryx cannot see the project's own CLI, so the astryx command you started answers. Run the project's CLI through Yarn (`yarn astryx`) to use it directly.

content.text: Part of {@link namespace:global}: what global mode is and how each part works.

docs.name: motion
docs.title: Motion
docs.description: Duration and easing tokens for animations and transitions.

content.text: Motion serves two purposes: it makes interfaces easier to understand, and it makes them more pleasant to use. A panel animating open helps the eye track what changed and where new content sits in the layout. These moments reduce cognitive load and make the interface feel responsive.
At the same time, well-tuned motion gives an application a sense of craft and polish that users notice, even if they can't name it.
The design system provides duration and easing tokens that keep these moments consistent across your application.
Nine duration tokens in fast, medium, and slow bands.

Motion duration primitives. Three bands: fast (micro-interactions), medium (entrance/exit), slow (continuous). Min/max variants derive from base × ratio. Of a theme's two `motion` knobs, `tempo` (0.75–1.5) scales every duration here; `character` leaves durations alone. A duration scale beats `tempo` for the bands it sets, and explicit `tokens` beat both. `tempo` leaves these unscaled: finger tracking, momentum, the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard, the press's onset delay, cancel distance and tap flash, hover-intent delays, gesture thresholds, Spinner's and Skeleton's loops, and the 200 ms Reduce Motion cap.

Four easing curves. `--ease-standard` decelerates, for state changes. `--ease-entrance` is for things arriving and `--ease-move` for things moving on screen; a theme's `character` sets both, and at `standard` they equal `--ease-standard`. `--ease-exit` accelerates, for things leaving: it moves off from rest and leaves fast, so the travel stays visible for the whole duration, and it is the same at every `character`.

Easing curves for animations and transitions. Of a theme's two `motion` knobs, `character` sets `--ease-entrance` and `--ease-move`: `crisp` decelerates without overshoot, `expressive` overshoots slightly, and at `standard` both equal `--ease-standard`; `--ease-exit` keeps its own curve at every character. `tempo` leaves curves alone. A duration scale's own fields win over the knobs, and explicit `tokens` win over everything. No curve here shapes motion that follows a finger or the system (dragging, momentum, the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard), and the press's clocks, hover-intent delays and gesture thresholds keep their timing whatever the character.

Some parts of the interface benefit from animation. Panels, dialogs, and collapsible sections are disorienting when they appear instantly, so animation gives the eye something to follow. Toasts and notifications need just enough entrance to be noticed without startling. State changes like a switch flipping or a selection highlighting feel more intentional with a brief transition.
The common thread is that these are moments where the user needs to understand what happened.

Table row hovers. List item highlights. Anything the user does dozens of times per minute. Adding perceptible duration to these interactions makes the interface feel like it's catching up to the cursor. Keep these fast enough that the user never notices a delay.

Animations that block interaction are worse. If a user has to wait for a panel to finish sliding before they can click something inside it, the animation has become an obstacle. Motion should never stand between the user and their next action.

items: Not everything needs an animated exit. Elements the user is moving away from, such as tooltips, hover cards, and dropdown menus, can disappear instantly. The user has already shifted their attention. Animate the exit only when it helps orient the user, like a panel closing or a dialog dismissing to reveal what's underneath.
When you do animate exit, match the entrance. A panel that slides in from the right should slide back out to the right.

Direction should match the action. Navigating deeper into content should feel like moving forward. Going back should feel like returning. This keeps the user oriented in the structure of the application.

Contextual UI should feel connected to its trigger. A dropdown should expand from the button that opened it. A popover should appear near the element it describes. This doesn't apply to global UI like command palettes or toasts, which have their own fixed positions.

content.text: Some users experience motion sensitivity; animation that feels polished to one person can cause discomfort for another. When the OS reduced-motion setting is on, Astryx components change at once under a mouse or trackpad, and under a finger they cross-fade instead of moving: opacity only, in 200 ms or less. A value that changes in place, such as a progress fill, takes its new value at once under any pointer. Do the same in your own animations with `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`, adding `(pointer: coarse)` for the touch cross-fade.

Set transition durations and easing from the motion tokens, so a theme that retunes motion retunes your animations too. Ease something arriving on `--ease-entrance` and something moving on screen on `--ease-move`, so it follows the theme's `character`, and something leaving on `--ease-exit`, which stays the same at every `character`.

content.label: Applying motion tokens

content.text: A theme sets how motion feels with two knobs in `defineTheme`'s `motion`. They drive the CSS motion tokens; the springs of touch motion don't read them yet. Every theme follows each person's Reduce Motion setting; no theme loosens it.

items: `tempo` scales every motion duration: 1 is Astryx's own, 0.75 the quickest and 1.5 the slowest (values outside are clamped).

`character` sets how lively motion is: `'crisp'` decelerates without overshoot, `'standard'` is Astryx's own, and `'expressive'` overshoots slightly on entrances and moves. Exits and fades never overshoot.

content.label: A quicker, crisper theme

content.text: Some motion never follows the knobs, because it tracks a finger or the system: finger tracking, momentum and the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard, the press model's onset delay, cancel distance and tap flash (its release fade follows tempo), hover-intent delays, gesture thresholds, the loops of busy indicators such as Spinner and Skeleton, and the 200 ms Reduce Motion cross-fade.

Precedence, lowest to highest: the knobs, then a duration scale (`fast`, `medium`, `slow`, `ratio`) for the durations it sets, then explicit `tokens`. A theme with no `motion` renders exactly as before.

items: Animate transitions that involve spatial change: panels opening, content expanding, elements entering the screen.
Use fast tokens for small, frequent interactions. Use medium tokens for larger transitions that rearrange the layout.
Honor reduced motion preferences at the OS level.
Let hover states or high-frequency interactions feel like they're lagging behind the user.
Let animation delay when a user can interact with new content. The transition should complete before (or not block) the next action.
Move elements in ways that contradict where they came from or where they're going.

docs.name: non-css-processing
docs.title: Non-CSS Processing
docs.description: Resolve token values outside the DOM for charts, canvas, SVG, and config objects using resolveThemeTokens() and useTheme().

content.text: Use `resolveThemeTokens()` or `resolveThemeToken()` when code outside React needs token values for a known theme and mode. Use `useTheme()` inside client components when the values should come from the nearest Theme and active mode.

content.label: Resolve tokens without React context
Resolve tokens from the nearest Theme

items: Use the returned `tokens` object as a memo dependency; it is stable until the active theme or mode changes.
Use data visualization tokens such as `--color-data-categorical-blue` for chart series instead of reusing arbitrary UI colors.
Prefer CSS variables for SVG elements when possible (`fill="var(--color-accent)"`); use token resolver APIs when an API requires a string value in JavaScript.
Use token resolver APIs for ordinary DOM styling. Use CSS variables, StyleX tokens, xstyle, or library aliases instead.

Assume the returned values reflect every CSS cascade override. They resolve tokens for the current theme and mode; local media-surface overrides and arbitrary CSS overrides may not be represented in the returned map.

docs.name: other-libraries
docs.title: Other Libraries
docs.description: Panda, Chakra, MUI, Emotion, styled-components, Theme UI, UnoCSS, and the interop checklist.

sections.title: Panda, Chakra, and Other Semantic Token Systems

content.text: Libraries like Panda CSS and Chakra UI have first-class semantic token objects. Put system CSS variables at the leaves of those objects so product code can use the library's semantic names while the system still owns the values.

content.label: Semantic token aliases
Panda-style usage
content.code:
<section
  className={css({
    bg: 'background.surface',
    color: 'text.primary',
    borderColor: 'border.default',
    p: '4',
    rounded: 'container',
  })}
/>

content.text: If a semantic-token library needs to generate its own light/dark CSS from raw values, align its mode selector with Theme (`data-theme="light|dark"`) and generate that adapter from system theme data. Otherwise it can drift from nested or runtime themes.

`MUI` expects palette slots such as primary, background, text, and divider. Map those slots to system variables for ordinary component styling. Use raw values only when MUI or your code needs to parse colors for contrast, alpha, lighten, or darken calculations.

content.label: MUI palette mapped to system vars

content.text: If MUI owns color mode in an app, generate the light and dark palette values from system theme data and keep Theme mode synchronized. If Theme owns color mode, keep both MUI schemes pointing at the same system CSS variables.

sections.title: Emotion, styled-components, Theme UI, and Styled System

content.text: Runtime CSS-in-JS libraries such as `Emotion` and `styled-components` usually accept arbitrary theme objects. Keep those objects semantic, but store system CSS variable references as the values. This keeps generated classes stable while the system updates values through the CSS cascade.

content.label: Generic CSS-in-JS theme object

content.text: Avoid rebuilding CSS-in-JS theme objects with raw color values on every mode switch. CSS variables let the class names stay the same while the browser resolves the active values.
Utility generators such as UnoCSS can put system variables in their theme config or shortcuts. Keep classes semantic (`bg-surface`, `text-primary`) and let the values point at system tokens.

content.label: UnoCSS-style config

content.text: Static utility extractors cannot see dynamically constructed class names. Prefer explicit class strings or the library's safelist/source-registration mechanism.

items: Import the reset/base CSS and a theme CSS file early enough for first paint. For production SSR, prefer built themes from `{@command theme build}` or published `/built` theme imports plus `theme.css`.
Choose one owner for color mode. Theme uses `data-theme="light|dark"` and `color-scheme` to resolve `light-dark()` tokens.
Map the external library's semantic layer to system variables by intent, not by exact naming. For example, MUI `background.paper` maps to `--color-background-surface`.
Use {@link namespace:tokens} and focused token docs when building mappings. Keep mappings small at first: text, surface/body/card/popover, border, accent, status, spacing, radius, typography, shadow.
Use token resolver APIs only for non-CSS APIs that need resolved values.

docs.name: principles
docs.title: Principles
docs.description: Core design principles and rules for building with the design system.

content.text: A design system that prioritizes consistency, adaptability, and developer experience. Every decision flows from a few core ideas:

items: Components over primitives: use components for everything they cover before reaching for raw HTML
Semantic tokens over hardcoded values: colors, spacing, and radii are named by purpose, not appearance
Theme-agnostic code: your app code never references specific colors or measurements, so themes and dark mode work automatically
Open internals: every primitive is exported and composable, so you can build on top of it without fighting it

content.text: Eight rules that keep app code on-system.

items: Use components for everything they cover
Page layout is frame-first: pick the shell and budget regions before writing content (see {@link namespace:layout})
Dense data renders as rows (Table, List/Item), edge-to-edge with dividers; Card is for widgets, galleries, and settings groups
StyleX or Tailwind for custom styling; both are first-class (see {@link namespace:styling})
Semantic tokens, not hardcoded values (see {@link namespace:tokens})
CSS custom properties for colors, not hex values
Form inputs are controlled (value + onChange)
Use useLinkComponent() for navigation so consumers can plug in their framework router via LinkProvider

content.text: The design system supports multiple styling approaches. Every component accepts an `xstyle` prop for StyleX style overrides via `stylex.create()`. For layout and wrapper styling outside of components, use StyleX or Tailwind utilities; both resolve to the same design tokens.
See {@link namespace:styling} for the complete guide with examples.
Patterns that break theming, routing, or layout, and what to use instead.

items: Inline styles on raw elements. Use xstyle on components
Hardcoded colors (#fff). Use var(--color-*) or Tailwind semantic classes (text-primary, bg-surface)
Hardcoded spacing (16px). Use spacing tokens or Tailwind spacing utilities
Hardcoded <a> elements. Use useLinkComponent() so consumers can swap in their framework router via LinkProvider
Wrapping every list item or page section in a Card. Decide the frame first; dense data renders as rows (see {@link namespace:layout})
Badge as decoration. Reserve Badge for counts and enumerated states; use StatusDot or Token for status
Inventing props. Read component docs first

content.text: The design system provides semantic design tokens for spacing, color, radius, shadow, typography, and size. Tokens adapt to the active theme and color mode. Run {@link namespace:tokens} for the full reference with all values.

docs.title: Troubleshooting global mode
