docs.name: subcomponent
docs.title: Subcomponent
docs.description: Move one member of a component family into its own sibling doc without duplicating it in the parent.

content.text: Start with a component family doc. Move one public member into a sibling doc when it has its own source and enough behavior, props, or usage guidance to maintain separately. The parent still lists the member, but only by name.

items: Keep a small member inline when its whole contract stays clear in the family doc.
Use a sibling doc when the member needs focused search results, examples, usage guidance, or independent maintenance.
Give each member one documentation owner. Do not keep a full parent entry and a sibling doc for the same name.

content.label: components/AcmeDialog.doc.mjs

content.text: The name-only entry keeps `AcmeDialogHeader` in the family. Its description and props come only from the sibling file.

content.label: components/AcmeDialogHeader.doc.mjs

content.text: Every field is in {@link schema:component-doc}.

items: `subComponentOf` must exactly match the parent doc's `name`.
`description` explains this member's role in the family. `usage` is optional; add it when the member needs guidance beyond that sentence.
The CLI does not copy family fields such as `group`, `category`, or `keywords` from the parent to the child. Set any the child needs in its own doc.

docs.name: tailwind
docs.title: Tailwind
docs.description: The Tailwind v4 bridge, cascade layer order, and utility-class usage backed by system tokens.

content.text: The Tailwind v4 bridge at `@astryxdesign/core/tailwind-theme.css` maps Tailwind theme variables to system CSS variables with `@theme reference inline`, so utility classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, `border-border`, `rounded-lg`, and `shadow-md` stay in sync with the active theme without emitting competing runtime declarations.

content.label: globals.css

content.text: Pre-declare every layer before any imports. This keeps reset lowest, Tailwind preflight above reset, component/theme styles in the middle, and Tailwind utilities last so utility classes on `className` can intentionally override component defaults.

A layer's rank is set by the first stylesheet on the page that names it, so this order only holds when `globals.css` loads first. Make it the first import in the root layout or app entry, before any module that imports Astryx or theme CSS. That includes the `astryx-themes` module generated by `{@command theme add}` and any root component that imports a theme's `theme.css`. If a theme stylesheet loads first, Tailwind preflight overrides Astryx base styles and theme overrides lose. If `globals.css` cannot come first, move the `@layer` line into its own `layers.css` and import that first instead.

content.label: Root layout or app entry
content.code:
import './globals.css'; // first: declares the cascade-layer order

import {themes, defaultThemeSlug} from './astryx-themes';

content.label: Tailwind classes backed by system tokens
content.code:
<section className="rounded-lg border border-border bg-surface p-4 text-primary shadow-md">
  <Button label="Save" variant="primary" />
</section>

content.text: The Tailwind bridge is the concrete example of the general interop pattern: expose another library's semantic API, but point the values at system token variables.

docs.name: template-assets
docs.title: Assets
docs.summary: Make sure the template's styles, fonts, icons, images, and video still show up after an app copies it.

blocks.text: The copied file does not bring sibling assets with it ({@link generic:write-the-template-file}). Give every asset exactly one owner:

headers: How the copied source reaches it
rows: The value is small, editable, and belongs to the starting point
The asset should stay centrally maintained with the package
Import a stable public package path
The app must provide product-specific content or branding
Use an explicit placeholder or app public URL and say what to replace

blocks.text: Do not make a template look self-contained while it relies on an undocumented package file or app convention.

docs.name: template-doc-overview
docs.title: Template doc overview
docs.description: Understand what the template doc controls, keep it accurate as the UI changes, and check how Astryx lists the template.

content.text: Every template has a source file and a doc file. For `acme-dashboard`, the source is `templates/acme-dashboard.tsx` and the doc is `templates/acme-dashboard.doc.mjs`. Both begin with `acme-dashboard`, which is how Astryx knows they belong together.

rows: The UI source that an app copies and then owns.
How Astryx names, describes, categorizes, previews, and resolves the template before it is copied.

content.text: The integration manifest points Astryx to the `templates` directory; it does not list each template. Change the source and doc together whenever the purpose, preview, readiness, or replacement behavior changes. No automated check can tell whether the doc still describes the rendered UI.
The fields below apply to every page and block. The page, block, and replacement guides add the fields unique to each.
Every field is in {@link schema:template-doc}.

items: Set `type` to the kind you chose in {@link generic:start-a-template}. It decides which other fields the doc accepts.

The file name sets the template id ({@link generic:start-a-template}). Labels live in the doc: the terminal list prints `name`, and JSON listings print `displayName`. Changing either never changes the id.
Write the description for someone choosing between templates. The Doc metadata category in {@link generic:template-grading-rubric} defines what a complete description covers.

Name the ideas the template serves in `keywords`: the domains, tasks, and other names a builder might use for it, in lowercase, such as `['monitoring', 'uptime', 'on-call']` for a service-health dashboard. How search and build use them is in {@link generic:field-reference}, so the description can stay about the layout.

Add `isReady: false` as soon as you generate the doc, because a doc without `isReady` is listed as ready. Keep it until the template passes {@link generic:test-template-in-app} and the quality review.

content.text: Note: `keywords` needs `@astryxdesign/cli` 0.6.6 or later. A stable CLI before 0.6.6 rejects the field and drops that template, and one before 0.6.4 also hides your doc topics: `template --list` and `search` print one warning, and `docs` and `build` say nothing. Declare the CLI floor as an optional peer ({@link generic:versioning}); `integration verify` fails until you do.
Read the package-scoped template list after every doc change. Confirm the id, visible name, description, type, readiness, and package.

content.code: astryx --json template --list --package @acme/astryx-templates

content.label: Relevant list result
content.code:
{
  "id": "acme-dashboard",
  "name": "acme-dashboard",
  "displayName": "Acme Dashboard",
  "description": "An analytics dashboard for reviewing account health and recent trends.",
  "type": "page",
  "package": "@acme/astryx-templates",
  "isReady": false
}

docs.name: template-fonts
docs.title: Fonts
docs.description: Keep text in the app's typeface unless the template truly needs its own, and ship every font file it uses when it does.

content.text: Use Astryx typography components and theme values unless the template must demonstrate a specific licensed typeface. A copied template should normally inherit the app typography instead of installing a new global font.

items: Do not add a font only to make sample content look more polished.
Do not override the app body font from a template.
Use a custom face only for a real product or content requirement that the integration package owns.

content.text: Keep the font files beside a package-owned stylesheet. The stylesheet can use relative `url()` paths because it stays in the package, and the template imports the stylesheet by its public path ({@link generic:template-styles}).

content.label: styles/acme-dashboard.css

items: Ship WOFF2 when it satisfies the supported browsers. Add another format only when those browsers require it.
Declare every weight and style the template uses. Do not make the browser synthesize bold or italic because a file is missing.
Use `font-display: swap` unless the product requirement and performance test justify another value.
Confirm that the font license permits redistribution in the integration package.

content.text: Exporting the stylesheet does not publish the font files it points to. Include the font directory in the package as well ({@link generic:export-template-assets}).
When you test the template in an app ({@link generic:test-template-in-app}), also confirm the following.

items: Every font request succeeds from the built asset path.
Computed styles show the requested family, weight, and style.
Text stays readable with the fallback stack when a font loads slowly or fails.

docs.name: template-icons
docs.title: Icons
docs.description: Keep icons consistent and accessible by rendering them through Astryx, and ship custom product icons from your package.

content.text: Use `Icon` for a standalone icon. For a component icon prop, pass what that prop accepts: most, such as `Button` and `IconButton`, take an element like `<Icon icon={BellIcon} />`, and some menu and navigation items also accept the icon definition itself. This keeps sizing, color, and accessibility aligned with the system.

items: Use one supported icon set consistently inside a template.
Give an icon-only control its required visible or assistive label through the Astryx control API.
Do not paste raw `svg` and `path` markup when an existing icon definition fits.
Do not render a library icon directly when `Icon` or the receiving Astryx component can render it.
Declare an icon library other than Astryx as a dependency ({@link generic:export-template-assets}).

content.text: A product mark or missing domain symbol can stay package-owned. Export a compatible icon definition from a public package path, then import that path from the template.

content.label: templates/acme-dashboard.tsx

content.text: Export the icon path and include its file in the package ({@link generic:export-template-assets}).
When you test the template in an app ({@link generic:test-template-in-app}), also confirm the following.

items: Every icon state renders, including selected, disabled, loading, and narrow layouts.
Meaningful icons have an accessible name, and decorative icons add no duplicate spoken text.
No missing icon leaves an empty control.

docs.name: template-images-media
docs.title: Images and media
docs.description: Make sure every image and video still works after the copy, or becomes a clear placeholder the app replaces.

sections.title: Do not rely on sibling media

content.text: A reference such as `./hero.png` or `../assets/demo.mp4` stays unchanged in the copied file and normally breaks.

items: Use a stable public URL when the integration owner will continue to host the media.
Use an explicit app-owned placeholder when every app must supply product-specific media.
Use a package-owned JS or CSS entrypoint only when every supported app toolchain can resolve and emit the underlying asset.
Do not assume that a file inside `node_modules` is automatically served at a browser URL.

content.text: `/template-assets/<path>` is a preview-only fixture path. During copy, Astryx replaces a complete static image reference with an inline neutral SVG placeholder. It replaces a complete static video reference with an empty string because it cannot create a valid inline video.

items: Supported preview image suffixes are SVG, PNG, JPG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, and ICO.
Supported preview video suffixes are MP4, WebM, MOV, OGV, and M4V.
Keep the preview path as one complete static string. Concatenation, interpolation, method calls, module imports, and unknown file formats are rejected when Astryx cannot replace them safely.
Use this path only when a placeholder is the intended copied result. It is not a way to ship required product media.
Astryx serves `/template-assets` only in its own docs. A preview you host must serve that path itself.

content.text: When the app must provide the final asset, keep the replacement point obvious in the copied source. Preserve enough surrounding layout and example data that the template still teaches the pattern without pretending the final content is included.

items: Use accurate alternative text for informative images and `alt=""` for decoration.
Provide dimensions or an aspect-ratio container so loading does not shift the page.
For video, provide controls, a useful poster, and captions when the content requires them.
Do not leave an inaccessible, expiring, authenticated, or environment-specific URL in copied source.

content.text: When you test the template in an app ({@link generic:test-template-in-app}), also confirm the following.

items: The copied source shows the placeholder substitutions you expect.
The network log has no missing, redirected, blocked, or unauthorized media requests.
Each placeholder keeps the layout and says what the app must replace.

docs.name: template-styles
docs.title: Styles
docs.description: Keep the copied UI on the app's theme: use Astryx props and tokens first, keep editable styles in the file, and ship shared CSS from your package.

content.text: Use Astryx component props, layout primitives, and design tokens before writing custom CSS. This keeps the copied result aligned with the host theme and reduces the styling contract an app inherits.

items: Use Stack and Grid spacing props instead of margins between children.
Use component variants, sizes, padding, and alignment props before restyling internals.
Use public theme token exports for a value that Astryx does not expose as a prop.
Do not copy private generated class names or target component internals with selectors.

sections.title: Keep editable styles with the source

content.text: When a style belongs to the editable starting point, define it in the template file.
Use custom declarations only when no Astryx prop or token fits. Each one counts in the Custom CSS category of {@link generic:template-grading-rubric}.
When a stylesheet must stay package-owned, import it from the template by its public package path.

content.label: templates/acme-dashboard.tsx
content.code: import '@acme/astryx-widgets/styles/acme-dashboard.css';

content.text: Then export that path and include the file in the package ({@link generic:export-template-assets}). TypeScript 6 and later check side-effect imports by default, so this import type-checks only when the app or its framework declares `*.css` modules.

docs.name: templates
docs.title: Templates
docs.summary: Templates are ready-made UI pages or page sections built with Astryx. Apps copy them into their code and adapt them to their product.

blocks.text: In global mode: templates from an integration installed for the computer show up outside projects; inside a project, only templates from integrations the project installs. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: test-in-an-app
docs.title: Test an integration in an app
keywords: try an integration in an app
docs.description: Install your packed package in an app and run the commands its users will run.

sections.title: Install the packed package in an app

content.text: Pack the package beside its folder, so the next pack does not ship it, then install it in an app together with Core and the CLI. The app loads your package because it is a dependency.

items: Install the CLI in the app too: `astryx` runs the CLI from the app's `node_modules`.
The app holds a copy, not a link. After each change, pack again and run the same `{@pm install}`.
Reading your work inside the package shows your source. The app shows what npm would publish.

content.text: From the app folder, run the commands your users run. Each should show your contribution under your package name.

rows: Your section, with guides such as `deploying`

content.text: `--package` narrows `template --list` and `theme list` to one package. `component --list` ignores it and lists Core too, so look a component up by name. Last, import `AcmeCarousel` in the app's code and build the app, as your users will.
`{@command doctor}` checks the whole app, including every package it loaded. `doctor integration validate` checks your package as the app installed it.

content.code:
{@command doctor}
{@command doctor integration validate @acme/astryx-widgets}

id:      implicit-integrations
status:  [info]
label:   Implicitly linked integrations
message: 1 integration loaded from installed dependencies with no astryx.config entry: @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0 from dependencies, contributing components, templates, themes, docs, codemods.

items: The `implicit-integrations` row names each package the app loads with no config. `[info]` is expected.
The `docs-progressive-disclosure` row warns when one of your doc sections is over 32 KB. The `doctor integration` checks do not measure size.
`doctor integration validate @acme/astryx-widgets` prints `[ok] No integration issues found.` when the installed copy is sound.

docs.name: test-template-in-app
docs.title: Test in an app
docs.description: Prove the template works the way apps use it: installed from the packed package, copied, built, and rendered.

content.text: Install the packed package in a clean app as described in {@link generic:test-in-an-app}. Also install every library the copied source imports, such as its icon library. Pack and reinstall after every change.

items: Confirm the copied files: `src/app/acme-dashboard/page.tsx` and `src/components/acme-stat-card.tsx`.
Inspect the copied source for placeholder substitutions and relative references.
Import the copied block into a real page. A file that is never imported has not been tested.

content.text: Run the type check (`{@pm exec tsc --noEmit}`, or the app's own script) and the production build in every framework or bundler the integration supports. One toolchain passing does not prove another.

content.code:
{@pm exec tsc --noEmit}
{@pm run build}

items: Every import resolves from the copied location.
Production builds keep required side-effect CSS.
No import bypasses `exports`, and no dependency resolves only through workspace hoisting.

rows: Wide and narrow; include the smallest supported viewport
Every supported color mode and theme
Keyboard and pointer for the primary task
Realistic, empty, long, loading, and error states that the pattern supports
Successful CSS, font, icon, image, poster, and video requests
No console error, hydration mismatch, or missing-provider failure

content.text: Check the rendered hierarchy, reading order, focus order, clipping, overflow, and fallback states. A screenshot of one default state is not a complete test.
Grade the exact packed revision using the evidence from this test ({@link namespace:write-good-templates}).

docs.name: theme
docs.title: Theming
docs.description: How to use and create themes: see Use a theme for applying themes, and Author a theme for creating and customizing them.

sections.title: Wrap your app in a theme

content.text: Install a theme, import it with the CLI, and wire the generated module once. For the full guide — available themes, integration themes, dark mode, nested themes, and production builds — see {@link generic:use-a-theme}.

content.label: Wire the generated module once

content.text: Use `defineTheme` with token overrides, scale configs, and component style overrides. For the full guide — palette generation, extending themes, adaptations, custom variants, and production builds — see {@link generic:author-a-theme}.

content.label: Quick start

content.text: For a new coordinated color system, run `{@command theme palette generate palette.config.json --out palette.generated.ts}`. Review and commit the generated palette module and receipt, import its `palette` export, then reference stable stops from semantic tokens. Regenerating an accepted palette updates every mapped token that keeps those references; generation does not rewrite the theme.

content.label: Map semantic tokens to generated palette stops

content.text: A theme sets the dimension of each Icon size in its stylesheet: `width` and `height` on `components.icon['size:sm']` (or `xsm`, `md`, `lg`) resize that size's glyph, for semantic icon names and SVG components passed to `Icon` alike. Give the dimension in `px` or `rem`: a semantic icon takes its font size from it, so an `em` value would also grow its box. A size the theme leaves alone stays 12, 16, 20, or 24px at a 16px root (`xsm`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`) and scales with the root font size; `rem` keeps that scaling. The four size names are fixed.

content.label: Set Icon size dimensions

content.text: Light, dark, and system modes: {@link generic:use-a-theme}.

content.label: Light/dark tuple
content.code:
'--color-accent': ['#0064E0', '#2694FE'],
//                   ^light     ^dark

content.text: Install an integration and Astryx discovers its themes automatically. Import one with `{@command theme add <name> --package <integration>}`. Use `theme eject` only for an independent source fork. For the full walkthrough, see {@link generic:use-a-theme}.

docs.name: themes
docs.title: Themes
docs.summary: Author a theme in your integration; apps install, apply, and extend it like any theme.

blocks.text: In global mode: outside projects, the theme list includes themes from integrations installed for the computer, and `theme add` there only shows them; inside a project, it lists only themes from integrations the project installs. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

A theme contribution has editable `defineTheme` source plus a built module and production CSS. `integration add theme` scaffolds the source and declares the package exports; `theme build` writes the built outputs. An app installs the package, runs `theme add`, applies the theme from its generated app module, and customizes it with `extends` instead of copying source.

These guides cover the whole path: scaffold the source, generate its palette, define and build the theme, ship fonts and assets, run `integration verify`, and document how apps add and extend it. Applying a theme, including mode and SSR, works the same for every theme; see {@link generic:use-a-theme}.

docs.name: tokens-and-setup
docs.title: Tokens & Setup
docs.description: Using design tokens in custom styles and configuring a StyleX compiler for swizzled components.

content.text: When writing custom styles, use design tokens instead of hardcoded values. Tokens are CSS custom properties that adapt to the active theme and color mode. The system provides tokens for spacing, color, radius, shadow, typography, and size.

content.label: Using tokens in stylex.create
Using typed token imports in stylex.create

content.text: Both approaches work: var() strings or typed imports from tokens.stylex. The typed imports give autocomplete and catch typos at build time.

See {@link namespace:tokens} for the full token reference (all spacing, color, radius, shadow, and typography tokens with values). See {@link generic:author-a-theme} for how to override tokens via defineTheme.

sections.title: StyleX Build Setup (required for swizzled components)

content.text: Astryx components ship pre-compiled: `astryx.css` and each package's own stylesheet hold all of their styles, so consuming the published packages needs no StyleX setup. But `{@command swizzle <Component>}` copies the raw StyleX *source* into your app, and StyleX source requires a build-time StyleX compiler to produce atomic CSS. Without one, importing the component throws an error that starts `Unexpected 'stylex.create' call at runtime`, and the page does not render. If a swizzled component throws that error, the app is missing a StyleX compiler. The same applies if you author your own StyleX with `stylex.create()`.

rows: An SWC-based transform; see the Next.js note below

content.text: Next.js (App Router) is the sharp edge. StyleX's canonical compiler is a Babel plugin, but introducing a Babel config in Next.js disables the SWC compiler, and with it SWC-dependent features like `next/font`.

The repo's `apps/example-nextjs-stylex` takes the Babel path (`next/babel`, `@stylexjs/babel-plugin`, `@stylexjs/postcss-plugin`). Babel turns off SWC, so that app does not use `next/font`. To keep `next/font`, use an SWC transform such as `@stylexswc/nextjs-plugin`.

content.label: next.config.mjs: SWC-based StyleX transform (keeps next/font working)

items: Symptom of a missing compiler: importing a swizzled component throws an error that starts `Unexpected 'stylex.create' call at runtime`, and the page does not render.
A Babel config turns off SWC in Next.js; skip it if you need `next/font`.
Pure theming (defineTheme + astryx theme build) needs NO StyleX compiler; only swizzled/authored StyleX source does.
Keep loading `astryx.css` with a StyleX compiler in place. The compiler builds your own and swizzled source only; never add `node_modules/@astryxdesign` to its inputs.

docs.name: tokens-duration
docs.title: Duration Tokens
docs.description: Motion duration primitives. Three bands: fast (micro-interactions), medium (entrance/exit), slow (continuous). Min/max variants derive from base × ratio. Of a theme's two `motion` knobs, `tempo` (0.75–1.5) scales every duration here; `character` leaves durations alone. A duration scale beats `tempo` for the bands it sets, and explicit `tokens` beat both. `tempo` leaves these unscaled: finger tracking, momentum, the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard, the press's onset delay, cancel distance and tap flash, hover-intent delays, gesture thresholds, Spinner's and Skeleton's loops, and the 200 ms Reduce Motion cap.

Of a theme's two `motion` knobs, `tempo` (0.75–1.5) scales every duration here; `character` leaves durations alone. A duration scale beats `tempo` for the bands it sets, and explicit `tokens` beat both. `tempo` leaves these unscaled: finger tracking, momentum, the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard, the press's onset delay, cancel distance and tap flash, hover-intent delays, gesture thresholds, Spinner's and Skeleton's loops, and the 200 ms Reduce Motion cap.

docs.name: tokens-ease
docs.title: Easing Tokens
docs.description: Easing curves for animations and transitions. Of a theme's two `motion` knobs, `character` sets `--ease-entrance` and `--ease-move`: `crisp` decelerates without overshoot, `expressive` overshoots slightly, and at `standard` both equal `--ease-standard`; `--ease-exit` keeps its own curve at every character. `tempo` leaves curves alone. A duration scale's own fields win over the knobs, and explicit `tokens` win over everything. No curve here shapes motion that follows a finger or the system (dragging, momentum, the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard), and the press's clocks, hover-intent delays and gesture thresholds keep their timing whatever the character.

docs.name: troubleshooting
docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.description: Find the message the CLI printed while you build, verify, or install an integration, and apply its fix.

content.text: These appear while you start the package or run the CLI in it. Each row quotes what the CLI prints.

rows: `No package.json found. Run this command inside an integration package.`
Run `{@pm-only npm "writes package.json" init -y}` and `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set name=@acme/astryx-widgets}` first, in the package folder.
Component commands read Core. Run `{@pm install @astryxdesign/core --dev}` in the package.
`core_not_found`: `Could not resolve @astryxdesign/core, so component names could not be checked.`
`Error: unknown subcommand 'integration verify'`, or `Error: Pass --check to verify the integration tarball.`
Your CLI is older than `integration verify`. Run `{@pm install @astryxdesign/cli@latest --dev}`. On the older CLI, the same check is `integration pack --check`.
The old name still runs the same check. Switch to `{@command integration verify}`; the old name will be removed in a later release.

content.text: `{@command integration verify}` prints each failure as a `[fail]` line. Add `--json` to see its issue code, such as `component_export_missing`.

rows: `component_export_missing`: `Component "AcmeCarousel" advertises import "@acme/astryx-widgets/components/AcmeCarousel", but that packed module does not export "AcmeCarousel".`

package.json has no `exports` map, or the module does not export the name. Keep `export function AcmeCarousel`, and add the entry: `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'exports[./components/AcmeCarousel]=./components/AcmeCarousel.tsx'}`. When the quoted name is a file name, such as `acme-carousel`, set the doc's `name` to the component the file exports. A type-only export does not count.
`template_export_missing`: `Template "acme-dashboard" public import "@acme/astryx-widgets/templates/acme-dashboard" does not have a default export.`

Run `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'exports[./templates/acme-dashboard]=./templates/acme-dashboard.tsx'}`, and keep `export default` in the source. Start new packages with `"exports": {}` so each add writes these.
`component_import_unresolvable` or `template_import_unresolvable`: `…Package subpath './components/AcmeCarousel' is not defined by "exports"…`

The `exports` map has no entry for it. Run `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'exports[./components/AcmeCarousel]=./components/AcmeCarousel.tsx'}`, or `'exports[./templates/acme-dashboard]=./templates/acme-dashboard.tsx'` for a template.
`component_import_unresolvable`: `…but a consumer cannot resolve it: Cannot find package '@acme/old-name'`
You renamed the package after the add wrote each doc's `import`. Change `import` in every component doc to the new name.
`Declared templates root "templates" has 0 of 2 expected files in the pack list. Add "templates" to "files" in package.json.`
`docs_tree_needs_cli`: `The package ships a namespace doc or a placed guide but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.`

Run `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.4'}` and `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json}`.
`replaces_needs_cli`: The package has a template that sets `replaces` but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.

Run `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.4'}` and `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json}`. A stable CLI before 0.6.4 rejects `replaces`, drops that template, and hides your doc topics.
`component_replaces_needs_cli` (a warning): The package has a component that sets `replaces` but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer, or a peer range that admits an earlier CLI.

Run `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.7'}` and `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json}` to turn the replacement on. Until then apps see no change ({@link generic:replace-a-core-component}).
`keywords_needs_cli`: The package has a template that sets `keywords` but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.

Run `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.6'}` and `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json}`. What an older CLI does with the field is in {@link generic:template-doc-overview}.
`themes_need_cli`: The package ships a theme but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.

Run `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.4'}` and `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json}`. A CLI older than published 0.6.4 cannot read typed theme descriptors, so it drops your themes and can hide your doc topics.
`section_ids_need_cli`: The package has a doc section that sets `id` but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.
The same fix as `themes_need_cli`, or drop the section `id`s: a CLI older than published 0.6.4 rejects them and hides your doc topics.
`doc_tokens_need_cli`: The package writes doc tokens (`{@@command …}`, `{@@pm …}`, `{@@pm-only …}`) in its docs, but its @astryxdesign/cli peer admits a CLI before 0.7.4.

Run `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.7.4'}` and `{@pm-only npm "edits package.json" pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json}`. A CLI before 0.7.4 prints each token as written, so readers see raw tokens.

content.text: These appear in an app that installs your package, or in the doctor checks that predict them.

rows: `Error: No component named "AcmeCarousel"` for a component your package documents.

Its doc still names its file. Set `name` to the export, such as `name: 'AcmeCarousel'` in `acme-carousel.doc.mjs`. A family member is listed only when the module its family doc imports exports it ({@link generic:component-family}).
`{@command component Dialog}` opens Core's `Dialog`, not yours.

A name that Core, a legacy docs package, or another package's file already has stays theirs. Run `{@command component Dialog --package @acme/astryx-widgets}`, or give your component a name of its own.
`Error: Template "dashboard" is ambiguous — narrow it with --type and/or --package.`

Your template id matches a Core id. Rename it, such as `acme-dashboard`, or set `replaces: 'dashboard'` to take its place. `{@command doctor integration templates}` warns about this before you publish.
The guide stays hidden until its `placement` names a namespace and slot your package declares. For `"…" names no doc`, fix the link target.
Error: Unknown topic "acme". The docs of @acme/astryx-widgets did not load; run `{@command doctor integration docs}` in that package to see why.
One invalid doc hides all of your docs. Run `{@command doctor integration docs}` in the package and fix the `invalid_doc` it names.
`cli-command` warns: `Loaded integrations declare different CLI commands`

Two packages the app loads set different `cliCommand` values, so the CLI prints the package manager's command. Agree on one command, or remove the package that does not belong. See {@link generic:cli-command}.
Your `cliCommand` is not one line of plain text of at most 120 characters, so it is ignored. Fix the value; the rest of the manifest still loads.
`{@command upgrade}` runs none of your codemods

The app must list your package in `integrations` in `astryx.config`, or pass `--integration @acme/astryx-widgets`. It runs a codemod folder only when its version is after `--from` and at most the installed `@astryxdesign/core`.
Your docs section, templates, or themes are missing only in some apps

Those apps run a CLI too old to read them ({@link generic:checks} lists which field needs which CLI). Update `@astryxdesign/cli` there, and keep your optional `@astryxdesign/cli` peer so npm checks the app's CLI against it when the app installs your package.

content.text: What each check catches is in {@link generic:checks}.

docs.name: type-scale
docs.title: Type Scale
docs.description: Line height, semantic type scale tokens, display text, Heading and Text components, and custom type scales via defineTheme.

content.text: Line heights are computed from a tiered target ratio and snapped to a 4px vertical grid. Small text (<20px) targets 1.5, medium text (20–31px) targets 1.4, and large text (≥32px) targets 1.25. A minimum gap of fontSize + 4px is enforced. The result is a unitless ratio stored in each --text-*-leading token.

The 4px grid matters: every line box aligns to 4px increments, which keeps baselines, spacing, and component heights predictable. The expandTypeScale utility computes these automatically when you provide a base and ratio, so you should never need to set line-height manually.

Semantic tokens that combine size, weight, and line-height into a single type style. Each token triplet (--text-*-size, --text-*-weight, --text-*-leading) is consumed by Text and Heading. Use the component props rather than composing raw font tokens.
Semantic tokens for headings, body, labels, code, supporting text, and display text. References font size and weight tokens. Override via typography.scale in defineTheme.

Display variants (display-1, display-2, display-3) continue the geometric progression above heading-1, at steps +6, +5, and +4. They use normal weight (400) instead of semibold, and tighter line-heights (~1.2), since large text reads better with less leading. Use display types for hero banners, marketing headlines, and data callouts, not for document headings.

Display text often needs heading semantics for accessibility. Use the type prop on Heading to apply display styling while preserving the correct HTML element: `<Heading level={1} type="display-1">` gives you display-1 styling with an `<h1>` tag, so screen readers see the correct document outline.
Use `Heading` for document structure and `Text` for everything else; each maps its props to the type scale tokens.

content.label: Heading for document structure
Text for body, label, and display text
content.code:
import {Text} from '@astryxdesign/core/Text';

<Text type="body">Body text at the base scale.</Text>
<Text type="large">Emphasized body text.</Text>
<Text type="label">Form label</Text>
<Text type="supporting">Helper text, timestamps, metadata.</Text>
<Text type="code">{'const x = 1;'}</Text>

// Display without heading semantics (data callouts, decorative)
<Text type="display-2">$1.2M Revenue</Text>

content.text: Change the whole ramp with `base` and `ratio` in `defineTheme`; every font size and line height recomputes from them.

docs.description: Do/don't rules for using the type scale, headings, display text, and semantic tokens.

items: Use Heading for document headings and Text for everything else; they apply the full type scale automatically.
Adjust typography holistically: change base and ratio in defineTheme to shift the entire ramp (e.g. { base: 16, ratio: 1.25 } for editorial, { base: 12, ratio: 1.125 } for dense UI).

Use display types with as="h1" (or h2/h3) when display text is a page heading; this preserves accessibility while giving you display-level sizing. Or better, use `<Heading level={1} type="display-1">` which handles both semantics and styling.
Let line-height snap to the 4px grid via the type scale; expandTypeScale computes leading automatically from base and ratio.
Use the supporting type for secondary information: timestamps, helper text, metadata, captions.
Use accessibilityLevel on Heading when the visual hierarchy doesn't match the document outline (e.g. sidebar or card headings).
Set font-size or line-height manually; use the semantic type scale tokens so the full ramp stays consistent and 4px-grid-aligned.
Skip heading levels (e.g. h1 to h3); screen readers rely on an unbroken hierarchy. Use accessibilityLevel to decouple visual from semantic level.
Use display types for body content or in-page sections; they're designed for hero/marketing/data-callout contexts only.
Override individual size tokens (--font-size-lg) to "tweak" a heading; adjust base/ratio instead so proportions remain coherent across the entire scale.
Use raw numeric font-weight values (400, 600); reference the semantic weight tokens so themes can remap them.

docs.name: uninstall
docs.title: Uninstall and reset
docs.description: Remove your global install, the agent guide it keeps, and the folders it uses, or reset them to start over.

content.text: While the CLI is still installed, remove the agent guide from your home folder:

content.code: {@command init --user --remove-agents}

content.text: Or delete `~/.agents/skills/astryx` and the links to it listed in {@link generic:computer-agent-guide}.

content.code:
{@pm remove @astryxdesign/cli --global}
# with Volta: volta uninstall @astryxdesign/cli

content.text: Projects are unaffected: each keeps the CLI it installs, if any.
Delete either folder to reset it; Astryx recreates what it needs on the next run.

rows: Cache: versions for projects, saved discover answers
Settings: update checks, the agent guide setting, and its links

content.text: On Linux, `XDG_CACHE_HOME` and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` move them when set to absolute paths.
This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works.

docs.name: updates
docs.title: Updates and notices
docs.description: Your global install checks for a newer version once a day and prints a two-line notice after a command succeeds. It never upgrades itself or a project.

content.text: Once a day, never in your first day, your global install checks the registry's `latest` version in the background, without slowing the command. When a newer one exists, a command that succeeds prints two lines on standard error, at most once a day:

content.code:
A new release of Astryx is available: 0.7.2 → 0.7.3
To upgrade, run: npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest

items: The command is the one for the package manager that installed your global install: `npm i -g`, `pnpm add -g`, `yarn global add`, `bun add -g`, or `volta install`. A global folder moved with the package manager's own setting (`BUN_INSTALL`, Yarn's `global-folder`, `PNPM_HOME`, or npm's prefix) counts while that setting names it; an app's own copy never runs the update check.
When the newest version needs a newer Node than your computer runs, the second line says which Node to install first.

Inside a project, the notice is about the project's version, and names the project's install and `upgrade` commands. The install command always adds the CLI next to Core, so a project that installed only Core gets its own CLI too, as recommended.

content.code:
A new release of Astryx is available: 0.7.1 → 0.7.3
To upgrade, run: pnpm add @astryxdesign/core@0.7.3 @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.3, then pnpm exec astryx upgrade --from 0.7.1 --apply

content.text: No notice prints with `--json`, after a failed command, when the `CI` environment variable is set, or when `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER` is set; with either variable set, the CLI does not check the registry either. Unlike some CLIs, a notice prints even when standard error is not a terminal, because agents run the CLI without one.

`{@command doctor}` shows the same thing at any time, in its `newest-release` check, along with why the last notice did not print, if one did not. When the last check ran, and when each notice printed, are kept in `state.json` in the settings folder ({@link generic:reference}).
This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works. Upgrading a project: {@link command:upgrade}.

docs.name: upgrading
docs.title: Upgrading
docs.description: Update your package for each Astryx release, and help apps upgrade with it.

sections.title: Update for a new Astryx release

content.text: When Astryx ships a release, bump your devDependencies, rerun the checks, widen your peer ranges, and ship a codemod for each change that breaks apps.

items: Run every check in {@link generic:checks}, not only the ones shown.
Codemod folders are named for Core versions: {@link generic:codemods}.
Release the result as a new version of your package; see {@link generic:publishing}.

content.text: After an app installs a new Core, `{@command upgrade}` runs the codemods for the versions it crossed. It is a dry run by default; `--apply` writes the changes.

content.code:
Integrations: @acme/astryx-widgets
<n> codemods to run
Applying integration codemods...
  Rename AcmeCarousel delay to interval (v0.7.0, @acme/astryx-widgets)
[ok]     [ok] src/Hero.tsx

items: `--from` is the `@astryxdesign/core` version the app had before, and the target is the installed Core.
`--integration` names your package. Without it, or an `integrations` entry in `astryx.config`, the upgrade skips your codemods, even when the app has your package installed.
`<n>` includes Core's codemods for the same versions, which run first.
Put this command in your release notes.

content.text: Upgrades never write files that the app marks as generated, vendored, or ignored. When such a file still needs a codemod change, the upgrade stops with `ERR_CODEMOD_PROTECTED` and exit code 1.

items: Generated: an `@generated` comment at the top of the file, or `linguist-generated` in `.gitattributes`.
Vendored: `linguist-vendored` in `.gitattributes`.
Ignored: a match in `.gitignore` or `.hgignore`.

content.code:
!     ! src/gen/Gen.tsx - protected by @generated in the leading comment block
ERR_CODEMOD_PROTECTED: 1 protected file still requires a codemod change:
  src/gen/Gen.tsx — @generated in the leading comment block
Upgrade incomplete: protected changes remain

content.text: The upgrade still writes every other file. Its options and exit codes are in {@link command:upgrade}.

docs.name: use-a-theme
docs.title: Use a theme
docs.description: Apply a theme to your app: install, import with the CLI, wire the generated module, switch dark mode, nest themes, and choose runtime or built for production.

sections.title: Wrap your app in a theme

content.label: Install and add a theme
content.code:
{@pm install @astryxdesign/theme-neutral}
{@command theme add neutral}

content.label: Wire the generated module once
Switch among added themes

content.text: `theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported theme becomes the default. `theme use <slug>` changes that default, and `theme remove <slug>` removes a non-default theme.

Customize a package theme with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`, then build and add that local theme. Use `theme eject` only when you want an independent source fork that no longer receives the package owner's updates. For the full authoring guide, see {@link generic:author-a-theme}.

A theme copied by the released `theme add` stays app source. The upgrade does not move, delete, or rewrite it. It only writes the missing same-stem descriptor with `maintained: false`, so the copy becomes a local theme.

content.label: Add descriptors to earlier copies
content.code: {@command upgrade --from 0.6.4 --path . --apply}

content.text: Before the upgrade runs, theme commands skip a descriptor-less copy in `src/themes`. `theme list` and doctor name it as unmigrated and show the upgrade command. A script that meant to copy source now runs `theme eject` with the same arguments. A script that meant to make the app use a theme runs `theme add`.

`ASTRYX_THEME` is no longer read. Run `theme add <slug>` and `theme use <slug>` to choose the default in a generated app theme module. When that module exists, component metadata reads its recorded default theme. Without the module, the released `package.json#astryx.theme` lookup keeps its meaning.
Install the theme package you want with `{@pm install @astryxdesign/theme-<name>}`, then import its slug with `theme add <slug>`. The CLI imports the package's built outputs for you.

rows: Muted, minimal aesthetic with Figtree typography. A good starting point.
Golden, buttery surfaces with blue accents; Sarina + Outfit type.
Warm brown tones and cozy beige; Fraunces + Albert Sans type.
Dark-only atmospheric theme; deep blue-gray surfaces, distressed display type.
Earthy greens; DM Sans + Playwrite US Trad type.
Warm stone and slate tones; Montserrat + Figtree type.
Playful Y2K pop; periwinkle body, holographic accents, Poppins + Crimson Text.

content.text: Every first-party package exports its built theme at `@astryxdesign/theme-{name}/built`, production CSS at `/theme.css`, and font loading CSS at `/fonts.css`. `theme add` writes those imports into the generated app module.
`<Theme>` takes `theme` (required), `mode` (`'system'` by default, or `'light'`/`'dark'`), and `children`. For every prop, run `{@command component Theme}`.

sections.title: Using a Theme from an Integration

content.text: Install the integration as a direct dependency. Astryx discovers its themes and guides without an `astryx.config` entry. A theme can be added only when the installed package exports its built module and production stylesheet.

content.label: Install, inspect, and add

content.text: `theme add` keeps the owner package in the app record and imports its built module, stylesheet, and optional font stylesheet. Package updates continue to reach the app. Run `theme eject ocean --package @acme/brand-integration` only to copy the source and descriptor into `src/themes/ocean` as an independent local fork.
Use [light, dark] tuples in token values for automatic mode switching. Use mode='system' (default) on Theme to follow OS preference.

content.label: Light/dark tuple
content.code:
'--color-accent': ['#0064E0', '#2694FE'],
//                   ^light     ^dark

content.label: Toggle with a button

content.text: To create a theme with custom dark mode colors, see {@link generic:author-a-theme}.
Wrap different sections in separate `<Theme>` providers.

content.label: Dark sidebar with light content
content.code:
<Theme theme={lightTheme} mode="light">
  <Layout
    header={<LayoutHeader>...</LayoutHeader>}
    start={
      <Theme theme={darkTheme} mode="dark">
        <LayoutPanel>{/* Dark sidebar */}</LayoutPanel>
      </Theme>
    }
    content={<LayoutContent>{/* Light content */}</LayoutContent>}
  />
</Theme>

content.text: Themes work in two modes:

rows: Pre-compiled .css file loaded with the page
In static CSS: present during SSR
Tokens yes, component overrides flash on hydration
App wiring, in development and production

items: Use `theme add` for production apps; it wires the built module and CSS.
Import `themes` and `defaultThemeSlug` from the generated module once, and keep that wiring in development too.
While you edit a local theme, run `{@command theme build --watch}` so its built files stay current.
Run `{@command theme build}` for custom themes to get the built artifacts.
Use runtime themes in production SSR apps; component overrides will flash on hydration.
Import /built without the CSS file; component overrides won't apply.
Import package theme source into app runtime code.
Hand-edit the generated theme module; `theme add`, `theme remove`, and `theme use` regenerate it.

content.text: To build a custom theme for production, see the Build section of {@link generic:author-a-theme}.

docs.name: use-a-theme-in-an-app
docs.title: Use and extend the theme
docs.description: An app installs the integration and applies or extends your theme, the same as any theme.

content.text: Install the integration, then run `theme add` with its slug and package. The command records the package owner and regenerates one app theme module that imports the built theme, production CSS, and optional font CSS. Use `theme eject` only to copy source into an independent local fork.

content.code:
{@pm install @acme/astryx-widgets}
{@command theme add ocean --package @acme/astryx-widgets}

content.text: `theme list` shows the available, added, and default themes. Use `theme use <slug>` to change the default, `theme remove <slug>` to stop importing one, and `theme eject <slug>` only when the app needs an independent source fork. Applying a theme — `mode`, SSR, and the production build — works the same for every theme; see {@link generic:use-a-theme}.

For ordinary customization, do not copy the package source. Import the built theme and derive a new one with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`, overriding only the tokens the app changes. Use `theme eject` only when the app must own an independent source fork. See {@link generic:define-the-theme}.

In global mode: install the theme package in each app that uses the theme; inside a project, the CLI ignores packages installed for the computer. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

docs.name: use-integrations
docs.title: Use integrations
docs.description: Install, discover, and use integration packages that add components, templates, themes, and docs to your app.

content.text: Integration packages extend Astryx with extra components, templates, themes, docs, and codemods. They are published as regular npm packages.
Search for what you need:

content.code:
astryx search carousel
astryx discover

content.text: `search` looks across everything the CLI knows (components, docs, templates, themes, and hooks), so a word like "carousel" finds it whether it is a component, a template, or a doc page. `discover` lists every integration the project has, and, with a discover source, packages it could add.
Install the package with your package manager. Integrations autolink: the CLI finds them among your dependencies, so installing is all it takes:

content.code: {@pm install @acme/brand-integration}

content.text: Run `astryx doctor` to confirm everything is wired up. If you need to load a package that is not a direct dependency, add it explicitly to `astryx.config.mjs`:

content.label: Optional: explicit config entry

content.text: Once installed, the integration's contributions appear alongside Core:

items: `astryx component --list` shows its components next to Core components.
`astryx template --list` includes its page and block templates.
`astryx theme list` lists its themes; add one with `astryx theme add <slug> --package @acme/brand-integration`.
`astryx docs` shows any guides it provides.
`astryx search <query>` finds everything, from every installed integration.

content.text: Import components at the subpath the integration documents. Run `astryx component <Name>` to see the exact import:

content.code: import {AcmeCarousel} from '@acme/brand-integration/components/AcmeCarousel';

content.text: For themes, see {@link generic:use-a-theme}. To build an integration of your own, see {@link namespace:authoring}.
Run `astryx doctor` to see integration issues: missing roots, invalid contributions, or a CLI version mismatch. The doctor check is the one place every issue for every package is listed.

content.code: astryx doctor

docs.name: verify-packed-template
docs.title: Verify the packed package
docs.description: Catch missing files, exports, and CLI requirements before you publish, and know what still needs the app test.

content.code: {@command integration verify}

content.text: `integration verify` runs `{@pm-only npm "the tarball the registry receives" pack}`, including lifecycle scripts, unpacks the `.tgz` file into a temporary app without installing its dependencies, and checks the unpacked integration. It publishes nothing and removes the `.tgz` file and the temporary app.

items: It validates the manifest, every template doc, its source file, and the templates directory.
It checks that the manifest and every template file are in the `.tgz` file.
It checks that each packed template keeps the same id, type, `name`, and `replaces` as your working copy. It does not compare template source or other doc fields.
It resolves each template through its public package path in the unpacked package.
It checks that the resolved template module has a default export.
It checks the CLI peer that features such as template replacement require.

content.text: Each failure prints a `[fail]` line with its message; add `--json` to see each issue code. {@link generic:troubleshooting} lists the common messages and their fixes. Fix every error, and review every warning before publishing.

sections.title: Know what it does not prove

content.text: `integration verify` checks the packed templates and their public entrypoints. It does not copy a template into an app or run a browser build, so it cannot show the following.

items: Whether a relative helper or stylesheet survives the copy.
Whether the copied file type-checks in every supported app toolchain.
Whether package-owned CSS, fonts, icons, images, or media load in a browser.
Whether layout, color modes, keyboard and pointer input, and real content work.
Whether a template id collides with Core, or whether a `replaces` target exists. Run `{@command doctor integration templates}` for those.
How the template scores on quality.

docs.name: versioning
docs.title: Versioning
docs.description: Version your package, declare its peers, and keep apps on older CLIs working.

content.text: Version your package with semver: a major version for a breaking change, a minor version for a new feature, and a patch for a fix.

items: Before 1.0.0, npm treats each minor version as breaking: an app that asks for `^0.6.0` never gets `0.7.0`. Bump the minor version for a breaking change, and the patch for anything else.
Ship a codemod with each breaking change so apps can migrate; see {@link generic:codemods}.

content.text: A breaking change stops code, commands, or links that worked in an app from working after the upgrade. For an integration, these names are part of its API.

headers: What stops working in the app
rows: A topic name or route, such as `acme/deploying`
Reads of the old name, and links to it from other docs
Imports written from the old path
Imports of that path, which fail with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`

content.text: List each breaking change in your release notes, with the codemod that migrates it. Any changelog tool works. If `package.json` has a `files` allowlist, add `CHANGELOG.md` to it so npm packs it.
Declare the Astryx packages that your code imports as peer dependencies, in `peerDependencies`, so the app installs one copy of each. Keep each range as wide as your tests prove.

rows: Your code imports Core, as a theme does with `@astryxdesign/core/theme`
The Core versions you test, such as `^0.6.0`
Your code imports that theme package
You ship a docs section, a placed guide, a template that sets `replaces` or `keywords`, a component that sets `replaces`, a doc section with an `id`, or a theme
`>=0.6.6` when you ship a template that sets `keywords`, `>=0.6.7` when a component sets `replaces`, otherwise `>=0.6.4`. Optional in `peerDependenciesMeta`

content.text: `integration verify` fails a package that needs the CLI peer and lacks it, or whose range admits a stable CLI too old for what it ships. `integration add doc --parent` and `integration add theme` write the peer for you.

When the CLI is outside that range, `doctor integration validate` and `integration check` list a `cli_peer_version` note naming your package. A note fails nothing, `--strict` included, and `integration verify` does not report it. Below the range the note gives the commands that install a newer Core and CLI together, as dev dependencies in your own package folder, and then run `upgrade --apply`. Above it, in an app the note asks for a release of your package that supports that CLI, and in your own package folder it asks you to test your package with that CLI and widen the range.
An app may run an older CLI than the one you build with. A CLI reads what it knows and skips the rest, but some newer files make an older CLI hide your docs.

items: An unknown field in `astryx.integration.mjs` is ignored with an `unknown_manifest_key` warning, and the rest of the manifest still loads.
A named export that the CLI does not know is ignored with no warning, so `debug` and `gapReport` are safe to add.
Published 0.6.3 and earlier print each `{@link ...}` as written.

Published 0.6.3 and earlier reject a template that sets `replaces` or `keywords`, drop that template, and hide every doc topic your package ships. Published 0.6.4 and 0.6.5 still drop a template that sets `keywords`.
Published 0.6.3 and earlier cannot read a docs section, a section `id`, or a theme folder that `integration add theme` writes. They can then hide every doc topic your package ships.
Published 0.6.2 and 0.6.3 still load your components, but published 0.6.0 and 0.6.1 cannot read the component docs that `integration add component` writes: `component AcmeCarousel` fails there.
An app on an older CLI lists a component whose doc names another export of its file under the file name, and lists no family members, so `component AcmeCarousel` fails there.

content.text: `integration verify` requires the CLI peer for a docs section, a placed guide, a template `replaces` or `keywords`, a doc section with an `id`, and a theme. A CLI too old for one of them cannot read it, and when it hides your topics, `docs` gives no warning.

sections.title: Name codemod folders after Core versions

content.text: Name each codemod folder after the Core version whose upgrade should run it, not after your package's version. Which folders an app runs, and when, is in "Choose when a codemod runs" in {@link generic:codemods}.

docs.name: who-answers
docs.title: Which version runs, and why
docs.description: Inside a project, the project's own CLI answers, whichever astryx command you start; in a project with only Core, the astryx command you started answers. Outside a project, your global install answers. How to see which one did.

sections.title: In a project, the project's version

items: The project installs the CLI, as recommended: that CLI answers, whatever its version, as it always has. When you type the global astryx command instead, it passes the run to the project's CLI, with the same arguments, input, output, and exit status, so either command gives the same answer.

The project installs only Core, or nothing is installed yet, as in a fresh clone: the astryx command you started answers, as it always has. When its version differs from the project's Core, a hint after the command, once a day, names the command that adds the CLI at Core's version.

The project's CLI is installed but cannot start: the CLI version equal to the project's Core answers instead (from the installed Core, else the lockfile, else the newest one the declared range allows), installed once into a cache.

content.text: Components come from `@astryxdesign/core`, and templates, docs, and agent guides come from the CLI. In a project, that Core is the one the project installs, so component commands work offline once the project's dependencies are installed. Outside a project, or in a project with nothing installed yet (a fresh clone), they use the answering version's own Core, from beside the CLI or the cache; when that Core cannot be downloaded, the error says to install the project's dependencies. When the project's CLI and Core are different versions, `{@command doctor}` warns and prints the command that brings them to one version.

sections.title: Outside a project, your global install

content.text: In a folder that belongs to no project, your global install answers as a brand-new project on its version would, so you and your agents can read every component and doc. It never installs a newer version by itself.
A few commands work on your computer rather than a folder, such as `{@command init --user}`: your global install answers them in any folder.
In a project with only Core, the hint looks like this, after the command, at most once a day per project:

content.code: astryx: this project has no Astryx CLI installed; answered by CLI 0.7.2 while its Core is 0.6.8. To match, run: npm install @astryxdesign/cli@0.6.8

content.text: Otherwise, in text mode, one line on standard error names the version, unless the project's own CLI answered directly:

content.code:
astryx: answered by this project's CLI 0.6.8, handed over from CLI 0.7.2
astryx: answered by CLI 0.6.8 with Core 0.6.8, the release that matches this project's Core
astryx: answered by CLI 0.7.2 with Core 0.7.2, outside a project
astryx: answered by CLI 0.7.2 with Core 0.7.2, for this computer

content.text: With `--json` nothing extra prints; every result carries `meta.answeredBy` instead ({@link generic:reference}):

content.code: {"meta": {"answeredBy": {"cli": "0.7.2", "core": "0.6.8", "copy": "starting"}}}

content.text: Commands the CLI prints for you to run start with a name that reaches the same version: the project's runner (such as `pnpm exec astryx`) in a project, `astryx` outside a project when your global install answered, and otherwise the CLI pinned to the version, such as `{@pm dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.6.8}`. An integration can name its own command: {@link generic:cli-command}.

This page is part of {@link namespace:global}, which explains what global mode is and how each part works. To check your computer, run `{@command doctor}` outside any project ({@link command:doctor}). Monorepos: {@link generic:monorepos}.

docs.name: working-with-ai
docs.title: Working with AI
docs.description: How to set up AI coding tools to generate correct component code.

content.text: The design system is built to be AI-friendly: consistent naming, predictable prop patterns, and a CLI that feeds structured documentation directly into AI context windows. But models still need the right context to avoid falling back to generic React patterns or inventing props.
The CLI includes a built-in agent docs system that generates context files for your AI tool of choice. One command sets up everything your AI needs to write correct component code.
Tell your AI to install the CLI and set itself up:

content.label: Paste this into your AI
content.code: Install @astryxdesign/cli and run `astryx init --features agents` to set up your Astryx context. Read the generated file.

content.text: That's it. The `init --features agents` command generates everything your AI needs (component index, behavioral rules, CLI reference, and package guidance from configured integrations) from the installed project. After a dependency bump, `{@command upgrade --from <old version>}` reports a stale block and adding `--apply` refreshes it.

By default this writes the instructions to `AGENTS.md` (the tool-agnostic standard most agents read), in the project root: the nearest folder whose `package.json` declares an Astryx package, else the nearest with any `package.json`. The search stops at the repository root. In the home folder, or in a settings folder in it outside a project, init writes no agent docs: every folder of the home folder whose name starts with a dot (`~/.claude`, `~/.gemini`, `~/.codex`) is a settings folder, and such a folder itself never counts as a project, even with a `package.json`; a project below it with its own `package.json`, such as an agent worktree, is set up normally. Claude Code skips `AGENTS.md` when the project has a `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so init also writes them to that file, even when it imports `AGENTS.md`: Claude Code does not follow that import in a session started in a subfolder. When both files exist, root `CLAUDE.md` gets the copy and a copy in `.claude/CLAUDE.md` is removed, unless the project ignores `CLAUDE.md`, in which case a `.claude/CLAUDE.md` the project commits keeps a copy. Gemini CLI reads only `GEMINI.md`, so init adds a one-line import of `AGENTS.md` there, unless `GEMINI.md` already imports it. `upgrade` keeps the copies in sync. The block between the Astryx markers belongs to Astryx: init and `upgrade` write, refresh, and remove it whatever the project's ignore rules or generated markers say, and never change the text around it. To target a specific tool's file instead:

content.label: Manual options
content.code:
{@command init --features agents --agent claude}    # CLAUDE.md if present, else .claude/CLAUDE.md
{@command init --features agents --agent cursor}    # .cursorrules if present, else AGENTS.md
{@command init --features agents --agent codex}     # AGENTS.md (Copilot, Codex, etc.)
{@command init --features agents --agent hermes}    # .hermes.md or HERMES.md if present, else AGENTS.md
{@command init --features agents --agent muse}      # AGENTS.md (Muse)
{@command init --features agents --agent all}       # every agent file present except GEMINI.md, else AGENTS.md and .claude/CLAUDE.md

content.text: With `--agent all`, `GEMINI.md` keeps its one-line import of `AGENTS.md`. With `--agent claude` or `--agent all`, as by default, when `CLAUDE.md` gets the instructions, `.claude/CLAUDE.md` gets none and a copy already there is removed, unless the project ignores `CLAUDE.md`: a fresh clone does not have it, so a `.claude/CLAUDE.md` the project commits gets a copy too, with `--agent claude` and `--agent all` alike. `init --remove-agents` removes them at the project root and in the folder it runs in.

For agents that work outside any one project, your global install keeps one short Astryx skill, `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, linked into the skill folders agent tools read, such as `~/.claude/skills/astryx`. It tells agents Astryx is there and when to use it; `{@command init --user}` writes it now or, with `--remove-agents`, turns it off. Inside a project, agents follow that project's own agent docs. See {@link generic:computer-agent-guide}.
The generated context teaches your AI a 3-step workflow before writing any UI code:

items: `{@command build "<idea>"}`: get the page template to start from (always one: the closest match, or the app shell), two other templates, and the blocks and components for the parts it lacks
`{@command template <name> <path>}`: scaffold that template into the project, keep its frame and spacing, and replace its content
`{@command component <Name>}`: read props and examples for every component used

content.text: It also includes rules that prevent common mistakes (start every page from a template, no raw divs, no style={{}}, use tokens not magic values), a CLI quick reference, and package-labeled integration guidance when a configured manifest declares `agentDocs`. After setup, you shouldn't need to manually correct your AI on these conventions; the agent docs handle it at the system level.

Cursor reads project rules from `.cursor/rules/`. To keep the Astryx context in a rule of its own, write it there. Give a path relative to the project root, such as `.cursor/rules/astryx.mdc`; an absolute path is refused.

content.label: Install as a Cursor project rule
content.code: {@command init --features agents --agent-docs-path .cursor/rules/astryx.mdc}

content.text: Rerunning the same command rewrites only the Astryx block, so frontmatter you add above it (such as `alwaysApply: true`) stays.
Paste this into your AI before writing any component code. If your AI can't answer these questions, it'll know to install the agent docs first.

content.label: Paste this into your AI
content.code:
Before writing any Astryx code, check your knowledge:

1. What is the correct import path for Button?
2. How do you make a Dialog non-dismissible?
3. What prop does Selector use for its items?

If you don't know all three, run `astryx init --features agents` to generate agent docs, then read the generated file.

content.text: AI agents frequently invoke the CLI with incorrect paths (e.g. node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/bin/docs.mjs instead of astryx.mjs), leading to silent failures. Adding an npm script alias with the correct path eliminates this entirely.

content.label: package.json

content.text: With this alias, agents run `npm run astryx -- component --list` instead of guessing the binary path. The `--` separator is standard npm convention for passing flags to scripts.

content.label: Reliable CLI invocation
content.code:
npm run astryx -- component --list
npm run astryx -- component Dialog --dense
npm run astryx -- docs styling --full --detail brief
npm run astryx -- docs tokens --dense

content.text: For a shorter read, add `--detail brief` (one line per section) or `--detail compact`. `--dense` swaps in a shorter text where a doc ships one. Use them when pasting CLI output into a web-based AI tool like ChatGPT or Claude.

content.label: Short output for pasting into AI conversations

content.text: Astryx ships a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that any MCP-compatible AI tool can connect to. Instead of manually pasting CLI output, the AI can query the Astryx design system directly, searching for components, reading full documentation, and pulling code examples on demand.
The MCP server exposes two tools: search(query) for discovering components, doc topics, and templates; and get(name) for retrieving full documentation with props, usage, and examples.

Add the server to your MCP config file. The entry is a remote HTTP server, and the exact shape differs per client, so use the snippet for the tool you run. An entry with an unrecognized transport is skipped with a warning rather than an error, which reads as a server that connects but exposes no tools.

content.label: Claude Code (.mcp.json)

content.text: Claude Code can also write that entry from the terminal:

content.code: claude mcp add --transport http astryx https://astryx.atmeta.com/mcp

content.label: Cline (cline_mcp_settings.json) - type is streamableHttp
Cursor (.cursor/mcp.json) - remote servers take no type field

content.text: Claude Desktop is the exception: claude_desktop_config.json holds local stdio servers, so a remote server is added through Settings, then Connectors, then Add custom connector, pasting the URL above.

Once connected, your AI tool can search for components by natural language (e.g. "dropdown menu", "success message") and retrieve full documentation without any manual CLI invocation. The server uses the same keyword index from component docs, so search quality improves automatically as component documentation is updated.

In global mode: your global install keeps one Astryx skill in your home folder, linked into the folders agent tools read, so agents outside any project know Astryx is there; inside a project, its own agent docs come first. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:computer-agent-guide}.

docs.name: write-good-templates
docs.title: How to write good templates
docs.summary: Write templates people trust: what good means, the rubric that scores it, and how to grade one with an agent.

blocks.text: A good template does more than render. It gives an app a clear product starting point that is easy to understand, safe to change, and complete after Astryx copies it out of the package. A rubric scores that quality so you can grade as you build.

items: Its purpose and primary task are clear before someone reads every detail.
It composes Astryx components instead of rebuilding their behavior with raw HTML or custom styles.
Its hierarchy, spacing, interactions, and reading order still work at narrow widths and in every supported color mode.
Its source, imports, styles, fonts, icons, images, and media still work from the copied location.
Its metadata makes the template easy to find and accurately explains when to use it.
Its example content is realistic enough to expose overflow, empty-space, and hierarchy problems.

blocks.text: Grade the first runnable version, again after each source, doc, dependency, or asset change, and in full before every release. Grade the source, doc, copied file, and rendered app together; none of them is enough alone.

items: Read every scoring rule in {@link generic:template-grading-rubric}.
Fix publication blockers first, then every reasonable deduction.
Repeat the full grade on the packed package in a clean app ({@link generic:test-template-in-app}).
To have an agent grade and improve the template, use {@link generic:grade-template-with-agent}.

blocks.text: Keep each scorecard with its package revision and rubric version.

docs.name: write-the-template-file
docs.title: Write the template file
docs.description: Astryx copies just this one file into an app, so write it to work on its own there: where it lands, what it can import, and what it exports.

content.text: `{@command template}` copies exactly one source file. It does not copy sibling helpers, stylesheets, fonts, icons, images, or media. Plan for that before you add supporting files.
Astryx refuses to replace an existing file unless the caller passes `--overwrite` or `-f`.

sections.title: Keep edited code in one file

content.text: Put every helper that the app is expected to edit in the template source. Small local components, example data, constants, and event handlers can live above or below the default component in the same file.

items: Inline a helper when it is part of the editable starting point.
Move a helper into the integration package only when it should stay package-owned and update with the package.
Do not import `./helper`, `./styles`, or any other sibling file.
Do not create routes, configuration, or extra files at runtime. Give the app one explicit source file to own.

sections.title: Use imports that work in the app

content.text: After the copy, imports resolve from the app, not from the template directory. Every bare import must name a package the app installs, and every package path must be public.

items: Import Astryx components from their public Core paths.
Import integration-owned components, helpers, icons, or styles only through paths the package exports ({@link generic:export-template-assets}).
Avoid adding another library when Astryx or platform APIs already provide the behavior.

content.text: The source must default-export one React component. Named helpers inside the file are fine.

items: Add `use client` as the first statement only when hooks, event handlers, browser APIs, or a component passed as a prop, such as `icon={BellIcon}`, need a client boundary.
Keep a static template server-compatible when it needs no client behavior.

templates.name: AlertDialog — Delete

templates.name: useAppShellMobile — Custom Mobile Trigger

templates.description: App shell with SideNav header providing app identity, no TopNav needed.
